questions.question: The respective number of significant figures for the numbers 23.023, 0.0003 and 2.1×10⁻³ are:
questions.explanation: In 23.023 every digit is significant because the zeros lie between non-zero digits, giving 5. In 0.0003 the leading zeros only locate the decimal point, so only the 3 counts, giving 1. In 2.1×10⁻³ the significant figures are those of the mantissa 2.1, giving 2. Hence the respective counts are 5, 1, 2; options b and c wrongly count the leading zeros or the power of ten, and d undercounts 23.023.

questions.question: Which among the following is the supplementary Quantity:
questions.answer: (c) Solid angle
questions.explanation: The SI has exactly two supplementary quantities, plane angle (radian) and solid angle (steradian), so solid angle is the only supplementary quantity listed. Mass, time and luminosity are base quantities measured in kilogram, second and candela. Hence c.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Mass  (b) Time  (c) Solid angle  (d) Luminosity

questions.question: The unit of solid angle is
questions.answer: (b) Steradian
questions.explanation: Solid angle is a supplementary quantity and its SI unit is the steradian (sr), defined as the angle subtended at the centre of a sphere by an area equal to the square of the radius. Second, kilogram and candela are the units of time, mass and luminous intensity respectively, so they are base units. Hence b.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Second  (b) Steradian  (c) Kilogram  (d) Candela

questions.question: The quantity having the same unit in all system of unit is:
questions.answer: (b) time
questions.explanation: The second is the unit of time in the MKS, CGS and FPS systems alike, so time keeps the same unit in every system. Mass is measured in kilogram, gram or pound; length in metre, centimetre or foot; and temperature in kelvin, degree Celsius or degree Fahrenheit. Hence b.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) mass  (b) time  (c) length  (d) temperature

questions.question: Random errors can be eliminated by:
questions.answer: (a) taking number of observations and their mean.
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter unpredictably above and below the true value, so repeating the measurement many times and taking the mean makes the positive and negative deviations cancel statistically. Eliminating the cause removes a systematic error, not a random one. Using several instruments or being careful may reduce scatter but cannot eliminate it. Hence a.

options.text: taking number of observations and their mean.
measuring the quantity with more than one instrument

questions.optionsRaw: (a) taking number of observations and their mean.  (b) measuring the quantity with more than one instrument  (c) eliminating the cause  (d) careful observations
questions.correctAnswer: (a) taking number of observations and their mean.

questions.question: Systemic error can be:
questions.answer: (a) either positive or negative
questions.explanation: A systematic error shifts every reading in the same sense, and that shift may make readings too large (positive) or too small (negative), as with a zero error of either sign or faulty calibration. It is not restricted to one sign, and zero error is only one cause of it rather than the general description. Hence a.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) either positive or negative  (b) negative only  (c) positive only  (d) zero error

questions.question: [MLT⁻²] is dimensional formula of:
questions.answer: (b) force
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration, so [F] = [M][LT⁻²] = [MLT⁻²]. Strain is a pure ratio and dimensionless, displacement has dimensions [L], and pressure is force per area with dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻²]. Hence b.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) strain  (b) force  (c) displacement  (d) pressure

questions.question: Which of the following pair has the same dimension?
questions.answer: (c) impulse and momentum
questions.explanation: Impulse is force multiplied by time, [MLT⁻²][T] = [MLT⁻¹], which is exactly the dimension of momentum mv. Moment of inertia [ML²] does not match torque [ML²T⁻²]; surface tension [MT⁻²] does not match force [MLT⁻²]; specific heat [L²T⁻²θ⁻¹] does not match latent heat [L²T⁻²]. Hence c.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) moment of inertia and torque  (b) surface tension and force  (c) impulse and momentum  (d) specific heat and latent heat

questions.question: Dependent variable is:
questions.answer: (b) effect
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the quantity that responds to a change deliberately made in the experiment, so it is the effect and is plotted on the y-axis. The independent variable is the cause that the experimenter varies. Hence b.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) cause  (b) effect  (c) cause and effect  (d) reason

questions.question: Dimensions of kinetic energy is the same as that of :
questions.answer: (c) Work
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so [KE] = [M][L²T⁻²] = [ML²T⁻²], the same as work (force × distance). Acceleration is [LT⁻²], velocity [LT⁻¹] and force [MLT⁻²], none of which matches. Hence c.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Acceleration  (b) Velocity  (c) Work  (d) Force

questions.question: Give an example of (I) a physical quantity which has a unit but no dimensions. (II) a physical quantity which has neither unit not dimensions. (III) a constant which has a unit. (IV) a constant which has no unit.
questions.answer:
(I) Plane angle (or solid angle): its unit is the radian (steradian), but angle = arc/radius is a ratio of two lengths, so it is dimensionless, [M⁰L⁰T⁰].
(II) Strain (or refractive index): strain = change in length/original length, a pure ratio, so it has neither unit nor dimensions.
(III) Gravitational constant G: from G = Fr²/m₁m₂ its unit is N m² kg⁻² and its dimensions are [M⁻¹L³T⁻²], so it is a constant that has a unit.
(IV) Dielectric constant (relative permittivity) K: it is the ratio of two permittivities, a pure number with no unit and no dimensions.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is between a unit and a dimension: angles carry a unit but no dimensions, while ratios of like quantities have neither. Do not confuse a constant such as G, which carries units, with a dimensionless constant such as K or the coefficient of friction.

questions.question: When rounding the product or quotient of two measurements, is it necessary to consider significant digit?
questions.answer: Yes. When measurements are multiplied or divided, the result can be no more reliable than the least reliable factor, so it must be rounded to the same number of significant figures as the factor having the fewest significant figures. For example, 4.16 cm × 2.0 cm = 8.32 cm² is rounded to 8.3 cm² because 2.0 has only two significant figures. Exact numbers such as the 2 in diameter = 2r, and defined conversion factors, do not limit the significant figures. Rounding should be done only at the final step to avoid accumulated rounding error.
questions.explanation: The rule follows from fractional uncertainty: the factor with the fewest significant figures has the largest percentage uncertainty and therefore controls the precision of the product or quotient.

questions.question: Drive the equation for period of oscillations of a mass suspended on a vertical spring by dimensional analysis. i.e., T = 2π√(m/k)
questions.answer:
Let T ∝ m^a k^b, where m is the mass and k the spring constant. The spring constant is force per unit extension, so [k] = [MLT⁻²]/[L] = [MT⁻²]. Writing the dimensions,
[T] = [M]^a [MT⁻²]^b = [M]^(a+b) [T]^(−2b).
Comparing powers: for M, a + b = 0; for T, −2b = 1, so b = −1/2 and a = +1/2.
Hence T = C√(m/k), where C is a dimensionless constant. Dimensional analysis cannot fix C; experiment or theory shows C = 2π, giving T = 2π√(m/k).
questions.explanation: The dimensional method gives only the form of the relation; the dimensionless constant 2π must be found experimentally. A common mistake is to take [k] as the dimension of force, [MLT⁻²], instead of force per length, [MT⁻²].

questions.question:
Find the dimensions of the following.
(a) work
(b) energy
(c) power
(d) momentum
questions.answer:
Using the defining equations and the base dimensions [M], [L] and [T] for mass, length and time:
(a) Work: W = Fd, so [W] = [MLT⁻²][L] = [ML²T⁻²].
(b) Energy: energy is the capacity to do work, so [E] = [ML²T⁻²], the same as work.
(c) Power: P = W/t, so [P] = [ML²T⁻²]/[T] = [ML²T⁻³].
(d) Momentum: p = mv, so [p] = [M][LT⁻¹] = [MLT⁻¹].
Work and energy are therefore dimensionally identical, which is why both are measured in joules, while momentum is measured in kg m s⁻¹, equivalently N s.
questions.explanation: Build each derived dimension from its defining equation. Work and energy share [ML²T⁻²]; power is work per unit time; momentum is mass times velocity, which has the same dimensions as impulse.

questions.question: You measure the radius of a wheel to be 4.16 cm. If you multiply by 2 to get diameter, should you write the result as 8 cm or as 8.32 cm? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Write the diameter as 8.32 cm. The factor 2 is an exact counting number in d = 2r, not a measured quantity, so it has unlimited significant figures and does not reduce the precision of the result. The radius 4.16 cm has three significant figures, so the diameter also has three: 8.32 cm. Writing 8 cm would round the result to one significant figure and discard real measured precision. Significant-figure rules apply to measured factors, not to exact multipliers.
questions.explanation: Only measured quantities limit significant figures; exact numbers such as 2, or π treated as exact, do not. Rounding 8.32 cm to 8 cm would wrongly imply that the radius was known only to the nearest centimetre.

questions.question: If y = a+bt+ct² where y is in meters and t in seconds, what is the unit of c?
questions.answer: By the principle of homogeneity, every term of y = a + bt + ct² must have the same unit as y, namely the metre. The term ct² therefore has unit m, so c has unit m/s² (m s⁻²), because t² has unit s². For completeness, a is in m and b is in m/s. Numerically, c is measured in m s⁻², the same as an acceleration.
questions.explanation: Additive equations are dimensionally homogeneous: terms with different units cannot be added. Compare the dimensions of each term separately rather than treating the equation as a whole.

questions.question: Differentiate between accuracy and precision.
questions.answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another, or how finely an instrument can read. A stopwatch that is always 2 s fast is precise but inaccurate, because its readings agree with each other yet are shifted from the truth. A set of readings scattered widely about the true value is accurate on average but imprecise. Accuracy is spoiled mainly by systematic errors, precision mainly by random errors. An accurate measurement must also be precise, but a precise measurement need not be accurate.
questions.explanation: Remember that accuracy refers to the target (true value) and precision to the grouping of readings. Systematic error shifts the whole group and reduces accuracy; random error spreads the group and reduces precision.

questions.question: Define dependent and independent variables.
questions.answer: An independent variable is the quantity that the experimenter deliberately changes or controls; it is the cause and is plotted on the x-axis. A dependent variable is the quantity whose value changes in response to the independent variable; it is the effect and is plotted on the y-axis. For example, in studying a simple pendulum, the length L is the independent variable and the period T is the dependent variable, because T is measured for each chosen L. Other quantities kept fixed, such as the mass of the bob, are controlled variables.
questions.explanation: Identify the variable you set and the variable you measure as a consequence. Plotting the independent variable on the x-axis makes the slope of the graph physically meaningful.

questions.question: Differentiate systematic error and random error.
questions.answer: Systematic error is a consistent deviation of readings from the true value in the same direction, caused by faulty calibration, zero error or a biased observer; repeating the measurement does not remove it, but it can be corrected once the cause is found. Random error is an unpredictable scatter of readings above and below the true value, caused by fluctuations in conditions or in the observer; it cannot be corrected individually but is reduced by taking many readings and averaging. Systematic error affects accuracy, whereas random error affects precision.
questions.explanation: The signature of systematic error is a repeated shift; the signature of random error is scatter. Averaging cancels random error but not systematic error.

questions.question: Enlist the limitations of dimensional analysis?
questions.answer:
Limitations of dimensional analysis:
1. It cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants such as 2π or ½; it gives only the form of an equation.
2. It cannot derive relations containing trigonometric, logarithmic or exponential functions, because their arguments must be dimensionless and their series contain several terms.
3. It cannot distinguish between quantities having the same dimensions, for example work and torque, or stress and pressure.
4. It cannot derive an equation involving a sum of terms, such as s = ut + ½at², completely, because each term must be treated separately.
5. It fails when a quantity depends on more than three mechanical quantities, since only three equations (for M, L and T) are available.
questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis checks homogeneity and predicts dependence on variables, but it is blind to pure numbers and to the physical distinction between quantities of identical dimensions.

questions.question: Describe least count of Vernier and screw gauge micrometer.
questions.answer:
Vernier callipers: least count = smallest main-scale division − smallest vernier-scale division. When 10 vernier divisions equal 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm, LC = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. Reading = main-scale reading before the vernier zero + (coinciding vernier division × LC).
Screw gauge: LC = pitch/number of circular-scale divisions. If the screw advances 0.5 mm per revolution and the circular scale has 50 divisions, LC = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Reading = sleeve reading + (circular-scale division × LC), with any zero error corrected.
questions.explanation: The least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can read. For the vernier it comes from the difference between one main-scale and one vernier division; for the screw gauge it comes from pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.

questions.question: Describe extrapolation methods.
questions.answer: Extrapolation is the process of extending a graph or trend line beyond the range of the measured data in order to predict values of the dependent variable outside the observed interval. For example, a straight-line V–I graph obtained for currents up to 2 A may be extrapolated to estimate the voltage at 3 A, or a cooling curve may be extended to predict the temperature after a longer time. Extrapolation is reliable only when the same physical law is expected to hold beyond the data; if the trend changes, for example because a component heats up or saturates, the extrapolated value can be badly wrong. It is therefore less reliable than interpolation.
questions.explanation: Extrapolation assumes the established trend continues unchanged, whereas interpolation stays inside the measured range. Always state this assumption when quoting an extrapolated result.

questions.question: Discuss graphs and its various types by supported an example?
questions.answer:
A graph is a visual representation of the relationship between two quantities, with the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis. Each axis is labelled with its symbol, unit and a suitable scale, and the graph carries a title.
1. Line graph: points joined by a straight line or smooth curve. Example: for uniformly accelerated motion the velocity–time graph is the straight line v = u + at; its slope gives the acceleration and its intercept gives u. The distance–time graph for the same motion is a parabola.
2. Scatter graph with a best-fit line: experimental points are plotted and a smooth line of best fit is drawn, whose slope and intercept are then interpreted. Example: plotting V against I for a metallic conductor gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is the resistance R.
3. Bar chart: bars of height proportional to the value of a quantity, used when one variable is categorical or discrete. Example: comparing the densities of copper, aluminium and iron, or the energy consumption of different appliances.
4. Pie chart: a circle divided into sectors whose angles are proportional to the parts of a whole. Example: showing the percentage of total electrical energy used by lighting, heating, motors and other devices in a home.
5. Histogram: adjacent bars showing the frequency distribution of continuous data, for example the distribution of measured lengths of a batch of screws.
To plot correctly, choose a scale that uses most of the graph paper, plot each point accurately, draw a smooth best-fit line rather than joining every point, and state what the slope and intercept mean. A graph reveals trends, maxima and anomalies that a table of numbers can hide.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that a graph's slope and intercept carry physical meaning; always label the axes with units and draw a best-fit line instead of a zig-zag through every point.

questions.question: Elaborate rules of significant figures. State the rules for the determining the number of significant figures in a given measurement.
questions.answer:
Rules for determining the number of significant figures in a measurement:
1. All non-zero digits are significant: 23.023 has five.
2. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: the zeros in 205 and 1.008 count.
3. Leading zeros are never significant; they only locate the decimal point: 0.0003 has one significant figure.
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 2.500 has four.
5. Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous; write 1500 as 1.5×10³ (two) or 1.500×10³ (four) to be clear.
6. In scientific notation all digits of the mantissa are significant: 2.1×10⁻³ has two.
7. Exact numbers (counted objects and defined conversions such as 1 km = 1000 m) have unlimited significant figures and do not restrict the answer.
8. When rounding, if the first discarded digit is greater than 5 round up, if it is less than 5 leave the digit unchanged, and if it is exactly 5 round to the nearest even digit.
9. In multiplication and division the result carries the least number of significant figures among the factors; in addition and subtraction it carries the least number of decimal places.
Examples: 4.16 × 2.0 = 8.32 → 8.3 (two significant figures); 12.11 + 0.3 = 12.41 → 12.4 (one decimal place); 3.67 ± 0.25 has three significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty is (0.25/3.67) × 100 = 6.8%.
questions.explanation: The rules exist so that a calculated result does not claim more precision than the measurements allow. The most common mistakes are counting leading zeros and retaining too many digits after multiplying.

questions.question: What are the uses of dimensional analysis? Explain each of them.
questions.answer:
Uses of dimensional analysis:
1. Checking the correctness of an equation. Every term on both sides of a correct equation must have the same dimensions. For s = ut + ½at², [ut] = LT⁻¹·T = L and [at²] = LT⁻²·T² = L, matching [s] = L, so the equation is dimensionally correct.
2. Deriving relations between physical quantities. If T depends on m and k, write T ∝ m^a k^b, substitute [k] = MT⁻² and solve the power equations to obtain T = C√(m/k). Similarly, the speed of a transverse wave on a string is found to be v ∝ √(F/μ).
3. Converting units from one system to another. Since 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², applying the conversion factors gives 1 N = 10⁵ dyne; the dimensional formula guarantees that the conversion is consistent.
4. Finding the dimensions, and hence the unit, of a physical constant or quantity such as G, h or the gas constant R.
5. Predicting how one quantity varies with others, for example that the period of a pendulum depends on √(l/g), which guides the design of experiments.
6. Checking the plausibility of an answer: a result with the wrong dimensions must be wrong.
Limitations: dimensional analysis cannot supply dimensionless constants, cannot handle trigonometric or exponential relations, and cannot distinguish quantities of the same dimensions. Nevertheless it is a quick and powerful first check in physics.
questions.explanation: The strength of the method is homogeneity; its blind spot is pure numbers. Use it to check and predict, not to obtain a complete equation with constants.

questions.question: A vernier and micrometer are shown as under. Observe their readings and write correctly. [Vernier: main scale graduated in cm; the vernier zero lies between 3.3 cm and 3.4 cm, the 4th vernier division coincides with a main-scale division, least count = 0.01 cm. Micrometer: sleeve scale reads 5.5 mm, the 28th circular-scale division lies on the datum line, least count = 0.01 mm.]
questions.answer:
Vernier reading:
Main-scale reading = 3.3 cm (the last main-scale mark before the vernier zero)
Vernier-division coincidence = 4
Vernier least count = 0.01 cm
Vernier-scale reading = 4 × 0.01 = 0.04 cm
Total = 3.3 + 0.04 = 3.34 cm

Micrometer reading:
Sleeve (main-scale) reading = 5.5 mm (the last sleeve mark exposed before the thimble edge)
Circular-scale division = 28
Least count = 0.01 mm
Circular-scale reading = 28 × 0.01 = 0.28 mm
Total = 5.5 + 0.28 = 5.78 mm

Both readings are internally consistent. The vernier fraction 0.04 cm is smaller than 0.10 cm, the value of ten vernier divisions, and the micrometer fraction 0.28 mm is smaller than 0.50 mm, the value of fifty circular-scale divisions. If either instrument had a zero error, the same amount would be subtracted from the observed reading; here the scales are taken as correctly zeroed. Recording 3.34 cm rather than 3.3 cm preserves the precision of the vernier, and 5.78 mm rather than 5.5 mm preserves the precision of the micrometer. The same procedure applies at any other position of the sliding jaw or thimble: read the main scale first, then the fractional scale, and add the two. The main scale is read in cm for the vernier and in mm for the micrometer, so the final answers are quoted to 0.01 cm and 0.01 mm respectively.
questions.explanation: In both instruments the total reading is the main-scale reading plus the fraction read on the secondary scale. For the vernier the fraction is the coinciding vernier division multiplied by the least count (0.01 cm); for the micrometer it is the circular-scale division multiplied by the least count (0.01 mm). A common mistake is to add the number of the coinciding division directly instead of multiplying by the least count.
questions.figure: Two scale diagrams: a vernier callipers with a centimetre main scale and a 0–10 vernier scale, and a micrometer screw gauge with a sleeve scale in mm and a 0–50 circular scale.

questions.question: What is the percent uncertainty in the measurement 3.67 ± 0.25 m?
questions.answer:
Given: measured value x = 3.67 m, absolute uncertainty Δx = 0.25 m
Formula: percentage uncertainty = (Δx/x) × 100%
Substitution: (0.25/3.67) × 100%
Calculation: 0.06812 × 100% = 6.812%
Result: percentage uncertainty ≈ 6.8%
questions.explanation: Divide the absolute uncertainty by the measured value and multiply by 100. The printed answer 6.8% matches; it is quoted to two significant figures because 0.25 has two.

questions.question: What is the area, and its approximate uncertainty, of a circle with radius 3.7 × 10⁴ cm
questions.answer:
Given: r = 3.7 × 10⁴ cm, so Δr ≈ 0.05 × 10⁴ cm (half a unit in the last place)
Formula: A = πr²; ΔA/A = 2Δr/r
Substitution: A = π(3.7 × 10⁴)² = π(1.369 × 10⁹)
Calculation: A = 4.30 × 10⁹ cm²
ΔA/A = 2(0.05/3.7) = 0.0270 = 2.7%
ΔA = 0.0270 × 4.30 × 10⁹ = 0.116 × 10⁹ cm² ≈ 0.12 × 10⁹ cm²
Result: A = (4.3 ± 0.12) × 10⁹ cm²
questions.explanation: The area matches the printed 4.3×10⁹ cm². Using the half-unit uncertainty in r gives 0.12×10⁹ cm²; the printed 0.11×10⁹ cm² corresponds to rounding the fractional uncertainty to about 2.5% (0.11/4.3 = 2.6%), so the two agree within rounding.

questions.question: An aero plane travels at 850 km/h. How long does it take to travel 1.00 km?
questions.answer:
Given: v = 850 km/h, s = 1.00 km
Formula: t = s/v
Substitution: t = 1.00/850 h = 1.1765 × 10⁻³ h
Calculation: t = 1.1765 × 10⁻³ × 3600 s = 4.235 s
Result: t ≈ 4.24 s
questions.explanation: Divide the distance by the speed and then convert hours to seconds. 3600/850 = 4.2353 s, which rounds to 4.24 s (three significant figures); the printed 4.23 s is a truncation, differing by 0.01 s.

questions.question: A rectangular holding tank 25.0 m in length and 15.0 m in width is used to store water for short period of time in an industrial plant. If 2980 m³ water is pumped into the tank. What is the depth of the water?
questions.answer:
Given: l = 25.0 m, w = 15.0 m, V = 2980 m³
Formula: V = l × w × d, so d = V/(l × w)
Substitution: d = 2980/(25.0 × 15.0) = 2980/375.0
Calculation: d = 7.9467 m
Result: d ≈ 7.95 m
questions.explanation: The base area is 375 m², and dividing the volume by it gives 7.95 m. The printed answer 7.95 m matches; three significant figures are kept, consistent with 25.0 and 15.0.

questions.question: Find the volume of rectangular underground water tank has storage facility of 1.9 m by 1.2 m by 0.8 m.
questions.answer:
Given: l = 1.9 m, w = 1.2 m, h = 0.8 m
Formula: V = l × w × h
Substitution: V = 1.9 × 1.2 × 0.8
Calculation: V = 1.824 m³
Result: V = 1.824 m³ (1.8 m³ to two significant figures)
questions.explanation: Multiply the three dimensions: 1.9 × 1.2 = 2.28 and 2.28 × 0.8 = 1.824. The printed 1.824 m³ matches; strictly, the data have two significant figures, so 1.8 m³ would also be acceptable.

questions.question:
Two students derive following equations in which x refers to distance traveled, v the speed, the acceleration, and t the time and the subscript (o) means a quantity at time t=0:
(a) x = vt² + 2at and
(b) x = v₀ t + 2at², which of these could possibly be correct according to dimensional check?
questions.answer:
(a) x = vt² + 2at
[vt²] = LT⁻¹ × T² = LT
[2at] = LT⁻² × T = LT⁻¹
Neither term has the dimension of x, [L], and the two terms do not match each other, so (a) is incorrect.

(b) x = v₀t + 2at²
[v₀t] = LT⁻¹ × T = L
[2at²] = LT⁻² × T² = L
Both terms and x have dimensions [L], so (b) is dimensionally correct.

Result: (a) Incorrect, (b) Correct.
questions.explanation: The printed key (a) Incorrect, (b) Correct is confirmed. Dimensional analysis cannot check the dimensionless factor 2; the correct kinematic equation is x = v₀t + ½at², so (b) has the right dimensions but a wrong numerical coefficient.

questions.question: One hectare is defined as 10⁴ m². One acre is 4 × 10⁴ ft². How many acres are in one hectare? (Hint: 1 m = 3.28 ft.)
questions.answer:
Given: 1 hectare = 10⁴ m², 1 acre = 4 × 10⁴ ft², 1 m = 3.28 ft
Formula: 1 m² = (3.28)² ft²; number of acres = area in ft²/(4 × 10⁴ ft²)
Substitution: 1 hectare = 10⁴ × (3.28)² ft² = 10⁴ × 10.7584 ft²
Calculation: = 1.07584 × 10⁵ ft²
Acres = 1.07584 × 10⁵/(4 × 10⁴) = 2.6896
Result: 1 hectare ≈ 2.69 acres
questions.explanation: Square the length conversion factor as well as converting the number. The printed 2.69 acres matches; using 3.28 ft/m gives 2.6896, which rounds to 2.69.

questions.question: A watch factory claims that its watches gain or lose not more than 10 seconds in a year. How accurate is this watch, express as percentage?
questions.answer:
Given: maximum error = 10 s, 1 year = 365 × 24 × 3600 s
Formula: percentage accuracy = (error/total time) × 100%
Substitution: t = 365 × 24 × 3600 = 3.1536 × 10⁷ s
Calculation: (10/3.1536 × 10⁷) × 100% = 3.171 × 10⁻⁷ × 100% = 3.17 × 10⁻⁵ %
Result: accuracy ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ %
questions.explanation: The fractional error is 10/3.15×10⁷ ≈ 3.2×10⁻⁷, which is 3.2×10⁻⁵ percent. The printed 3.16×10⁻⁵ % differs only in the third digit because of the year length used (365.25 days gives 3.17×10⁻⁵ %); the result is about 3×10⁻⁵ %.

questions.question:
The diameter of Moon is 3480 km. What is the volume of the Moon? How many Moons would be needed to create a volume equal to that of Earth?
(Hint: Radius of Earth = 6380 km)
questions.answer:
Given: d(Moon) = 3480 km, so r(Moon) = 1740 km = 1.74 × 10⁶ m; r(Earth) = 6380 km = 6.38 × 10⁶ m
Formula: V = (4/3)πr³; N = V(Earth)/V(Moon) = [r(Earth)/r(Moon)]³
Substitution: V(Moon) = (4/3)π(1.74 × 10⁶)³
Calculation: (1.74 × 10⁶)³ = 5.268 × 10¹⁸ m³
V(Moon) = 4.1888 × 5.268 × 10¹⁸ = 2.207 × 10¹⁹ m³
N = (6.38 × 10⁶/1.74 × 10⁶)³ = (3.667)³ = 49.3
Result: V(Moon) ≈ 2.2 × 10¹⁹ m³; about 49.3 Moons would be needed.
questions.explanation: Both answers match the printed values (2.2×10¹⁹ m³, 49.3). The ratio of volumes equals the cube of the ratio of radii, so the common factor 4π/3 cancels.

questions.question: To get a resultant displacement of 10m, two displacement vectors of magnitude 6m and 8m should be combined:
questions.answer: (d) Perpendicular to each other
questions.explanation: For vectors of 6 m and 8 m, R² = 6² + 8² + 2(6)(8)cosθ = 100 + 96cosθ. A resultant of 10 m requires 100 = 100 + 96cosθ, so cosθ = 0 and θ = 90°, i.e. the vectors must be perpendicular. Parallel gives 14 m, antiparallel 2 m, and 45° gives about 12.96 m, so the other options fail.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Parallel  (b) Antiparallel  (c) At an angle of 45°  (d) Perpendicular to each other

questions.question: The velocity of a particle at an instant is 10 m/s and after 5sec the velocity of particle is 20m/s. The velocity at 3 sec before in before 10m/s is:
questions.explanation: The acceleration is a = (20 − 10)/5 = 2 m/s². Going back 3 s from the instant when v = 10 m/s, v = 10 − 2(3) = 4 m/s, so the answer is 4 m/s. Options 8 and 7 would come from adding the velocity change or using a wrong time, and 6 from using a = 1.33 m/s²; the printed options omit units.

questions.question: A ball is thrown upwards with a velocity of 100 m/s. It will reach the ground after:
questions.answer: (b) 20 sec
questions.explanation: With g = 10 m/s² the time to reach the top is u/g = 100/10 = 10 s, and the downward journey takes the same time, so the total is 20 s. 10 s is only the ascent, 5 s would require g = 20 m/s², and 40 s is double the correct total. Using g = 9.8 m/s² gives about 20.4 s.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 10 sec  (b) 20 sec  (c) 5 sec  (d) 40 sec

questions.question: Two projectiles are fired from the same point with the same speed at angles of projection 60° and 30° respectively. Which one of the following is true?
questions.answer: (a) The range will be same
questions.explanation: R = u²sin2θ/g, and for 60° and 30° sin120° = sin60°, so the ranges are equal. The maximum heights H = u²sin²θ/2g differ because sin²60° ≠ sin²30°, and the times of flight T = 2u sinθ/g also differ. The landing speeds are equal, but the landing velocities point at different angles, so their velocities as vectors are not the same and (c) is not true.

options.text: Their maximum height will be same
Their landing velocity will be same
their time of flight will be same

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The range will be same  (b) Their maximum height will be same  (c) Their landing velocity will be same  (d) their time of flight will be same

questions.question: The ratio of numerical values of average velocity and average speed of a body is always:
questions.answer: (b) Unity or less
questions.explanation: Average speed uses the total path length, while the magnitude of average velocity uses the net displacement; since path length is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement, the ratio is at most 1. It equals unity for straight-line motion without reversal and is less than unity when the path bends or reverses. Hence the ratio is unity or less, not always less.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Unity  (b) Unity or less  (c) Unity or more  (d) Less than unity

questions.question: If the average velocities of a body become equal to the instantaneous velocity, body is said to be moving with:
questions.answer: (b) Uniform velocity
questions.explanation: Average velocity over any interval equals the instantaneous velocity at every instant only when the velocity is constant in both magnitude and direction, that is, uniform velocity. Uniform acceleration still changes the instantaneous velocity, so the average over an interval generally differs from the instantaneous value. Variable velocity or variable acceleration would also make the two unequal.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Uniform acceleration  (b) Uniform velocity  (c) Variable velocity  (d) Variable acceleration

questions.question: At the top of a trajectory of a projectile, the acceleration is:
questions.answer: (d) g
questions.explanation: At the top of the trajectory the vertical component of velocity is zero, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration remains g downward throughout the flight. Acceleration does not vanish when velocity does. It is neither maximum nor minimum at the top; its magnitude is the same g at every point when air resistance is neglected.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) maximum  (b) minimum  (c) zero  (d) g

questions.question: At what angle the range of projectile becomes equal to the height of projectile?
questions.explanation: Setting R = H gives u²sin2θ/g = u²sin²θ/2g, so 4cosθ = sinθ and tanθ = 4, giving θ = 75.96° ≈ 76°. Option (b) is printed without the degree sign; 45° gives the maximum range, where R = 4H, not R = H. At 30° or 65° the range and height are also unequal.

questions.question: The angle at which dot product becomes equal to the cross product is:
questions.explanation: For two vectors, A·B = ABcosθ and |A×B| = ABsinθ. Equating the two gives cosθ = sinθ, so tanθ = 1 and θ = 45°. At 65°, 76° or 30° the cosine and sine are unequal, so the dot and cross products differ.

questions.question: If the dot product of two non-zero vectors vanishes; the vectors will be:
questions.answer: (c) perpendicular to each other
questions.explanation: A·B = ABcosθ vanishes for non-zero A and B only when cosθ = 0, that is, θ = 90°, so the vectors are perpendicular. Parallel vectors give the maximum positive dot product and antiparallel vectors the maximum negative product. Zero is a value of the product, not a direction.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) in the same direction  (b) opposite direction to each other  (c) perpendicular to each other  (d) zero

questions.question: Is the range equivalent to the horizontal distance in the projectile motion, or do they have distinct meaning? Explain
questions.answer: They are related but not identical. The horizontal distance travelled after time t is x = v₀cosθ·t, which grows continuously during the flight. The range is the particular horizontal distance between the point of projection and the point where the projectile returns to the same horizontal level, obtained by putting t equal to the total time of flight: R = v₀cosθ × (2v₀sinθ/g) = v₀²sin2θ/g. Thus the range is the total horizontal displacement for a complete flight, whereas horizontal distance means the x-coordinate at any instant. If the projectile lands at a different height, the horizontal distance to the landing point is not given by the standard range formula.
questions.explanation: Range is a special value of horizontal distance evaluated at the landing time, not a different physical quantity. The standard formula applies only when launch and landing heights are equal.

questions.question: If air resistance is taken into account in case of projectile motion, then what parameters of projectile are influenced?
questions.answer: With air resistance, the drag force opposes the velocity and grows with speed, so it changes both components of motion. The maximum height reached is lower, the time of flight is shorter, and the horizontal range is reduced compared with the vacuum case. The path is no longer a symmetric parabola: the descending branch is steeper than the ascending one, and the projectile lands with a smaller speed than it was launched. The horizontal velocity is no longer constant because drag has a horizontal component. The angle for maximum range is also reduced below 45°. Spin can add lift or side force, further modifying the trajectory.
questions.explanation: Drag removes mechanical energy and couples the horizontal and vertical motions, so the ideal projectile equations no longer hold. The trajectory becomes asymmetric, and both range and maximum height decrease.

questions.question: What are some real-life examples of projectile motion? Can motion of an aero plane be considered as projectile motion? Explain
questions.answer: Examples include a cricket ball thrown to a fielder, a football kicked towards the goal, a javelin in flight, a shell fired from a gun, water spurting from a horizontal pipe and a stone thrown from a cliff. In each case, after release the only significant force is gravity (air resistance neglected), so the object follows a parabolic path. An aeroplane in powered flight is not a projectile: its engines provide continuous thrust, its wings provide lift and its control surfaces change the forces, so its motion is not determined solely by its initial velocity and gravity. A glider with its engine off, or an aircraft in a ballistic phase, only approximates projectile motion.
questions.explanation: The defining test is whether gravity alone acts after launch. Thrust, lift and control forces disqualify a powered aeroplane from being treated as a projectile.

questions.question: Where do we use the concept of speed and velocity in our daily life? Can you give some examples?
questions.answer: Speed, a scalar, tells how fast a body moves along its path, while velocity, a vector, also gives the direction. In daily life a car's speedometer reads speed only, and a speed limit of 60 km/h is a scalar restriction. Weather reports and air-traffic control use velocity because the direction of a wind or an aircraft matters: a plane heading north at 300 km/h in a 50 km/h east wind has a velocity different from its heading. Navigation and GPS use displacement and velocity to give the direction of travel. An athlete's average speed describes a race, whereas collision analysis or escape problems require velocity. Thus speed suffices when direction is irrelevant, and velocity is needed when direction affects the outcome.
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of velocity but carries no direction; distance divided by time gives average speed, whereas displacement divided by time gives average velocity.

questions.question: Can an object have an initial velocity of zero and still experience uniformly accelerated motion
questions.answer: Yes. Uniformly accelerated motion means the acceleration is constant, not that the velocity is non-zero. If an object is released from rest, its initial velocity is zero while its acceleration remains constant, for example g downward for a dropped stone or a constant 3 m/s² for a car starting from rest. The velocity then grows as v = at, and the distance as s = ½at². The condition u = 0 merely selects one particular case of the equations of motion; it does not prevent the acceleration from being uniform. A body remaining at rest would not accelerate, but a body starting from rest certainly can.
questions.explanation: Do not confuse zero initial velocity with zero acceleration. Constant acceleration and u = 0 are independent conditions.

questions.question: What are three equations of uniformly accelerated motion and how they are derived?
questions.answer:
For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration a, initial velocity u and displacement s in time t, the three equations are:
(1) v = u + at
(2) s = ut + ½at²
(3) 2as = v² − u²

Derivation of (1): By definition a = (v − u)/t for constant acceleration, so v = u + at. Equivalently, a = dv/dt, and integrating from 0 to t gives v − u = at.

Derivation of (2): The displacement is the area under the v–t graph, a trapezium with parallel sides u and v and width t: s = ½(u + v)t. Substituting v = u + at gives s = ½(u + u + at)t = ut + ½at². Alternatively, integrating v dt = (u + at)dt gives the same result.

Derivation of (3): Eliminate t between (1) and (2). From (1), t = (v − u)/a. Substituting in (2): s = u(v − u)/a + ½a(v − u)²/a² = [2uv − 2u² + v² − 2uv + u²]/2a = (v² − u²)/2a, so 2as = v² − u².

These equations apply only when the acceleration is constant and the motion is along a straight line. For example, a car starting from rest with a = 2 m/s² reaches v = 20 m/s in 10 s and covers s = ½(2)(10)² = 100 m.
questions.explanation: All three follow from the definitions of acceleration and velocity for constant a; equation (3) is obtained by eliminating t. They are valid only for uniform acceleration in one dimension.

questions.question: How does the horizontal component of velocity in projectile motion behaves?
questions.answer:
Once a projectile is launched and air resistance is neglected, the only force acting on it is its weight, which is vertical. There is therefore no horizontal force and hence no horizontal acceleration: aₓ = 0. Consequently the horizontal component of velocity, vₓ = v₀cosθ, remains constant in magnitude and direction throughout the flight. It is the same at launch, at the top of the path and at landing.
The horizontal displacement after time t is therefore x = vₓt = (v₀cosθ)t, which increases uniformly with time. The vertical component, by contrast, changes as v_y = v₀sinθ − gt, so the velocity vector continually changes direction while its horizontal component stays fixed.
At the top of the trajectory v_y = 0 but vₓ is still v₀cosθ, so the speed at the top is not zero unless θ = 90°. The constant vₓ is what carries the projectile forward, while gravity controls the vertical motion and the time of flight. Because vₓ is constant, the x–t graph is a straight line through the origin, whereas the y–t graph of height against time is a parabola.
If air resistance is included, a horizontal drag component appears and vₓ decreases during the flight, so the above result is an idealisation valid for low speeds and short ranges.
questions.explanation: The key point is that gravity has no horizontal component, so vₓ = v₀cosθ is constant. A common error is to assume that the horizontal velocity becomes zero at the top, where only the vertical component vanishes.

questions.question: What is the significance of the area under a velocity-time graph in the context of accelerated motion?
questions.answer:
On a velocity–time graph the velocity is plotted against time, so a small interval of time dt corresponds to a thin strip of area v dt. Since v dt is the displacement ds during that interval, the area under the graph between two times equals the displacement of the body during that interval.
For uniformly accelerated motion the graph is a straight line. The area between t = 0 and t is a trapezium with parallel sides u and v and width t, so s = ½(u + v)t. Substituting v = u + at gives s = ut + ½at², which is the second equation of motion. Thus the area under a v–t graph is not merely a geometrical quantity; it directly yields the displacement and leads to the kinematic equations.
The area is counted as positive above the time axis and negative below it, because velocity in the opposite direction corresponds to negative displacement. If the graph crosses the time axis, the net area gives the net displacement, while the total unsigned area gives the distance travelled.
The slope of the same graph gives the acceleration, so a v–t graph contains the complete kinematics: slope = a, area = s. For example, if velocity rises uniformly from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 10 s, the area is ½(5 + 15)(10) = 100 m, the displacement.
questions.explanation: Area under v–t = displacement, while slope of v–t = acceleration. Signed areas must be used when the velocity reverses.

questions.question: How do the initial launch angle and velocity affect projectile motion?
questions.answer:
For a projectile launched with speed v₀ at angle θ to the horizontal (air resistance neglected), the three characteristic quantities are:
Range R = v₀²sin2θ/g
Maximum height H = v₀²sin²θ/(2g)
Time of flight T = 2v₀sinθ/g

Effect of initial speed: for a fixed angle, R, H and T all increase with v₀; R and H are proportional to v₀², while T is proportional to v₀. Doubling the launch speed therefore quadruples the range and maximum height but only doubles the time of flight.

Effect of launch angle: for a fixed speed, the range is greatest at θ = 45°, where sin2θ = 1, and falls to zero at 0° and 90°. Two angles that add to 90° (complementary angles, e.g. 30° and 60°) give the same range, because sin2θ = sin(180° − 2θ). Maximum height increases with θ, reaching v₀²/2g at 90°, while the time of flight also increases with θ. At 45°, H = R/4. For instance, doubling v₀ from 10 m/s to 20 m/s at 45° increases the range from v₀²/g = 10.2 m to 40.8 m, a fourfold rise.
The angle thus trades range against height and time: a low angle gives a flat, fast trajectory, a high angle a lofty, slow one. With air resistance the optimum angle for range falls below 45°, and the ideal formulas no longer apply.
questions.explanation: Range depends on sin2θ (maximum at 45°, equal for complementary angles), whereas height and time depend on sinθ and increase all the way to 90°. Speed affects range and height quadratically.

questions.question: Explain the concept of independence between horizontal and vertical motion in projectile motion
questions.answer:
Projectile motion is two-dimensional, but the horizontal and vertical motions can be treated separately because the only acceleration is vertical (g). There is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal motion is uniform; the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated. The two sets of equations are:
Horizontal: vₓ = v₀cosθ (constant), x = (v₀cosθ)t
Vertical: v_y = v₀sinθ − gt, y = (v₀sinθ)t − ½gt²
The two motions are independent in the sense that neither the acceleration nor the velocity component in one direction affects the other. The single quantity that links them is the time t, which is the same for both.
A striking demonstration is the simultaneous fall experiment: one ball is dropped from rest while another is projected horizontally from the same height at the same instant. Both reach the ground together, because the vertical motion of each is identical free fall; the horizontal velocity of the second ball does not delay its fall. Likewise, the horizontal range is unaffected by the value of g, while the time of flight is unaffected by the horizontal speed.
This independence allows each direction to be solved with one-dimensional equations and then combined vectorially. It holds only while air resistance is neglected, since drag couples the components.
questions.explanation: The shared time is the link between the components; gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal motion stays uniform. The dropped-and-projected ball demonstration is the classic test.

questions.question: A helicopter is ascending at the rate of 12 m/s. At a height of 80 m above the ground, a package is dropped. How long does the package take to reach the ground?
questions.answer:
Given: u = +12 m/s (upward), a = −g = −9.8 m/s², displacement s = −80 m (ground below the release point)
Formula: s = ut + ½at²
Substitution: −80 = 12t − 4.9t², i.e. 4.9t² − 12t − 80 = 0
Calculation: t = [12 ± √((−12)² − 4(4.9)(−80))]/(2 × 4.9) = [12 ± √(144 + 1568)]/9.8 = [12 ± 41.38]/9.8
Positive root: t = 53.38/9.8 = 5.447 s
Result: t ≈ 5.4 s
questions.explanation: The package initially moves upward with the helicopter, so u = +12 m/s while the displacement to the ground is negative. The printed answer 5.4 s matches; with g = 10 m/s² the result is 5.38 s. The negative root is discarded.

questions.question: Two tug boats are towing a ship each exerts a force of 6000 N, and the angle between two ropes is 60°. Calculate the resultant force on the ship?
questions.answer:
Given: F₁ = F₂ = 6000 N, θ = 60°
Formula: R = √(F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cosθ)
Substitution: R = √(6000² + 6000² + 2(6000)(6000)cos60°)
Calculation: R = 6000√(1 + 1 + 2 × 0.5) = 6000√3 = 6000 × 1.7321
Result: R = 10392 N ≈ 1.04 × 10⁴ N, directed along the bisector, 30° from each rope
questions.explanation: Equal forces at 60° combine to √3 times one force. The printed 10392 N matches. The resultant lies midway between the ropes because the forces are equal.

questions.question:
A car starts from rest and moves with a constant acceleration. During the 5th second of its motion, it covers a distance of 36 meters. Calculate:
(a) acceleration of the car
(b) the total distance covered by the car during this time.
questions.answer:
Given: u = 0, distance in the 5th second s₅ = 36 m, n = 5, total time t = 5 s
Formula: s_n = u + (a/2)(2n − 1); total distance s = ut + ½at²
Substitution: 36 = 0 + (a/2)(2 × 5 − 1) = 4.5a
Calculation: a = 36/4.5 = 8 m/s²
s = 0 + ½(8)(5)² = 4 × 25 = 100 m
Check: s₅ − s₄ = 100 − ½(8)(4)² = 100 − 64 = 36 m
Result: (a) a = 8 m/s²; (b) s = 100 m
questions.explanation: The distance covered in the nth second uses s_n = u + a(2n − 1)/2, which gives 4.5a for n = 5. The printed answers 8 m/s² and 100 m match, and the check confirms 36 m during the fifth second.

questions.question: Show that the range of projectile at complementary angles are same with examples?
questions.answer:
To show: R(θ) = R(90° − θ).
Let a projectile be launched with speed v₀ at angle θ. Its range is R(θ) = v₀²sin2θ/g.
For the complementary angle (90° − θ),
R(90° − θ) = v₀²sin[2(90° − θ)]/g = v₀²sin(180° − 2θ)/g.
Since sin(180° − 2θ) = sin2θ,
R(90° − θ) = v₀²sin2θ/g = R(θ).
Hence complementary angles give equal ranges.

Example 1: θ = 30° and 60°. With v₀ = 20 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s²,
R(30°) = (400 × sin60°)/9.8 = (400 × 0.8660)/9.8 = 35.3 m,
R(60°) = (400 × sin120°)/9.8 = (400 × 0.8660)/9.8 = 35.3 m.
Example 2: θ = 15° and 75° give R = (400 × sin30°)/9.8 = (400 × 0.5)/9.8 = 20.4 m for both.
The maximum range occurs at θ = 45°, which is its own complement, R = v₀²/g = 40.8 m.
questions.explanation: The identity sin(180° − 2θ) = sin2θ is the whole proof. The pair 45° is self-complementary and gives the maximum range; complementary pairs share a range but have different heights and times of flight.

questions.question: At what angle the range of projectile becomes equal to the height of projectile?
questions.answer:
Given: range R equals maximum height H
Formula: R = v₀²sin2θ/g and H = v₀²sin²θ/(2g)
Substitution: v₀²sin2θ/g = v₀²sin²θ/(2g)
Calculation: 2sinθcosθ = sin²θ/2; for θ ≠ 0, dividing by sinθ gives 4cosθ = sinθ, so tanθ = 4
θ = tan⁻¹(4) = 75.96°
Result: θ ≈ 76°
Check: R = H = 0.47v₀²/g at this angle.
questions.explanation: The printed answer 76° matches. At 45° the range is four times the height (R = 4H), which is why 45° is not the answer; tanθ = 4 follows from equating the two expressions.

questions.question: A marter shell is fired at a ground level target 500 m distance with an initial velocity of 90 m/s. What is the launch angle?
questions.answer:
Given: R = 500 m, v₀ = 90 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula: R = v₀²sin2θ/g, so sin2θ = Rg/v₀²
Substitution: sin2θ = (500 × 9.8)/(90)² = 4900/8100
Calculation: sin2θ = 0.60494
2θ = 37.22° or 2θ = 180° − 37.22° = 142.78°
θ = 18.61° or θ = 71.39°
Result: θ ≈ 71.4° (the high trajectory; the low trajectory is 18.6°)
questions.explanation: The printed answer 71.4° corresponds to the larger angle; 18.6° gives the same range. The sine equation has two solutions because sin2θ is positive in both the first and second quadrants. Using g = 10 m/s² would give about 19.0° and 71.0°.

questions.question: The rate of change of linear momentum of a body is called a:
questions.answer: (a) Linear force
questions.explanation: Newton's second law in its general form is F = dp/dt, so the rate of change of linear momentum is the net linear force acting on the body. Power is the rate of doing work (dW/dt); impulse is the change of momentum produced over a time interval (J = FΔt), not its rate; angular force (torque) is the rate of change of angular momentum. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Linear force  (b) Angular force  (c) Power  (d) Impulse

questions.question: The term mass refers to the same physical concept as:
questions.answer: (b) inertia
questions.explanation: Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia, the resistance of a body to any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion; the larger the mass, the larger the force needed for a given acceleration (m = F/a). Weight is the gravitational pull on that mass (W = mg) and changes with g, while force and acceleration are dynamic quantities, not measures of inertia. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) weight  (b) inertia  (c) force  (d) acceleration

questions.question: Which one of the following force is also called as self adjusting force ?
questions.answer: (a) frictional force
questions.explanation: Static friction adjusts its own magnitude from zero up to a maximum value μsN so that it exactly balances the applied force and the body does not slip; it is therefore called a self-adjusting force. Tension, weight and thrust are fixed by the load, the mass and the pressure respectively and do not change themselves to match an applied force. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) frictional force  (b) tension  (c) Weight  (d) Thrust

questions.question: The laws of motion shows the relationship between:
questions.answer: (d) force and acceleration
questions.explanation: Newton's second law, F = ma, states that the net force acting on a body determines the acceleration produced, with mass as the constant of proportionality (the inertia). The first law defines force through its effect on motion and the third law relates action and reaction forces, so the laws primarily link force with acceleration. Mass and acceleration are connected only through the force, and the velocity-acceleration relation belongs to kinematics, not to dynamics. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) velocity and acceleration  (b) mass and velocity  (c) mass and acceleration  (d) force and acceleration

questions.question: The motion of rocket in the space is according to the law of conservation of:
questions.answer: (b) linear momentum
questions.explanation: The rocket expels hot gases backwards; the momentum given to the gases is equal and opposite to the momentum gained by the rocket, so the total linear momentum of the rocket-gases system stays constant when no external force acts. This is Newton's third law applied to an isolated system, that is, conservation of linear momentum. Energy is also conserved but does not determine the thrust, mass is not conserved because fuel is ejected, and no rotation is involved. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Energy  (b) linear momentum  (c) mass  (d) angular momentum

questions.question: A bomb of mass 12 kg initially at rest explodes into two pieces of masses 4kg and 8kg . The speed of 8kg mass is 6 m/s. The kinetic energy The kinetic energy of 4 kg mass is:
questions.explanation: The bomb is initially at rest, so the fragments must carry equal and opposite momentum: 4 × v = 8 × 6 = 48 kg·m/s, giving v = 12 m/s for the 4 kg piece. Its kinetic energy is ½ × 4 × 12² = 288 J. The 8 kg piece carries ½ × 8 × 6² = 144 J, so 32 J, 48 J and 114 J would violate momentum conservation; note also that the printed stem repeats 'The kinetic energy' (typo in the book). Hence (d).

questions.question: If momentum is increased by 20% then K.E increases by:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy and momentum are related by K.E = p²/2m, so for a given mass K.E ∝ p². If p becomes 1.20p, then K.E becomes (1.20)² = 1.44 times its original value, an increase of 44%. A 20% increase in kinetic energy (the common mistaken answer) would require only about a 10% increase in momentum, and 55%, 66%, 77% do not follow from any square of 1.2. Hence (a).

questions.question: The kinetic energy of body of mass 2kg and momentum of 2 Ns is:
questions.answer: (a) 1 J
questions.explanation: Using K.E = p²/2m with p = 2 N·s and m = 2 kg gives K.E = (2)²/(2 × 2) = 1 J. This corresponds to a speed v = p/m = 1 m/s, and ½mv² = 1 J confirms it. Options 2 J, 3 J and 4 J would need momenta of 2.83, 3.46 and 4 N·s respectively for the same mass, so they are inconsistent with the data. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 1 J  (b) 2 J  (c) 3 J  (d) 4 J

questions.question: For the same kinetic energy, the momentum is maximum for:
questions.answer: (d) alpha particle
questions.explanation: From K.E = p²/2m, p = √(2mK); for the same kinetic energy p ∝ √m, so the heaviest particle has the largest momentum. The masses are about 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg (electron), 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (proton), 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (deuteron) and 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (alpha particle), so the alpha particle carries the greatest momentum and the electron, being lightest, the least. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) an electron  (b) a proton  (c) a deuteron  (d) alpha particle

questions.question: A 3kg bowling ball experiences a net force of 15N. What will be its acceleration.
questions.answer: (c) 5 m/s²
questions.explanation: From Newton's second law a = F/m = 15/3 = 5 m/s². The printed options contain a duplication: (a) and (d) are both 35 m/s², so neither can be a unique answer (35 would come from misreading 15 N as 105 N). 7 m/s² would require a mass of about 2.14 kg, which is not the given mass. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 35 m/s²  (b) 7 m/s²  (c) 5 m/s²  (d) 35 m/s²

questions.question: State Newton's second law of motion.
questions.answer: Newton's second law states that the rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force acting on it and takes place in the direction of that force. In symbols, F ∝ dp/dt, or F = k dp/dt; with SI units k = 1, so F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt. For a body of constant mass this becomes F = ma: the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass, and it is always along the net force. The law is a vector equation, so forces must be added vectorially, and it holds only in an inertial frame. One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
questions.explanation: Key point: the law is about the net (resultant) force and the rate of change of momentum; for constant mass it reduces to F = ma, and both F and a are vectors.

questions.question: How does mass affect an object's acceleration?
questions.answer: For a given net force the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass: a = F_net/m. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration produced by the same force, because the same force must change the motion of twice as much inertia; tripling the mass reduces the acceleration to one third. Mass is therefore the measure of a body's inertia, its resistance to a change in velocity. The relation a ∝ 1/m holds only when the force is kept constant; if both change, the two effects combine in the single equation a = F/m. Since force and acceleration are vectors, a is always along F_net, and a graph of a against 1/m for a fixed force is a straight line through the origin.
questions.explanation: Key point: a = F/m gives inverse proportionality between acceleration and mass for constant force; mass is inertia, not weight.

questions.question: What are the different types of forces that can act on an object?
questions.answer: The forces acting on an object are grouped into contact forces and non-contact (field) forces. Contact forces need physical touch: the normal reaction (perpendicular to a surface), friction (static or kinetic, along the surface and opposing relative motion), tension in strings and ropes, applied push or pull forces, thrust (for example from ejected gases), the elastic force of a spring (F = −kx) and air resistance or drag. Non-contact forces act over a distance without touching: gravitational force or weight (W = mg), electric force, magnetic force, and at nuclear dimensions the strong and weak nuclear forces. For a body on a rough inclined plane the usual forces are its weight, the normal reaction and friction; inside a lift they are the weight and the normal reaction or the tension in the cable. The net force is the vector sum of all the forces acting.
questions.explanation: Key point: classify forces as contact (normal, friction, tension, thrust, spring, drag) and non-contact (gravitational, electric, magnetic, nuclear); weight is a field force, not a contact force.

questions.question: How do you calculate net force?
questions.answer: The net force is the vector sum of all the forces acting on a body: F_net = ΣF. Choose convenient x and y axes, resolve every force into components (Fx = F cosθ, Fy = F sinθ, with θ measured from the x-axis), then add the components algebraically: F_net,x = ΣFx and F_net,y = ΣFy. The magnitude is F_net = √(Fx² + Fy²) and its direction is θ = tan⁻¹(Fy/Fx) measured from the x-axis. In a one-dimensional problem a sign convention is enough: take right or up as positive and add with signs. The net force then fixes the acceleration through a = F_net/m; if the sum is zero the body is in equilibrium and moves with constant velocity. For example, 10 N east and 4 N west give a net force of 6 N east.
questions.explanation: Key point: add forces as vectors (resolve into components), never as scalars; the net force alone determines acceleration by a = F_net/m.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: In the absence of a net external force, the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant in magnitude and direction. For two bodies interacting with each other, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. The law follows from Newton's second and third laws: the internal action and reaction forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so their impulses cancel and no net momentum is created or destroyed. Momentum is a vector, so the law applies separately to each direction and signs must be used for opposite motions. It holds for elastic and inelastic collisions, for explosions, for the recoil of a gun and for rocket propulsion, and it applies to the system as a whole rather than to the individual bodies, each of which may gain or lose momentum.
questions.explanation: Key point: total momentum of an isolated system is constant because internal action-reaction impulses cancel; it is a vector law and applies to the whole system.

questions.question: What is the difference between elastic and inelastic collisions?
questions.answer: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ and ½m₁u₁² + ½m₂u₂² = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂². In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂); momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not, part of it being converted into heat, sound and permanent deformation. Partly inelastic collisions lie between the two, described by the coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach), with e = 1 for elastic and e = 0 for perfectly inelastic collisions. Collisions between gas molecules or hard steel balls are nearly elastic, while a bullet embedding in a block, two lumps of clay sticking together, and a car crash are inelastic. Momentum conservation holds in both types.
questions.explanation: Key point: momentum is conserved in both types; only elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy, while inelastic ones convert some kinetic energy into heat, sound and deformation.

questions.question: How does impulse relate to force and time?
questions.answer: Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts: J = FΔt, a vector in the direction of the force and measured in N·s (equivalent to kg·m/s). From Newton's second law F = Δp/Δt we obtain J = Δp = mv − mu, so the impulse equals the change in momentum of the body; this is the impulse-momentum theorem. For a force that varies with time, the impulse is the area under the force-time graph, J = ∫F dt, and the average force is F_av = Δp/Δt. The same change of momentum can be produced by a large force acting for a short time or by a small force acting for a long time, because the product FΔt is fixed. This is why airbags and crumple zones lengthen the collision time to reduce the force.
questions.explanation: Key point: J = FΔt = Δp is the impulse-momentum theorem; lengthening the contact time for the same Δp reduces the force.

questions.question: How does friction influence the motion of an object?
questions.answer: Friction is the resistance force between two surfaces in contact that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion. Kinetic friction f_k = μ_kN acts opposite to the direction of sliding, so it decelerates a moving body and dissipates kinetic energy as heat and sound. Static friction adjusts itself up to a maximum f_s = μ_sN, and it is this friction that lets a body start moving, allows us to walk, enables a car to drive and brake, and supplies the centripetal force for a car on an unbanked curve. Friction also causes wear of machine parts and reduces efficiency, which is why lubricants and ball bearings are used. On a rough incline it opposes the component of weight, and it is the reason a body needs a minimum force before it begins to slide.
questions.explanation: Key point: friction opposes relative motion and is self-adjusting up to μsN; it both enables motion (walking, driving, braking) and dissipates energy as heat.

questions.question: Explain Newton's Second Law of Motion and how it relates force, mass, and acceleration. Provide an example to illustrate the concept.
questions.answer:
Statement. Newton's second law states that the rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force: F ∝ dp/dt, or F = k dp/dt. In SI units k = 1, so F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt.

Relation with mass and acceleration. For constant mass, dp/dt = m dv/dt = ma, hence F = ma. This single vector equation contains three ideas. (i) Force and acceleration are directly proportional for a fixed mass, so doubling F doubles a. (ii) Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force, a = F/m, which identifies mass as the measure of inertia. (iii) Acceleration is always along the net force, not along the velocity — in uniform circular motion a points to the centre while v is tangential. The law uses the net force, the vector sum of all forces, so a body with several forces may still have zero acceleration when they cancel. It holds only in inertial (non-accelerating) frames, and if mass itself changes (a rocket) the general form F = dp/dt must be used.

Example. A 1200 kg car at rest is acted on by a constant net force of 2400 N for 5 s. Then a = F/m = 2400/1200 = 2 m/s², so v = at = 10 m/s and s = ½at² = 25 m. If the same car carries a 600 kg load (m = 1800 kg), the same force gives a = 2400/1800 = 1.33 m/s², showing the inverse dependence on mass. If instead the force is doubled to 4800 N with the original mass, the acceleration becomes 4 m/s², showing direct proportionality. Catching a ball with the hands moved back illustrates the same law in the form F = Δp/Δt: increasing the time reduces the force.
questions.explanation: Key principle: F = dp/dt reduces to F = ma for constant mass; force and acceleration are parallel vectors and mass measures inertia. Common mistake: using only the applied force instead of the net force, or treating F = ma as valid when mass changes.

questions.question: How does the conservation of momentum apply in each type of collision? Give real-life examples of both types of collisions.
questions.answer:
Law in collision form. When no net external force acts, the total momentum before and after a collision is the same: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. Momentum is a vector, so velocities to the left are taken negative.

Elastic collision. Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. For a head-on collision in which mass m₁ moves with u₁ and m₂ is at rest, solving the two conservation equations gives v₁ = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]u₁ and v₂ = [2m₁/(m₁ + m₂)]u₁. If m₁ = m₂, then v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u₁: the first body stops and the second moves off with its speed, as in a Newton's cradle or a head-on hit between equal billiard balls. If m₁ >> m₂, then v₁ ≈ u₁ and v₂ ≈ 2u₁, as when a heavy ball strikes a light one.

Inelastic collision. Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; part of it becomes heat, sound and deformation. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and move with the common velocity v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂), and the kinetic energy lost is ΔK = ½[m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)](u₁ − u₂)². A partly inelastic collision is described by the coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach), with 0 < e < 1.

Examples. Elastic: collisions between gas molecules in a container, hard steel balls striking each other, and alpha particles scattered by nuclei (approximately elastic). Inelastic: a bullet embedding itself in a wooden block (ballistic pendulum), two lumps of clay sticking together, a railway wagon coupling to a stationary one, and a car crash in which the vehicles lock together.

Why momentum is conserved in both. During contact the forces the bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite (Newton's third law) and act for the same time, so their impulses cancel; only the distribution of momentum between the bodies and the amount of kinetic energy change.
questions.explanation: Key principle: momentum is conserved in every collision because internal forces cancel; kinetic energy is conserved only when the collision is elastic. Common mistake: applying kinetic-energy conservation to inelastic collisions, or forgetting the signs of oppositely directed velocities.

questions.question: Explain how the concept of impulse is related to the change in momentum of an object. Provide an example of an everyday life where impulse plays a significant role.
questions.answer:
Definition. Impulse is the product of a force and the time interval for which it acts: J = FΔt. It is a vector in the direction of the force and is measured in N·s, which is the same as kg·m/s.

Impulse-momentum theorem. Newton's second law gives F = Δp/Δt, and multiplying by Δt gives FΔt = Δp = mv − mu. The impulse of the net force therefore equals the change in momentum of the body. For a force that varies with time, J = ∫F dt is the area under the force-time graph, and the average force is F_av = Δp/Δt. The theorem is simply Newton's second law integrated over the time of contact, and it holds for any body of constant mass.

Meaning. A required change of momentum fixes the product FΔt. A large force acting for a short time and a small force acting for a long time can produce the same impulse; increasing the contact time reduces the force, and shortening the time increases it.

Everyday example: catching a cricket ball. A 0.16 kg ball moving at 20 m/s has momentum 3.2 kg·m/s, so stopping it requires an impulse of 3.2 N·s. If the hands are held rigid and the ball stops in 0.01 s, the average force is F = Δp/Δt = 3.2/0.01 = 320 N, which hurts. If the hands are moved back so that the ball stops in 0.10 s, the same impulse acts over ten times as long and the force falls to 32 N. Car airbags and crumple zones, landing mats, bending the knees on landing, and the sand pit at a long jump use the same idea. The opposite case is a hammer blow or a karate strike, where a very short contact time gives a very large force for a modest momentum change, and a rubber ball bouncing back reverses momentum and so needs a larger impulse than one that simply stops.
questions.explanation: Key principle: J = FΔt = Δp; the impulse equals the area under the force-time graph. Common mistake: forgetting that a bouncing ball undergoes Δp = 2mv, not mv, so the impulse is twice as large.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of momentum. Provide an example from everyday life that demonstrates the principle of momentum conservation.
questions.answer:
Statement. In the absence of a net external force, the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant in magnitude and direction: Σp_initial = Σp_final. For two interacting bodies, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

Derivation from Newton's laws. Let bodies A and B collide. By Newton's third law the force of A on B is equal and opposite to the force of B on A: F_AB = −F_BA. Multiplying by the same contact time Δt gives F_ABΔt = −F_BAΔt, so Δp_B = −Δp_A, that is Δp_A + Δp_B = 0. The total momentum does not change. The law also follows at once from Newton's second law, since F_ext = dp/dt = 0 means p is constant.

Scope and conditions. Only external forces can change the momentum of a system; internal forces always occur in equal and opposite pairs, so they cancel. Momentum is a vector, so the law applies separately along each direction, and it holds for collisions of any type, for explosions, for recoil and for rocket motion. Unlike energy conservation in collisions, it is not affected by kinetic energy being converted into heat.

Everyday example — firing a gun. Before firing, the gun and bullet are at rest, so the total momentum is zero. When the bullet of mass m leaves with velocity v to the right, the gun of mass M must move with velocity V = −(m/M)v to the left (recoil), so that mv + MV = 0. A 10 kg gun firing a 20 g bullet at 500 m/s recoils at 1 m/s. A rocket works in the same way: the momentum of the ejected gases backwards equals the momentum of the rocket forwards, which is why a rocket can accelerate in empty space where there is nothing to push against. Two skaters pushing off each other, a person throwing a heavy ball while standing on frictionless ice, and the recoil of a cannon are further examples in which the total momentum stays zero although each body moves.
questions.explanation: Key principle: internal action-reaction pairs cannot change total momentum, so an isolated system keeps its total momentum; rocket propulsion and recoil are direct consequences. Common mistake: applying momentum conservation when a significant external force (friction, gravity along the motion) acts.

questions.question: A car weighing 9800 N is moving with a speed of 40 Km/h. On the Application of breaks it comes to rest after traveling a distance of 50 meters. Calculate the average retarding force?
questions.answer:
Given:
W = 9800 N, u = 40 km/h = 40 × 1000/3600 = 11.11 m/s, v = 0, s = 50 m, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula:
m = W/g; a = (v² − u²)/2s; F = ma
Substitution:
m = 9800/9.8 = 1000 kg
a = (0 − 11.11²)/(2 × 50) = −123.46/100
Calculation:
a = −1.235 m/s²
F = 1000 × (−1.235) = −1234.6 N
The negative sign shows that the force acts opposite to the motion, i.e. it is a retarding force.
Result:
Average retarding force = 1234.6 N ≈ 1.23 × 10³ N, which agrees with the printed answer 1234.57 N.
questions.explanation: Key formula: v² = u² + 2as gives the deceleration, then F = ma. Convert km/h to m/s first and obtain the mass from m = W/g; the retarding force is the magnitude 1234.57 N.

questions.question: A helicopter weighs 3920 N. Calculate the force on it if it is ascending up at the rate of 2m/s². What will be the force on helicopter if it is moving up with a constant speed of 4 m/s?
questions.answer:
Given:
W = 3920 N, a = 2 m/s² (upward), constant speed case a = 0, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula:
m = W/g
Ascending with acceleration: F = m(g + a)
Constant speed: F = mg
Substitution:
m = 3920/9.8 = 400 kg
F = 400 × (9.8 + 2) = 400 × 11.8
Calculation:
F = 4720 N (upward thrust of the rotor)
For constant speed: F = 400 × 9.8 = 3920 N
Result:
(a) While ascending at 2 m/s² the force is 4720 N.
(b) While moving up with a constant speed of 4 m/s the force is 3920 N.
Both values agree with the printed answers (4720 N, 3920 N).
questions.explanation: Key idea: the rotor must support the weight and also supply the upward acceleration, F − mg = ma, so F = m(g + a); at constant speed the acceleration is zero and F = mg regardless of the speed value.

questions.question: A 100 grams bullet s fired from a 10 kg gun with a speed of 1000m/s. What is the speed of recoil of the gun?
questions.answer:
Given:
m_b = 100 g = 0.1 kg, m_g = 10 kg, v_b = 1000 m/s, initial total momentum = 0
Formula:
m_b v_b + m_g v_g = 0, so v_g = −(m_b v_b)/m_g
Substitution:
v_g = −(0.1 × 1000)/10 = −100/10
Calculation:
v_g = −10 m/s
Result:
The recoil speed of the gun is 10 m/s in the direction opposite to the bullet. This agrees with the printed answer 10 m/s.
questions.explanation: Key formula: conservation of linear momentum for a system initially at rest, m_bv_b + m_gv_g = 0; the minus sign gives the direction of recoil and the speed is its magnitude.

questions.question: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second into a target. Each bullet weighs 20 gram and had a speed of 1500 m/s. Find the necessary force to hold the gun in position?
questions.answer:
Given:
n = 10 bullets/s, m = 20 g = 0.02 kg per bullet, v = 1500 m/s, u = 0
Formula:
F = (change in momentum per second) = n m v
Substitution:
F = 10 × 0.02 × 1500
Calculation:
F = 10 × 30 = 300 N
Result:
The force needed to hold the gun in position is 300 N, directed along the motion of the bullets (the gun presses back on the holder with 300 N). This agrees with the printed answer 300 N.
questions.explanation: Key formula: average force equals the momentum delivered per second, F = n m v; the holding force must equal the recoil force in magnitude and act forward.

questions.question: A 50 grams bullet is fired into a 10 kg block that is suspended by a long cord so that it can swing as a pendulum. If the block is displaced so that its center of gravity rises by 10cm, what was the speed of bullet?
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 50 g = 0.05 kg, M = 10 kg, h = 10 cm = 0.10 m, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula:
After the (perfectly inelastic) impact: v = √(2gh) for the block + bullet
Conservation of momentum: m u = (M + m) v, so u = (M + m)v/m
Substitution:
v = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.10) = √1.96 = 1.4 m/s
u = (10 + 0.05) × 1.4/0.05
Calculation:
u = 10.05 × 1.4/0.05 = 14.07/0.05 = 281.4 m/s
Result:
The speed of the bullet was 281.4 m/s, which agrees with the printed answer 281.4 m/s. (If the 10 kg block mass alone is used instead of 10.05 kg, the result is 280 m/s, a difference of about 0.5%.)
questions.explanation: Key method: two stages — an inelastic collision in which only momentum is conserved, followed by a rise in which only mechanical energy is conserved, ½(M + m)v² = (M + m)gh. Common mistake: applying energy conservation to the collision itself.

questions.question: A 70-gram ball collides with another ball of mass 140 gram. The initial velocity of the first ball is 9m/s to right while the second ball is at rest. If the collision were perfectly elastic, what would be the velocity of two balls after the collision?
questions.answer:
Given:
m₁ = 70 g = 0.07 kg, m₂ = 140 g = 0.14 kg, u₁ = 9 m/s (to the right), u₂ = 0, perfectly elastic collision
