Formula:
v₁ = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]u₁
v₂ = [2m₁/(m₁ + m₂)]u₁
Substitution:
m₁ + m₂ = 0.21 kg
v₁ = [(0.07 − 0.14)/0.21] × 9 = (−0.07/0.21) × 9
v₂ = (2 × 0.07/0.21) × 9 = (0.14/0.21) × 9
Calculation:
v₁ = −(1/3) × 9 = −3 m/s
v₂ = (2/3) × 9 = 6 m/s
Check:
Momentum before = 0.07 × 9 = 0.63 kg·m/s; after = 0.07 × (−3) + 0.14 × 6 = −0.21 + 0.84 = 0.63 kg·m/s ✓
K.E. before = ½ × 0.07 × 81 = 2.835 J; after = ½ × 0.07 × 9 + ½ × 0.14 × 36 = 0.315 + 2.52 = 2.835 J ✓
Result:
The 70 g ball rebounds with 3 m/s to the left (−3 m/s) and the 140 g ball moves with 6 m/s to the right. This agrees with the printed answers (−3 m/s, 6 m/s).
questions.explanation: Key formulas: for a head-on elastic collision with the second body at rest, v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂); the negative sign of v₁ means rebound. Both momentum and kinetic energy checks confirm the result.

questions.question: A truck weighing 2500 kg and moving with a velocity of 21m/s collides with a stationary car weighing 1000 kg. The truck and car move together after the impact. Calculate their common velocity?
questions.answer:
Given:
m₁ = 2500 kg, u₁ = 21 m/s, m₂ = 1000 kg, u₂ = 0, perfectly inelastic collision
Formula:
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v, so v = m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂)
Substitution:
v = (2500 × 21)/(2500 + 1000) = 52500/3500
Calculation:
v = 15 m/s
Check: momentum before = 52500 kg·m/s; momentum after = 3500 × 15 = 52500 kg·m/s ✓
Result:
The common velocity after the impact is 15 m/s in the original direction of the truck, which agrees with the printed answer 15 m/s.
questions.explanation: Key formula: conservation of momentum for a perfectly inelastic collision, v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂); kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision.

questions.question: One radian is about
questions.explanation: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius, so 2π rad = 360° and 1 rad = 180°/π = 57.3° ≈ 57°. The value 25° is far too small, 37° belongs to a 3-4-5 triangle often used in problems, and 45° would correspond to π/4 rad. Hence (d).

questions.question: Wheel turns with constant angular speed then:
questions.answer: (c) the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times
questions.explanation: Constant angular speed means ω = Δθ/Δt is fixed, so equal angles are turned through in equal times, θ = ωt. A point on the rim has constant speed but its velocity direction changes continuously, so its velocity is not constant (a is wrong); its centripetal acceleration also changes direction continuously, so the acceleration vector is not constant (b is wrong). Options (d) and (e) describe angular acceleration and deceleration respectively, which contradict constant ω. Hence (c).

options.text: each point on its rim moves with constant velocity
each point on its rim moves with constant acceleration
the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times
the angle through which the wheel turns in each second increases as time goes on
the angle through which the wheel turns in each second decreases as time goes on

questions.optionsRaw: (a) each point on its rim moves with constant velocity  (b) each point on its rim moves with constant acceleration  (c) the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times  (d) the angle through which the wheel turns in each second increases as time goes on  (e) the angle through which the wheel turns in each second decreases as time goes on
questions.correctAnswer: (c) the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times

questions.question: The rotational inertia of a wheel about its axle does not depend upon its
questions.answer: (d) speed of rotation
questions.explanation: Rotational inertia is I = Σmr², which depends on the total mass, on how that mass is distributed about the axis (shape, diameter and thickness, since mass near the rim contributes more than mass near the axle), and on the axis chosen. It does not depend on how fast the wheel happens to spin, because it is a purely inertial-geometric property measured in kg·m². Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) diameter  (b) mass  (c) distribution of mass  (d) speed of rotation

questions.question: A force with at given magnitude is to be applied to a wheel. The torque can be maximized by
questions.answer: (d) applying the force at the rim, tangent to the rim
questions.explanation: Torque is τ = rF sinθ, so for a fixed force magnitude it is largest when the lever arm r is greatest (force at the rim) and when θ = 90° (force perpendicular to the radius, i.e. tangent to the rim). A force near the axle has a small r, and a radial force has sinθ = 0 and therefore produces no torque at all, however large it is. Hence (d).

options.text: applying the force near the axle, radially outward from the axle.
applying the force near the rim, radially outward.
applying the force near the axle, parallel to a tangent to the wheel.
applying the force at the rim, tangent to the rim

questions.optionsRaw: (a) applying the force near the axle, radially outward from the axle.  (b) applying the force near the rim, radially outward.  (c) applying the force near the axle, parallel to a tangent to the wheel.  (d) applying the force at the rim, tangent to the rim
questions.correctAnswer: (d) applying the force at the rim, tangent to the rim

questions.question: An object rotating about a fixed axis, I is its rotational inertia and α is its angular acceleration. Its
questions.answer: (d) follows directly from Newton's second law.
questions.explanation: The printed stem is incomplete (it ends with 'Its'); the intended statement is 'Its Iα is'. The relation τ = Iα follows directly from Newton's second law in rotational form, τ = dL/dt with L = Iω for a fixed axis and constant I, so τ = I dω/dt = Iα. It is not a definition: torque is defined as τ = rF sinθ, rotational inertia as I = Σmr² and angular acceleration as α = dω/dt. Hence (d).

follows directly from Newton's second law.

questions.correctAnswer: (d) follows directly from Newton's second law.

questions.question: The angular momentum vector of Earth about its rotation axis, due to its daily rotation is, directed
questions.answer: (c) north
questions.explanation: Earth spins from west to east, so a point on the equator moves eastward. By the right-hand rule, curling the fingers of the right hand in the sense of rotation makes the thumb point along the axis towards the geographic north pole, which is the direction of L. A vector tangent to the equator would describe the instantaneous velocity of a surface point, not the angular momentum, and the direction of the Sun is unrelated to the rotation axis. Hence (c).

options.text: tangent to the equator towards east
tangent to the equator towards the west

questions.optionsRaw: (a) tangent to the equator towards east  (b) tangent to the equator towards the west  (c) north  (d) towards the Sun.

questions.question: A stone of 2 kg is tied to a 0.50 m long string and swung around a circle at angular velocity of 12 rad/s . The net torque on the stone about the center of the circle is:
questions.answer: (a) 0 N.m
questions.explanation: The stone moves in a circle at constant angular velocity, so its angular momentum about the centre does not change and the net torque must be zero. The only force is the tension, which acts along the string toward the centre, so r and F are antiparallel and τ = rF sin180° = 0. Option (d) 72 N·m comes from wrongly multiplying the centripetal force (mω²r = 2 × 144 × 0.5 = 144 N) by r without the sinθ factor, and 6 and 12 N·m have no basis in the data. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 0 N.m  (b) 6 N.m  (c) 12 N.m  (d) 72 N.m

questions.question: A man, with his arms at his sides, is spinning on a light frictionless turntable . When he extends his arms
questions.answer: (d) his angular momentum remains the same.
questions.explanation: The turntable is frictionless and light, so no external torque acts about the vertical axis and angular momentum L = Iω is conserved. Extending the arms moves mass away from the axis, so the rotational inertia I increases (not decreases) and the angular velocity ω = L/I decreases (not increases). Hence only (d) is correct.

options.text: his angular momentum remains the same.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) his angular velocity increases  (b) his angular velocity remains same  (c) his rotational inertia decreases  (d) his angular momentum remains the same.
questions.correctAnswer: (d) his angular momentum remains the same.

questions.question: A space station revolves around the earth as a satellite, 100 km above the Earth's surface. What is the net force on an astronaut at rest inside the space station?
questions.answer: (b) a little less than her weight on earth
questions.explanation: At a height of 100 km the gravitational field is g' = g(R/(R + h))² ≈ 9.8 × (6370/6470)² ≈ 9.5 m/s², only about 3% less than at the surface, so the gravitational force on the astronaut is a little less than her weight on Earth. She and the station are in free fall together, so she feels weightless and the normal reaction on her is zero, but the actual net force (gravity) is not zero — it provides the centripetal force for the orbit. It is certainly not less than half her weight. Hence (b).

options.text: equal to her weight on earth
a little less than her weight on earth
less than half her weight on earth

questions.optionsRaw: (a) equal to her weight on earth  (b) a little less than her weight on earth  (c) less than half her weight on earth  (d) zero (she is weightless)
questions.correctAnswer: (b) a little less than her weight on earth

questions.question: If the external torque acting on a body is zero, then its
questions.answer: (b) angular momentum is conserved
questions.explanation: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, τ = dL/dt, so zero external torque means dL/dt = 0 and L stays constant — the law of conservation of angular momentum. Angular momentum need not be zero; a body can continue spinning uniformly. Angular acceleration is zero (not maximum), since τ = Iα with τ = 0, and there is no such quantity as 'maximum rotational motion'. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) angular momentum is zero  (b) angular momentum is conserved  (c) angular acceleration is maximum  (d) rotational motion is maximum

questions.question: For an isolated rotating body, what is the relation between angular velocity and radius?
questions.answer: For a body rotating about a fixed axis, the linear speed of a point at radius r is v = rω, so ω = v/r: for a given linear speed the angular velocity is inversely proportional to the radius, and points farther from the axis move faster. For an isolated (torque-free) body, angular momentum L = Iω is conserved, so ω = L/I and the angular velocity is inversely proportional to the moment of inertia. Since I = Σmr² grows as the mass is moved farther from the axis, increasing the radius of the mass distribution increases I and reduces ω. For a single mass whirled on a string, I = mr², so at constant L, ω ∝ 1/r², and the string tension supplies the centripetal force.
questions.explanation: Key point: v = rω links speed and radius, while L = Iω = constant makes ω inversely proportional to I (and hence to r² for a point mass).

questions.question: When the moment of inertia of a rotating body is halved, then what will be the effect on angular velocity?
questions.answer: For an isolated rotating body no external torque acts, so angular momentum L = Iω is conserved. If the moment of inertia becomes I' = I/2, then ω' = L/I' = L/(I/2) = 2L/I = 2ω: the angular velocity doubles. The rotational kinetic energy K = L²/2I also doubles, the extra energy being supplied by the work done by the internal forces that pulled the mass closer to the axis, as when a skater pulls in her arms. Note that this conclusion assumes the body is isolated; if an external agency keeps the angular velocity constant or applies a fixed torque, ω need not double.
questions.explanation: Key principle: conservation of angular momentum, I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂; halving I doubles ω for an isolated body.

questions.question: Compare kinematics equation of linear motion and circular motion
questions.answer: Every linear kinematic equation for constant acceleration has a rotational analogue obtained by replacing s by θ, u by ω₀, v by ω and a by α: v = u + at ↔ ω = ω₀ + αt; s = ut + ½at² ↔ θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; v² = u² + 2as ↔ ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; average velocity (u + v)/2 ↔ average angular velocity (ω₀ + ω)/2; and s = vt for uniform velocity ↔ θ = ωt for uniform angular velocity. The dynamics correspond as well: F ↔ τ, m ↔ I and p ↔ L, so F = ma ↔ τ = Iα, and K = ½mv² ↔ K = ½Iω². The correspondence holds only for constant acceleration or angular acceleration; θ must be in radians, ω in rad/s and α in rad/s².
questions.explanation: Key point: the equations map one-to-one by s→θ, u→ω₀, v→ω, a→α; the analogy also extends to F→τ, m→I and p→L.

questions.question: Can a small force ever exert a greater torque than a larger force? Give reason.
questions.answer: Yes. Torque is τ = rF sinθ, so it depends on the lever arm r and on the angle θ as well as on the magnitude of the force. A small force applied far from the axis, perpendicular to the radius (sinθ = 1), can give a larger torque than a large force applied close to the axis or along the radius. For example, a 10 N force at 1.0 m produces 10 N·m, while a 100 N force at 0.05 m produces only 5 N·m; and a force directed through the axis produces no torque however large it is. This is why a long spanner loosens a tight bolt and why door handles are fixed far from the hinges.
questions.explanation: Key point: torque is not force; τ = rF sinθ, so the lever arm and direction can more than compensate for a small force.

questions.question: Give two real world applications of angular momentum
questions.answer: Gyroscope: a rapidly spinning rotor has a large angular momentum along its axis, and because no torque acts the direction of L stays fixed in space. This is used for navigation and inertial guidance in aircraft, ships and missiles, and for attitude control (reaction wheels) in satellites and space telescopes. Ice skater and divers: with arms and legs pulled in, the moment of inertia decreases and the angular velocity increases because L = Iω is conserved; extending the limbs again slows the spin before landing. Further examples are the tail rotor of a helicopter, which counteracts the reaction torque of the main rotor, and a spinning cricket or football, whose angular momentum keeps its axis steady in flight.
questions.explanation: Key point: conservation of angular momentum, I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂; the gyroscope keeps its axis direction because L is constant when no external torque acts.

questions.question: Derive relationship between torque and angular acceleration.
questions.answer: Consider a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis and made of particles of masses m₁, m₂ … at distances r₁, r₂ … from the axis. Because the body is rigid, every particle has the same angular acceleration α, and the ith particle has a tangential acceleration a_i = r_iα. The tangential force needed on it is F_i = m_i a_i = m_i r_i α. The torque of this force about the axis is τ_i = r_i F_i = m_i r_i² α. Summing over all particles, the internal torques cancel in pairs by Newton's third law, leaving the net external torque: τ = Σm_i r_i² α = Iα, where I = Σm_i r_i² is the moment of inertia. This is the rotational form of Newton's second law, τ = Iα. If I changes with time, the general form τ = dL/dt must be used.
questions.explanation: Key steps: a_t = rα, F = ma_t, τ = rF = mr²α, then sum over all particles to get τ = Iα. Note that internal torques cancel.

questions.question: List the moment of inertia dependent factors.
questions.answer: The moment of inertia I = Σmr² of a body about a chosen axis depends on: (i) the total mass of the body — doubling the mass doubles I; (ii) the distribution of mass about the axis — the farther the mass lies from the axis, the larger I, so a hoop (MR²) has twice the I of a solid disc (½MR²) of the same mass and radius; (iii) the position of the axis — I about the rim is larger than about the centre, as given by I = I_cm + Md²; (iv) the orientation of the axis relative to the body — a rod about its centre (ML²/12) differs from the same rod about one end (ML²/3); (v) the size and shape of the body. It does not depend on the angular speed of rotation.
questions.explanation: Key point: I depends on mass, mass distribution, and the position and orientation of the axis — but not on angular speed or on the torque applied.

questions.question: State and explain the law of conservation of angular momentum. Give two examples to illustrate it.
questions.answer:
Statement. If no net external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant in magnitude and direction: L = Iω = constant, or I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. Since torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, τ = dL/dt, zero torque means dL/dt = 0.

Explanation. For a particle, angular momentum is L = r × p, with magnitude L = mvr sinθ; for a rigid body about a fixed axis, L = Iω. The law follows from Newton's second law in rotational form, just as conservation of linear momentum follows from F = ma with F = 0. Internal torques — for example the forces a skater exerts on herself, or the forces between the parts of an exploding body — always occur in equal and opposite pairs and cancel, so only external torques can change L. Angular momentum is a vector, so the law holds separately for each component; a body may change its shape and its angular velocity, but the product Iω stays fixed. It also explains why a torque-free body keeps the direction of its axis fixed in space, the basis of gyroscopic stability.

Example 1 — the spinning skater. A skater spinning with arms outstretched has a large moment of inertia I₁ and a small angular velocity ω₁. Pulling the arms in reduces the moment of inertia to a fraction of its value, so ω₂ = I₁ω₁/I₂ becomes much larger and she spins rapidly; extending the arms again slows the spin. The rotational kinetic energy ½Iω² increases, and the extra energy comes from the work she does in pulling her arms inward against the tendency of the mass to move outward.

Example 2 — a planet in orbit. The gravitational force on a planet is directed towards the Sun, so it is a central force and its torque about the Sun is zero; hence the planet's angular momentum mvr sinθ is constant. The planet therefore moves fastest at perihelion, where r is smallest, and slowest at aphelion, and its radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal times (Kepler's second law). Divers tucking to somersault faster, and the large angular momentum of a gyroscope or a bicycle wheel, are further illustrations.
questions.explanation: Key principle: τ = dL/dt, so with no external torque Iω is constant; internal forces cannot change total L. Common mistake: thinking angular velocity alone is conserved — it is L, so ω changes when I changes.

questions.question: Discuss forces action on banked curve and derive relation between curve angle and velocity?
questions.answer:
Consider a car of mass m moving with speed v along a curve of radius r that is banked at an angle θ to the horizontal. For the design speed the road is taken as frictionless.

Forces acting. (i) The weight mg acting vertically downward through the centre of gravity; (ii) the normal reaction N acting perpendicular to the road surface, and therefore tilted from the vertical by the angle θ; (iii) if the speed differs from the design speed, friction along the surface, up or down the slope, which is neglected in the ideal case.

Resolution of forces. Take the vertical direction and the horizontal direction towards the centre of the curve. There is no acceleration vertically, so the vertical components balance: N cosθ = mg. The horizontal component of N is the only horizontal force and it provides the centripetal force: N sinθ = mv²/r.

Derivation. Dividing the horizontal equation by the vertical one, (N sinθ)/(N cosθ) = (mv²/r)/(mg), gives tanθ = v²/(rg). Hence the banking angle is θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg), and the design speed for a given banking angle is v = √(rg tanθ).

The normal reaction does two jobs: its vertical component N cosθ supports the weight, and its horizontal component N sinθ bends the velocity towards the centre. Because the road is tilted, no friction is needed at the design speed. At a higher speed the car tends to slide outward and friction down the slope is needed (with friction, tanθ = (v²/rg − μ)/(1 + μv²/rg)); at a lower speed it tends to slide inward. Banking is used on highway curves, railway bends (where the outer rail is raised) and velodromes. For example, r = 1.20 km and v = 105 km/h = 29.2 m/s give tanθ = (29.2)²/(1200 × 9.8) = 0.0723, so θ ≈ 4.1°.
questions.explanation: Key derivation: N cosθ = mg and N sinθ = mv²/r, so tanθ = v²/(rg). Common mistake: resolving the centripetal force along the slope instead of horizontally toward the centre.

questions.question: Derive the formula for centripetal acceleration using fundamental principles and equations, illustrating each step of the derivation
questions.answer:
A body moving on a circle of radius r with constant speed v has a continuously changing velocity direction, so it is accelerated. The acceleration is directed towards the centre and is called centripetal acceleration.

Method 1 — vector subtraction. Let the body be at A with velocity v₁ and, after a short time Δt, at B with velocity v₂, where |v₁| = |v₂| = v and the radius OA has turned through the angle Δθ. Because v₁ is perpendicular to OA and v₂ is perpendicular to OB, the angle between v₁ and v₂ is also Δθ. Draw v₁ and v₂ from a common point; the change Δv = v₂ − v₁ joins their tips, and the triangle formed by v₁, v₂ and Δv is similar to the triangle OAB, since both are isosceles with the same vertex angle Δθ. Therefore |Δv|/v = AB/r, that is |Δv| = v(AB)/r. Dividing by Δt gives |Δv|/Δt = (v/r)(AB/Δt). For small Δt the chord AB approaches the arc, so AB/Δt → v. Hence a_c = v²/r. As Δt → 0 the vector Δv becomes perpendicular to v, that is, it points towards the centre O.

Method 2 — calculus. Place the origin at the centre and let the body be at angle θ = ωt, so r = r(cosωt i + sinωt j). Differentiating once, v = dr/dt = rω(−sinωt i + cosωt j), whose magnitude is rω = v. Differentiating again, a = dv/dt = −rω²(cosωt i + sinωt j) = −ω²r. The magnitude is a_c = ω²r, and since v = ωr this is a_c = v²/r; the minus sign shows that a points opposite to r, i.e. towards the centre.

Interpretation. The acceleration is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of motion and not the speed. The force needed to produce it is F_c = mv²/r = mω²r, directed towards the centre; if this force is removed the body moves along the tangent, in agreement with Newton's first law. A car on a curve, a stone whirled on a string, a satellite in orbit and electrons in a magnetic field all move under such a centripetal force.
questions.explanation: Key result: a_c = v²/r = ω²r, directed towards the centre. The similar-triangles step |Δv|/v = AB/r and the limit AB/Δt → v are the essential parts; the direction follows because Δv becomes perpendicular to v.

questions.question: Derive the formula for the moment of inertia of a uniform rod or a solid sphere. Clearly illustrate each step of the derivation.
questions.answer:
Definition. The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is I = Σmr², the sum of mr² for all its particles; for a continuous body I = ∫r² dm, where r is the perpendicular distance of the element dm from the axis.

Uniform rod of length L and mass M about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its length. Take the centre O as origin with the x-axis along the rod, and consider an element of length dx at distance x from O. Its mass is dm = (M/L)dx. Then
I = ∫x² dm = ∫_{−L/2}^{+L/2} x² (M/L) dx = (M/L)[x³/3]_{−L/2}^{+L/2}
= (M/L)[(L/2)³/3 − (−L/2)³/3] = (M/L)(2/3)(L³/8) = ML²/12.

About an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod. Take the end as origin, so x runs from 0 to L:
I = ∫₀ᴸ x²(M/L)dx = (M/L)[x³/3]₀ᴸ = ML²/3.
The same result follows from the parallel-axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md² = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3.

Solid sphere of radius R and mass M about a diameter. Slice the sphere into thin discs perpendicular to the axis. A disc at distance x from the centre has radius y = √(R² − x²), thickness dx and mass dm = ρπy²dx, where ρ = 3M/(4πR³). Its moment of inertia about the diameter is dI = ½(dm)y² = ½ρπy⁴dx. Hence
I = ∫_{−R}^{+R} ½ρπ(R² − x²)² dx = ½ρπ[R⁴x − (2/3)R²x³ + x⁵/5]_{−R}^{+R} = (8/15)ρπR⁵.
Substituting ρ gives I = (2/5)MR².

Conclusion. I depends on the mass, on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis, and on the position of the axis: for the same rod, ML²/3 (end) is four times ML²/12 (centre), which is why the point of support matters.
questions.explanation: Key method: I = ∫r²dm with dm = (M/L)dx for the rod and dm = ρπ(R² − x²)dx for a disc slice of the sphere. Common mistake: measuring x from one end while using the centre formula, or forgetting the ½ factor for a disc.

questions.question: Define torque and explain how does it differ from force in linear motion?
questions.answer:
Definition. Torque (or moment of a force) is the turning effect of a force about a point or axis. If a force F acts at a position r from the axis, then τ = r × F, with magnitude τ = rF sinθ, where θ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is the newton metre (N·m). Torque is a vector along the axis of rotation, its sense being given by the right-hand rule, and it is taken as positive or negative according to whether it tends to produce anticlockwise or clockwise rotation. The quantity r sinθ is called the lever arm or moment arm.

Differences from force in linear motion.
1. Effect produced: a force produces linear acceleration, a = F/m; a torque produces angular acceleration, α = τ/I, i.e. a change in the rate of rotation.
2. Dependence on point of application: torque depends on where the force is applied (through r) and on its direction relative to r, so the same force gives different torques at different points; a force acting through the axis gives zero torque. A force on a particle is independent of any such choice.
3. Governing equations: F = ma and p = mv correspond to τ = Iα and L = Iω.
4. Equilibrium: a body in equilibrium needs both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. A body can have zero net force and still rotate, as when a couple acts on it.
5. Units and nature: N for force against N·m for torque; torque is a vector along the axis, force is a vector along its own line of action.

Example. A 20 N force applied at right angles to a door 0.8 m from the hinge gives τ = 0.8 × 20 = 16 N·m and opens the door easily; the same force applied 0.1 m from the hinge gives only 2 N·m, and applied along the door towards the hinge it gives no torque at all. This is why a long spanner is used to loosen a tight bolt: it increases the lever arm and hence the torque for the same force.
questions.explanation: Key point: torque is the rotational analogue of force, τ = rF sinθ, and it depends on the point of application as well as on the force; τ = Iα is the rotational counterpart of F = ma.

questions.question: A car mechanic applies a force of 800 N to a wrench for the purpose of loosening a bolt. He applies the force which is perpendicular to the arm of the wrench. The distance from the bolt to the mechanic's hand is 0.40 m. Find out the magnitude of the torque applied?
questions.answer:
Given:
F = 800 N, r = 0.40 m, θ = 90° (force perpendicular to the wrench arm)
Formula:
τ = rF sinθ
Substitution:
τ = 0.40 × 800 × sin90° = 0.40 × 800 × 1
Calculation:
τ = 320 N·m
Result:
The magnitude of the torque applied is 320 N·m, which agrees with the printed answer 320 N·m.
questions.explanation: Key formula: τ = rF sinθ; with the force perpendicular to the arm sinθ = 1, so τ is simply the product rF, and the large lever arm is what makes the bolt turn.

questions.question: A car accelerates uniformly from rest and reaches a speed of 22 m/s in 9 s. If the diameter of a tire is 58 cm, find (a) the number of revolutions the tire makes during this motion, assuming no slipping, and (b) the final rotational speed of the tire in revolutions per second.
questions.answer:
Given:
u = 0, v = 22 m/s, t = 9 s, diameter d = 58 cm = 0.58 m, so radius r = 0.29 m
Formula:
Distance travelled s = ½(u + v)t
Number of revolutions N = s/(2πr)
Final angular speed ω = v/r; revolutions per second f = ω/2π
Substitution:
s = ½(0 + 22) × 9 = 99 m
2πr = 2 × 3.1416 × 0.29 = 1.822 m
N = 99/1.822 = 54.3
ω = 22/0.29 = 75.86 rad/s
f = 75.86/(2 × 3.1416) = 12.07 rev/s
Calculation:
N = 54.3 revolutions
f = 12.07 ≈ 12 rev/s
Result:
(a) The tire makes about 54.3 revolutions (≈ 54 rev).
(b) The final rotational speed is 12.07 ≈ 12 rev/s, which agrees with the printed answer 12 rev/s.
Note: the book prints 55 rev for part (a); the exact value from s = 99 m and circumference 1.822 m is 54.3 rev, so 55 rev is a rounding of about 1% upward and does not affect the physics.
questions.explanation: Key steps: distance from average speed × time, revolutions = distance/circumference, and f = v/(2πr). Common mistake: using the diameter as the radius, or using the final speed instead of the average speed to find the distance.

questions.question: An ordinary workshop grindstone has a radius of 7.5 cm and rotates 6500 rev/min. (a) Calculate the magnitude of centripetal acceleration at its edge in m/s² and convert it into multiples of g. (b) What is the linear speed of a point on its edge?
questions.answer:
Given:
r = 7.5 cm = 0.075 m, rotational speed = 6500 rev/min, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula:
ω = 2πn/60 (n in rev/min)
a_c = ω²r = v²/r
v = ωr
Substitution:
ω = (2 × 3.1416 × 6500)/60 = 680.7 rad/s
a_c = (680.7)² × 0.075 = 4.634 × 10⁵ × 0.075
v = 680.7 × 0.075
Calculation:
a_c = 3.47 × 10⁴ m/s²
a_c/g = (3.47 × 10⁴)/9.8 = 3.55 × 10³ g
v = 51.05 m/s
Result:
(a) Centripetal acceleration = 3.47 × 10⁴ m/s² ≈ 3.55 × 10³ g.
(b) Linear speed of a point on the edge = 51 m/s.
Both values agree with the printed answers ((3.47×10⁴ m/s², 3.55×10³ g, 51 m/s)).
questions.explanation: Key formulas: convert rev/min to rad/s with ω = 2πn/60, then a_c = ω²r and v = ωr. Note that a_c is thousands of g, which is why grindstones must be rated for high speed.

questions.question: A satellite is orbiting the Earth with an orbital velocity of 3200 m/s. What is the orbital radius?
questions.answer:
Given:
v = 3200 m/s, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², M = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg
Formula:
For a circular orbit v = √(GM/r), so r = GM/v²
Substitution:
GM = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.98 × 10²⁴ = 3.989 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²
v² = (3200)² = 1.024 × 10⁷ m²/s²
r = (3.989 × 10¹⁴)/(1.024 × 10⁷)
Calculation:
r = 3.895 × 10⁷ m
Result:
The orbital radius is 3.90 × 10⁷ m (about 39,000 km from the Earth's centre), which agrees with the printed answer 3.897 × 10⁷ m within rounding.
questions.explanation: Key formula: the orbital speed is set by gravity providing the centripetal force, GMm/r² = mv²/r, giving v = √(GM/r) and r = GM/v².

questions.question: A satellite wishes to orbit the earth at a height of 100 km (approximately 60 miles) above the surface of the earth. Determine the speed, acceleration and orbital period of the satellite. (Given: M_earth = 5.98 x 10²⁴ kg, R_earth = 6.37 x 10⁶ m)
questions.answer:
Given:
h = 100 km = 1.00 × 10⁵ m, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, M = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
Formula:
r = R + h
v = √(GM/r)
a = v²/r = GM/r²
T = 2πr/v
Substitution:
r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 0.10 × 10⁶ = 6.47 × 10⁶ m
GM = 3.989 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²
v = √[(3.989 × 10¹⁴)/(6.47 × 10⁶)] = √(6.165 × 10⁷)
T = (2 × 3.1416 × 6.47 × 10⁶)/(7.85 × 10³)
Calculation:
v = 7.85 × 10³ m/s
a = (6.165 × 10⁷)/(6.47 × 10⁶) = 9.53 m/s²
T = (4.065 × 10⁷)/(7.85 × 10³) = 5.18 × 10³ s = 5178/3600 = 1.44 h
Result:
Speed = 7.85 × 10³ m/s, acceleration = 9.53 m/s², orbital period = 1.44 hours (about 86 min). All three agree with the printed answers (7.85×10³ m/s, 9.53 m/s², 1.44 hours).
questions.explanation: Key formulas: v = √(GM/r), a = GM/r² and T = 2πr/v with r = R + h. Common mistake: using the surface radius R instead of R + h, which is 1.6% larger here.

questions.question: A thin disk with a 0.3m diameter and a total moment of inertia of 0.45kg·m² is rotating about its center of mass. There are three rocks with masses of 0.2kg on the outer part of the disk. Find the total moment of inertia of the system?
questions.answer:
Given:
d = 0.3 m, so r = 0.15 m; I_disk = 0.45 kg·m²; three rocks, each m = 0.2 kg, at the outer edge r = 0.15 m
Formula:
I_total = I_disk + 3mr²
Substitution:
I_rocks = 3 × 0.2 × (0.15)² = 0.6 × 0.0225
I_total = 0.45 + 0.0135
Calculation:
I_rocks = 0.0135 kg·m²
I_total = 0.4635 kg·m²
Result:
The total moment of inertia of the system is 0.464 kg·m², which agrees with the printed answer 0.464 kg·m².
questions.explanation: Key idea: moments of inertia about the same axis add, I_total = I_disk + Σmr² for the rocks treated as point masses at the rim. Common mistake: using the diameter 0.3 m as the radius.

questions.question: What is the ideal banking angle for a gentle turn of 1.20 km radius on a highway with a 105 km/h speed limit (about 65 mi/h), assuming everyone travels at the limit?
questions.answer:
Given:
r = 1.20 km = 1200 m, v = 105 km/h = 105 × 1000/3600 = 29.17 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s²
Formula:
tanθ = v²/(rg), θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg)
Substitution:
v² = (29.17)² = 850.7 m²/s²
rg = 1200 × 9.8 = 11760 m²/s²
tanθ = 850.7/11760 = 0.07234
Calculation:
θ = tan⁻¹(0.07234) = 4.14°
Result:
The ideal banking angle is 4.14°, which agrees with the printed answer 4.14°.
questions.explanation: Key formula: for a frictionless banked curve N sinθ = mv²/r and N cosθ = mg, so tanθ = v²/(rg). Convert km/h to m/s before substituting.

questions.question: A 1500-kg car moving on a flat, horizontal road negotiates a curve as shown in Figure. If the radius of the curve is 35 m and the coefficient of static friction between the tires and dry pavement is 0.523, find the maximum speed the car can have and still make the turn successfully.
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 1500 kg, r = 35 m, μ_s = 0.523, g = 9.8 m/s², flat (unbanked) curve
Formula:
Static friction supplies the centripetal force: f_s = mv²/r, with f_s(max) = μ_sN = μ_smg
μ_smg = mv_max²/r, so v_max = √(μ_srg)
Substitution:
v_max = √(0.523 × 35 × 9.8) = √(179.4)
Calculation:
v_max = 13.39 m/s (about 48 km/h)
Result:
The maximum speed is 13.4 m/s, which agrees with the printed answer 13.5 m/s within rounding; the printed value corresponds to g = 10 m/s², which gives √(0.523 × 35 × 10) = 13.5 m/s.
questions.explanation: Key condition: on a flat curve friction alone provides the centripetal force, and the limiting case is f_s = μ_smg = mv²/r, so v_max = √(μ_srg). The mass cancels. The printed 13.5 m/s uses g ≈ 10 m/s²; with g = 9.8 m/s² the result is 13.4 m/s.
questions.figure: Figure on page 97: a 1500 kg car on a flat, horizontal curved road (unbanked) of radius 35 m; the curve is shown from above with the car turning, friction between the tyres and dry pavement providing the centripetal force.

questions.question: A system of points shown in figure 4.22. Each particle has same mass of 0.3 kg and they all lie in the same plane. What is the moment of inertia of the system about given axis? (Four particles, one at the axis point, one 40 cm above it, one 20 cm to its right and one 50 cm away to its lower left; the axis is perpendicular to the plane through the particle at the junction.)
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 0.3 kg for each of the four particles; distances from the axis (perpendicular to the plane through the particle at the junction): r₁ = 0 (particle on the axis), r₂ = 40 cm = 0.40 m, r₃ = 20 cm = 0.20 m, r₄ = 50 cm = 0.50 m
Formula:
I = Σmr² = m(r₁² + r₂² + r₃² + r₄²)
Substitution:
I = 0.3 × (0² + 0.40² + 0.20² + 0.50²)
I = 0.3 × (0 + 0.16 + 0.04 + 0.25)
Calculation:
I = 0.3 × 0.45 = 0.135 kg·m²
Result:
The moment of inertia of the system about the given axis is 0.135 kg·m², which agrees with the printed answer 0.135 kg·m².
questions.explanation: Key idea: I = Σmr² about the axis, each distance measured perpendicular to the axis; the particle lying on the axis contributes nothing. Convert cm to m before squaring.
questions.figure: Figure 4.22: four equal particles (0.3 kg each) in one plane — one at the junction on the axis, one 40 cm above it, one 20 cm to its right and one 50 cm away to its lower left; the axis is perpendicular to the plane of the particles and passes through the particle at the junction.

questions.question: (a) What is the angular momentum of a 2.9 kg uniform cylindrical grinding wheel of radius 20 cm when rotating 1550 rpm? (b) How much torque is required to stop it in 6 s?
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 2.9 kg, r = 20 cm = 0.20 m, n = 1550 rev/min, t = 6 s, final ω = 0
Formula:
I = ½mr² (uniform cylinder)
ω = 2πn/60
L = Iω
τ = ΔL/Δt = (0 − L)/t
Substitution:
I = ½ × 2.9 × (0.20)² = ½ × 2.9 × 0.04 = 0.058 kg·m²
ω = (2 × 3.1416 × 1550)/60 = 162.3 rad/s
L = 0.058 × 162.3
τ = (0 − 9.41)/6
Calculation:
L = 9.41 kg·m²/s
τ = −1.57 N·m
Result:
(a) Angular momentum = 9.4 kg·m²/s (the printed answer is 9.5 kg·m²/s, obtained by rounding I to 0.0583 kg·m² before multiplying; the difference is under 1%).
(b) Torque required to stop it = −1.6 N·m, the minus sign showing that the torque opposes the rotation; this agrees with the printed answer −1.6 N·m.
questions.explanation: Key formulas: I = ½mr² for a uniform cylinder, L = Iω and τ = ΔL/Δt. Common mistake: using I = mr² as for a hoop, which would double L and the torque.

questions.question: Determine the angular momentum of the Earth (a) about its rotation axis (Assume the Earth as uniform sphere), and (b) in its orbit around the Sun (Take Earth as a particle orbiting the Sun). The Earth has mass 6 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶m, and is 1.5 × 10⁸ km from the Sun.
questions.answer:
Given:
M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, orbital radius r = 1.5 × 10⁸ km = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m, one day T_day = 86400 s, one year T_year = 3.156 × 10⁷ s
Formula:
(a) I = (2/5)MR², ω = 2π/T_day, L = Iω
(b) v = 2πr/T_year, L = Mvr
Substitution:
(a) I = 0.4 × 6 × 10²⁴ × (6.4 × 10⁶)² = 0.4 × 6 × 10²⁴ × 4.096 × 10¹³ = 9.83 × 10³⁷ kg·m²
ω = 2π/86400 = 7.27 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s
L = 9.83 × 10³⁷ × 7.27 × 10⁻⁵
(b) v = (2 × 3.1416 × 1.5 × 10¹¹)/(3.156 × 10⁷) = 2.99 × 10⁴ m/s
L = 6 × 10²⁴ × 2.99 × 10⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹¹
Calculation:
(a) L = 7.15 × 10³³ kg·m²/s
(b) L = 2.69 × 10⁴⁰ kg·m²/s
Result:
(a) Angular momentum about its rotation axis = 7.2 × 10³³ kg·m²/s (printed 7.3 × 10³³ kg·m²/s; the small difference comes from rounding R and the day length).
(b) Angular momentum in its orbit = 2.7 × 10⁴⁰ kg·m²/s, which agrees with the printed answer.
questions.explanation: Key formulas: for a uniform sphere I = (2/5)MR² and L = Iω with ω = 2π/T; for the orbit L = Mvr with v = 2πr/T. Note the orbital angular momentum is about 10⁷ times larger than the spin angular momentum.

questions.question: Work done by centripetal force is always:
questions.answer: (c) Zero
questions.explanation: Centripetal force always acts along the radius, i.e. perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, so the angle θ between force and displacement is 90°. Hence W = Fd cos 90° = 0, whatever the magnitude of the force or of the speed. The force changes only the direction of motion, never the speed, so no energy is transferred. It is therefore neither maximum nor minimum but always zero.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Maximum  (b) Minimum  (c) Zero  (d) None of these

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg is moving with a momentum of 10 kg m/s . A force of 0.2 N acts on it in the direction of motion of the body for 10 seconds. The increase in kinetic energy is:
questions.explanation: Initial speed u = p/m = 10/5 = 2 m/s and a = F/m = 0.2/5 = 0.04 m/s², so after 10 s v = 2 + 0.04 × 10 = 2.4 m/s. Then ΔK = ½m(v² − u²) = 2.5 × (5.76 − 4) = 4.4 J. Equivalently the impulse adds 2 kg m/s to the momentum (10 → 12 kg m/s), and K = p²/2m gives 10 J → 14.4 J, again +4.4 J. The distractors come from using the momentum change or the acceleration alone.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of a light and a heavy object is same. Which object has maximum momentum?
questions.answer: (b) Heavy object
questions.explanation: Since K = p²/2m, we have p = √(2mK); for the same kinetic energy the momentum is proportional to √m. The heavier object therefore has the greater momentum, although it moves more slowly. The lighter object must move much faster for the same K, but its momentum is still smaller, so (a), (c) and (d) are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Light object  (b) Heavy object  (c) Both have same momentum  (d) N.O.T

questions.question: Two bodies of mass 1 kg and 2 kg have equal momentum. Then the ratio of their kinetic energies is:
questions.explanation: For equal momentum, K = p²/2m shows that kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass. Hence K₁/K₂ = m₂/m₁ = 2/1, i.e. the 1 kg body has twice the kinetic energy of the 2 kg body. Options (b), (c) and (d) ignore this inverse dependence on mass.

questions.question: A body fallen from height h . After it has fallen a height h/2 , its will possess :
questions.answer: (c) half potential half kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Initially all the energy is potential, mgh. After falling h/2 the body is at height h/2 above the ground, so U = mg(h/2) = mgh/2, and by conservation of energy K = mgh − mgh/2 = mgh/2. Thus PE and KE are equal at that instant, so none of the other descriptions fits.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) only potential energy  (b) only kinetic energy  (c) half potential half kinetic energy  (d) more kinetic and less potential

questions.question: Which of the following quantity can be calculated by multiplying force and velocity ?
questions.answer: (b) power
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t = Fd/t = Fv, when force and velocity are along the same direction (in general P = F·v = Fv cos θ), and it is measured in watts. Force multiplied by displacement gives work, force multiplied by perpendicular distance gives torque, and force divided by mass gives acceleration, so the other options are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) acceleration  (b) power  (c) torque  (d) work

questions.question: The minimum velocity given to an object so that it emerges out from the gravitational field of earth is about _________ :
questions.explanation: This is the escape velocity, v_e = √(2gR) = √(2 × 9.8 × 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 1.12 × 10⁴ m/s = 11.2 km/s. A speed of 5 km/s is far below this value, so the object would rise and fall back; 9.8 km/s merely repeats the numerical value of g in m/s²; 15.3 km/s is much larger than needed.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 11.2 km/s  (b) 15.3 km/s  (c) 5 km/s  (d) 9.8 km/s

questions.question: When one joule of work is done on a body in one second, power of body is said to be :
questions.answer: (a) One watt
questions.explanation: Power = work done / time taken = 1 J / 1 s = 1 W; the watt is defined exactly as one joule per second. The other options would require 0.5 J, 0 J and 100 J of work per second respectively, so they are inconsistent with the data.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) One watt  (b) 0.5 watt  (c) zero  (d) 100 watt

questions.question: The absolute potential energy of an object depends on:
questions.answer: (a) The object's mass and height
questions.explanation: Near the earth U = mgh, and in general U = −GMm/r, so gravitational potential energy depends on the mass of the object and on its position (height) relative to the reference level. Speed determines kinetic energy, not potential energy, and shape, size, colour and temperature play no part in gravitational PE.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) The object's mass and height  (b) The object's mass and speed  (c) The object's shape and size  (d) The object's color and temperature

questions.question: The escape velocity of a planet depends on which of the following factors?
questions.answer: (c) Both the mass and the radius of the planet
questions.explanation: The escape velocity is v_e = √(2GM/R), so it depends on both the mass M and the radius R of the planet; neither one alone fixes it (a massive but very large planet can have a small escape speed). Density by itself is also insufficient, because the same density with a different radius gives a different v_e. Hence only (c) is complete.

options.text: The mass of the planet only
The radius of the planet only
Both the mass and the radius of the planet

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The mass of the planet only  (b) The radius of the planet only  (c) Both the mass and the radius of the planet  (d) The density of the planet
questions.correctAnswer: (c) Both the mass and the radius of the planet

questions.question: How does work relate to the transfer of energy?
questions.answer: Work is the process by which energy is transferred from one body to another by a force acting through a displacement, W = F d cos θ. When positive work W is done on a body, its energy increases by exactly W; this is the work–energy theorem, W_net = ΔK. When the body does work on something else, its energy decreases by the same amount. Work is therefore energy in transit, not energy stored in a body, and its unit (joule) is the same as that of energy. For example, pushing a trolley transfers energy from the pusher to the trolley, while friction transfers part of it to the surroundings as heat. If the force is perpendicular to the displacement, no energy is transferred and W = 0.
questions.explanation: Stress that work is a process of energy transfer, not a stored quantity; the work–energy theorem gives the exact bookkeeping W_net = ΔK.

questions.question: How is power related to work and time?
questions.answer: Power is the rate at which work is done, i.e. the rate at which energy is transferred: P_av = W/t, and instantaneous power P = dW/dt = F·v. For the same amount of work, a shorter time means a larger power, so power measures how quickly, not how much, energy is transferred. The SI unit is the watt, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹, and the kilowatt (10³ W) and megawatt (10⁶ W) are common multiples. For example, a 100 W lamp converts 100 J of electrical energy every second, and a 1 kW motor does 1000 J of work each second.
questions.explanation: Key relation P = W/t; a common mistake is to think a more powerful machine does more work — it only does the same work faster.

questions.question: What is the difference between average power and instantaneous power?
questions.answer: Average power is the total work done divided by the total time taken, P_av = ΔW/Δt, and it gives no information about how the power varied during that interval. Instantaneous power is the power at one particular instant, P = lim(Δt→0) ΔW/Δt = dW/dt = F·v; it equals the slope of the work–time graph at that instant. For example, a crane that lifts a load slowly and then quickly has a small instantaneous power most of the time but a moderate average power for the whole lift. Average power is quoted for complete jobs (a car's power over a journey), instantaneous power for engines whose output changes from moment to moment.
questions.explanation: Average power uses the whole interval; instantaneous power is the limit Δt → 0 and equals F·v at that instant.

questions.question: How does gravitational potential energy change with height and mass?
questions.answer: For heights small compared with the earth's radius, gravitational potential energy is U = mgh, where h is the height above the chosen reference level and g is practically constant. U is directly proportional to the mass m and to the height h, so doubling either the mass or the height doubles the potential energy. For example, a 2 kg body raised 5 m has U = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J, while a 4 kg body at the same height has 196 J. At very large heights g is not constant and one must use U = −GMm/r, which becomes less negative, i.e. increases, as the height and hence r increases.
questions.explanation: U = mgh is linear in both m and h only near the earth's surface; for large heights the exact −GMm/r form must be used.

questions.question: What is the law of conservation of energy?
questions.answer: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, so the total energy of an isolated system remains constant. In mechanics, if only conservative forces act, K + U = constant, that is ½mv² + mgh = constant, so any loss of potential energy appears as an equal gain of kinetic energy and vice versa. When friction or air resistance acts, the mechanical energy lost reappears as heat and sound, so the total energy is still conserved. A swinging pendulum and a stone falling freely are simple illustrations of the law.
questions.explanation: Total energy of an isolated system is constant; mechanical energy alone is conserved only when non-conservative forces do no work.

questions.question: How does energy efficiency play a role in various energy transformations?
questions.answer: Energy efficiency compares the useful energy obtained from a device with the total energy supplied to it: η = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%. In every real transformation some energy is dissipated by friction, air resistance, electrical resistance or sound, so the efficiency is always less than 100%. A filament lamp converts only about 5% of the electrical energy into light, the rest becoming heat; a petrol engine is typically 25–40% efficient. Efficiency therefore decides running cost and fuel consumption — a 40% efficient engine wastes 60% of the fuel energy. Better design and lubrication raise η and conserve energy resources.
questions.explanation: η = useful output / total input × 100%; no real device reaches 100% because some energy is always degraded to heat.

questions.question: What is the work-energy theorem and how is it expressed mathematically?
questions.answer: The work–energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i². For a constant net force acting along the displacement, W = Fs = (ma)s, and since v_f² = v_i² + 2as we have as = (v_f² − v_i²)/2, giving W = ½m(v_f² − v_i²). For a variable force the same result follows on integrating, W = ∫F dx. The theorem holds for any combination of forces; work done by friction appears as a decrease of K, while work done by a driving force increases it.
questions.explanation: W_net = ΔK; remember that only the NET work (work of all forces) changes the kinetic energy.

questions.question: How is the work done by a variable force calculated?
questions.answer: When the force is not constant the work is not simply F × d. The displacement is divided into small elements Δx over which the force is practically constant, the work for each element being F Δx, and the total work is the limit of the sum: W = ∫F(x) dx between the initial and final positions. Graphically, this integral is the area under the force–displacement graph, counted positive above the axis and negative below it. For a spring obeying Hooke's law F = kx, the graph is a straight line and the area is a triangle, so W = ½kx². This method is used for springs, stretched wires, and any force that changes with position.
questions.explanation: W = ∫F dx = area under the F–x graph; a frequent error is to use the average force multiplied by distance without justification.

questions.question: How the work done in gravitational field is independent of path
questions.answer:
Consider a body of mass m moved slowly from a point A at height h₁ to a point B at height h₂ (h₂ > h₁) above a reference level in the earth's field, where g is constant.

Path 1 — vertical: the applied force must just balance the weight, F = mg upward, and the displacement is h₂ − h₁ upward, so W₁ = mg(h₂ − h₁).

Path 2 — along a smooth incline of length L making an angle θ with the horizontal: the force needed along the plane is mg sin θ and h₂ − h₁ = L sin θ, so W₂ = (mg sin θ)L = mg(h₂ − h₁) = W₁.

Path 3 — an arbitrary zig-zag curve: divide the path into elements ds making an angle α with the vertical. The work of the applied force on one element is mg ds cos α, but ds cos α = dy, the vertical rise of that element. Hence W₃ = ∫mg dy from h₁ to h₂ = mg(h₂ − h₁). All horizontal portions contribute nothing, because the force is perpendicular to them.

Thus the work depends only on the initial and final heights, not on the route, its length or its shape. This is the defining property of a conservative force. As a consequence the work done in carrying the body round any closed path back to A is zero, and a potential energy function U = mgh can be defined with W = −ΔU. For the exact inverse-square field the same reasoning gives U = −GMm/r.
questions.explanation: The key step is ds cos α = dy for every element; only the vertical rise matters, which is why gravity is conservative.

questions.question: Calculate gravitational potential energy at a certain height due to work against gravity.
questions.answer:
Gravitational potential energy is the energy a body possesses because of its position in the earth's gravitational field, and it is equal to the work done in raising the body from the reference level to that height at constant speed.

Let a body of mass m be lifted vertically through a height h near the earth's surface, where g may be taken as constant. To move it without acceleration the applied force must just balance its weight, F = mg, upward. The displacement h is also upward, so θ = 0° and
W = F h cos 0° = mgh.
This work is stored in the earth–body system as gravitational potential energy, so U = mgh, taking U = 0 at the reference level. For example, a 5 kg body raised to a shelf 4 m high has U = 5 × 9.8 × 4 = 196 J, and the same 196 J reappears as kinetic energy if the body falls back to the floor.

The result can also be obtained from the work done by gravity itself: when the body falls through h, gravity does +mgh of work, so ΔU = −W_gravity = −mgh, i.e. the potential energy falls by mgh.

For heights comparable with the earth's radius, g cannot be treated as constant. The work done in bringing the mass from infinity to a distance r from the earth's centre is W = −GMm/r, so U = −GMm/r; at a height h above the surface r = R + h and U = −GMm/(R + h). Between two heights, ΔU = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
questions.explanation: U = mgh is the work done against gravity at constant speed; its negative gradient gives the gravitational force.

questions.question: Describe that the gravitational PE is measured from a reference level and can be positive or negative, to denote the orientation from the reference level.
questions.answer:
Potential energy is always measured relative to a chosen reference level (datum) at which U is taken as zero — the floor of a room, the ground, sea level, or the earth's centre. The height h in U = mgh is measured from this level, and the sign of U shows on which side of the reference the body lies: a body above the reference has positive potential energy, a body below it has negative potential energy.

Example: take the ground as reference. A 2 kg ball on a table 1 m high has U = 2 × 9.8 × 1 = +19.6 J. The same ball 3 m down a well has h = −3 m, so U = 2 × 9.8 × (−3) = −58.8 J. If the table top is chosen as reference instead, the ball on the table has U = 0 and the ball on the floor has U = −19.6 J. The absolute values differ with the choice, but every change ΔU is the same, and only ΔU has physical meaning because it equals the work done.

The same convention is used for absolute potential energy, U = −GMm/r, measured from infinity where U = 0. Since r is finite, U is negative everywhere; as the body is raised, r increases and U becomes less negative, i.e. it increases towards zero. A negative value therefore does not mean 'negative energy'; it means the body is bound and lies below the zero-energy level at infinity, and the sign simply records its orientation with respect to the reference.
questions.explanation: Only differences of PE are physical; the sign records whether the body is above (+) or below (−) the chosen zero, or whether the bound system lies below U = 0 at infinity.

questions.question: Show that the work done in gravitational field is independent of path
questions.answer:
To show that the work done in a gravitational field is independent of path, compare two or more routes between the same two points A (height h₁) and B (height h₂).

Route 1, straight up: the applied force needed is mg upward and the displacement is (h₂ − h₁) upward, so W₁ = mg(h₂ − h₁).

Route 2, up a smooth incline of length L at angle θ to the horizontal: the force along the plane is mg sin θ and h₂ − h₁ = L sin θ, so W₂ = mg sin θ × L = mg(h₂ − h₁) = W₁.

Route 3, any curve: split it into elements ds making an angle α with the vertical. The work of the applied force on an element is mg ds cos α, and ds cos α = dy, its vertical rise. Summing, W₃ = ∫mg dy = mg(h₂ − h₁). Horizontal elements give zero work because the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

So every route gives the same W = mg(h₂ − h₁): the work depends only on the end heights. Equivalently, if the body goes A → B by one route and returns B → A by another, the total work in the closed loop is mg(h₂ − h₁) − mg(h₂ − h₁) = 0. This zero work around a closed path is the test of a conservative force, and it is what allows a potential energy function (mgh near the earth, −GMm/r in the exact field) to be defined. Friction, which gives different work for different paths and non-zero work in a closed loop, is non-conservative.
questions.explanation: Compare vertical, inclined and arbitrary paths; the closed-loop result W = 0 is the standard test of a conservative field.

questions.question: Define work by variable force. Calculate the work done from the force-displacement graph. [Take a force-displacement graph in which the force increases uniformly from 0 to 20 N over the first 4.0 m of displacement and then remains constant at 20 N from 4.0 m to 6.0 m.]
questions.answer:
Definition: when the force acting on a body does not remain constant during the displacement, the work cannot be found from a single product F d. The displacement is divided into very small intervals dx, so small that the force is practically constant over each. The work in one interval is dW = F(x) dx, and the total work is the limit of the sum:
W = ∫F(x) dx, taken between the initial and final positions x₁ and x₂.
Geometrically this integral is the area between the force–displacement curve and the displacement axis. Area above the axis is positive (force along the displacement), area below the axis is negative (force opposite to the displacement), and the net work is the algebraic sum.

Calculation from the graph [F rises uniformly from 0 to 20 N over 0 to 4.0 m, then stays at 20 N from 4.0 m to 6.0 m]:
(1) From x = 0 to 4.0 m the graph is a triangle: W₁ = ½ × base × height = ½ × 4.0 × 20 = 40 J.
(2) From x = 4.0 m to 6.0 m the graph is a rectangle: W₂ = 20 × (6.0 − 4.0) = 40 J.
Total work W = W₁ + W₂ = 40 + 40 = 80 J.

A simple physical example is a spring stretched by x, for which F = kx; the F–x graph is a straight line through the origin and the area is W = ½kx². For k = 200 N/m and x = 0.10 m, W = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1.0 J — not Fx = 2 J — which shows why the graphical (integral) method is essential for a variable force.
questions.explanation: Work is the area under the F–x graph; add the triangle and the rectangle, and note that area below the axis counts as negative work.
questions.figure: Force–displacement graph: F rises linearly from 0 to 20 N over 0–4.0 m, then stays constant at 20 N from 4.0 m to 6.0 m.

questions.question: A man pulls a trolley through a distance of 10 m by applying a force of 50 N which makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. Calculate the work done by the man?
questions.answer:
Given: F = 50 N; d = 10 m; θ = 60°.
Formula: W = F d cos θ.
Substitution: W = 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 500 × 0.5.
Calculation: W = 250 J.
Result: W = 250 J, which agrees with the printed answer (250 J).
questions.explanation: Only the horizontal component F cos θ does work; cos 60° = 0.5 halves the product Fd.

questions.question: A 100 kg man runs up a long flight of stairs in 9.8 second. The vertical height of the stair is 10 m. Calculate its power?
questions.answer:
Given: m = 100 kg; h = 10 m; t = 9.8 s; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: P = W/t = mgh/t.
Substitution: P = (100 × 9.8 × 10)/9.8.
Calculation: P = 9800/9.8 = 1000 W.
Result: P = 1000 W = 1 kW, which agrees with the printed answer (1000 Watts).
questions.explanation: The work done is only against gravity (mgh); the time happens to equal g numerically, so the power equals mh = 1000 W.

questions.question: When an object is thrown upwards. It rises to a height 'h'. How high is the object in terms of h, when it has lost one third of its original kinetic energy?
questions.answer:
Given: the object rises to a maximum height h, so its original kinetic energy K is converted completely into potential energy at the top: K = mgh.
Condition: at the required height y the object has lost one third of K, so its remaining KE is 2K/3 and the potential energy gained is K/3.
Formula: mgy = K/3.
Substitution: mgy = (mgh)/3.
Calculation: y = h/3.
Result: y = h/3, which agrees with the printed answer (h/3).
questions.explanation: Use K = mgh at the top, so losing one third of the KE means rising one third of h; the remaining 2/3 of K is still kinetic.

questions.question:
A 70 kg man runs up a hill through a height of 3 m in 2 seconds.
(a) How much work does he do against gravitational field?
(b) What is the average power output?
questions.answer:
Given: m = 70 kg; h = 3 m; t = 2 s; g = 9.8 m/s².
(a) Work against gravity:
Formula: W = mgh.
Substitution: W = 70 × 9.8 × 3.
Calculation: W = 2058 J.
Result: W ≈ 2.06 × 10³ J, which agrees with the printed answer (2060 J) after rounding to three significant figures.
(b) Average power output:
Formula: P = W/t.
Substitution: P = 2058/2.
Calculation: P = 1029 W.
Result: P ≈ 1.03 × 10³ W ≈ 1030 W, which agrees with the printed answer (1030 Watt).
questions.explanation: Work is done only against the vertical height (mgh), not along the slope; average power is that work divided by 2 s.

questions.question: A neutron travels a distance of 12 m in a time interval of 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ sec. Assuming its speed was constant, Find its kinetic energy? Take the mass of neutron 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
questions.answer:
Given: s = 12 m; t = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ s; m = 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Formula: v = s/t and K = ½mv², then K(eV) = K(J)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹).
Substitution: v = 12/(3.6 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.33 × 10⁴ m/s; K = ½ × 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ × (3.33 × 10⁴)².
Calculation: v² = 1.11 × 10⁹ m²/s²; K = 0.5 × 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ × 1.11 × 10⁹ = 9.44 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 9.44 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ eV = 5.90 eV.
Result: K ≈ 5.9 eV. The printed answer is 5.78 eV; the 2% difference arises because the printed value uses the more exact neutron mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, which gives 5.79 eV. With the mass quoted in the question (1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) the answer is 5.90 eV.
questions.explanation: Speed from uniform motion, then K = ½mv²; converting joules to eV means dividing by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

questions.question: A stone is thrown vertically upwards and can reach to a height of 10m, find the speed of stone, when it is just 2m above the ground?
questions.answer:
Given: maximum height h = 10 m; required height above ground y = 2 m; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: by conservation of energy, ½mv² = mg(h − y), so v = √(2g(h − y)).
Substitution: v = √(2 × 9.8 × (10 − 2)) = √(2 × 9.8 × 8).
Calculation: v = √156.8 = 12.52 m/s.
Result: v ≈ 12.5 m/s. The printed answer is 12.9 m/s, which does not follow from the given data: it would require g ≈ 10.4 m/s² or a fall of about 8.5 m. With g = 9.8 m/s² the correct value is 12.5 m/s, and even with g = 10 m/s² it is 12.6 m/s, so the printed figure appears to be a rounding or printing slip.
questions.explanation: The stone loses potential energy mg(h − y) and gains the same kinetic energy; the relevant drop is 8 m, not 10 m.

questions.question: The potential energy of a body at the top of a building is 200 Joules when it is dropped its kinetic energy just before striking the ground is 160 Joules, find the work done against the air resistance?
questions.answer:
Given: PE at the top = 200 J; KE just before striking the ground = 160 J.
Formula: work done against air resistance = loss of mechanical energy = PE_top − KE_ground.
Substitution: W = 200 − 160.
Calculation: W = 40 J.
Result: W = 40 J, which agrees with the printed answer (40 J).
questions.explanation: With no air resistance the KE at the ground would equal 200 J; the 40 J missing has been used up in doing work against air resistance.

questions.question: Find the energy equivalent of 1 gram?
questions.answer:
Given: m = 1 g = 1 × 10⁻³ kg; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Formula: E = mc².
Substitution: E = 1 × 10⁻³ × (3 × 10⁸)².
Calculation: E = 1 × 10⁻³ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ J.
Result: E = 9 × 10¹³ J, which agrees with the printed answer (9 × 10¹³ J).
questions.explanation: Mass must be converted to kilograms before using E = mc²; the square of 3 × 10⁸ is 9 × 10¹⁶.

questions.question: A 1Kilowatt motor pump, pumps the water from the ground to a height of 10 m. Find, how much litres of water it can pump in one hour?
questions.answer:
Given: P = 1 kW = 1000 W; h = 10 m; t = 1 hour = 3600 s; g = 9.8 m/s²; density of water = 1000 kg/m³.
Formula: useful work Pt = mgh, so m = Pt/(gh); the volume in litres equals the mass in kg because 1 litre of water has mass 1 kg.
Substitution: m = (1000 × 3600)/(9.8 × 10) = 3.6 × 10⁶/98.
Calculation: m = 3.67 × 10⁴ kg, i.e. V = 3.67 × 10⁴ litres.
Result: about 3.6 × 10⁴ litres in one hour, which agrees with the printed answer (3.6 × 10⁴ litre); with g = 10 m/s² the value is exactly 3.6 × 10⁴ litres.
questions.explanation: Convert 1 hour to 3600 s and 1 kW to 1000 W, then equate Pt to mgh; rounding g to 10 gives the printed value.

questions.question: A rocket of mass 2kg is launched in air, when it attains height of 15m the 400 Joules of its chemical fuel burns. Find the speed of rocket at maximum height?
questions.answer:
Given: m = 2 kg; h = 15 m; energy released by the fuel E = 400 J; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: ½mv² + mgh = E (conservation of energy from the ground), so v = √(2(E − mgh)/m).
Substitution: ½ × 2 × v² + 2 × 9.8 × 15 = 400, i.e. v² + 294 = 400.
Calculation: v² = 106, so v = 10.3 m/s.
Result: v ≈ 10.3 m/s ≈ 10 m/s, which agrees with the printed answer (10 m/s). Note that this is the speed of the rocket at the 15 m height where the fuel has burnt out; at the true maximum height of the flight (400/19.6 = 20.4 m) the speed is zero, so the printed answer refers to the burnout point.
questions.explanation: Equate the fuel energy to KE + PE at 15 m; at the actual top of the path the kinetic energy is zero, so the printed 10 m/s is the burnout speed.

questions.question: A motor pumps the water at the rate 500 gram/minute to the height of 120 m. If the motor is 50% efficient then how much input electric power is needed?
questions.answer:
Given: mass rate = 500 g/min = 0.5 kg/60 s = 8.33 × 10⁻³ kg/s; h = 120 m; η = 50% = 0.50; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: output power P_out = (m/t)gh, and efficiency η = P_out/P_in, so P_in = P_out/η.
Substitution: P_out = 8.33 × 10⁻³ × 9.8 × 120; P_in = P_out/0.50.
Calculation: P_out = 9.8 W; P_in = 19.6 W.
Result: P_in ≈ 20 W, which agrees with the printed answer (20 watt).
questions.explanation: The 50% efficiency doubles the electrical input compared with the mechanical output; remember to convert 500 g/min into kg/s.

questions.question: A completely submerged object always displaces its own ________
questions.answer: (b) volume of a fluid
questions.explanation: A completely submerged body occupies the space where fluid used to be, so the volume of fluid displaced equals its own volume; this is the geometrical basis of Archimedes' principle. It does not generally displace its own weight of fluid (otherwise it would be neutrally buoyant), so (a) is wrong unless the densities happen to be equal. Density and area are properties of the fluid, not quantities displaced, so (c) and (d) are meaningless here.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) weight of fluid  (b) volume of a fluid  (c) density of a fluid  (d) Area of fluid

questions.question: The pressure exerted on the ground by a man is greatest when:
questions.answer: (c) he stands on the toes of one foot
questions.explanation: Pressure is p = F/A, and the force is the man's weight in every case, so the pressure is greatest when the area of contact is smallest — standing on the toes of one foot. Two feet flat give the largest area and the least pressure, one flat foot is intermediate, and lying down spreads the weight over the whole body, giving the least pressure of all.

options.text: he stands with both feet flat on the ground
he stands flat on one foot
he stands on the toes of one foot
he lies down on the ground

questions.optionsRaw: (a) he stands with both feet flat on the ground  (b) he stands flat on one foot  (c) he stands on the toes of one foot  (d) he lies down on the ground
questions.correctAnswer: (c) he stands on the toes of one foot

questions.question: In a stationary homogeneous liquid:
questions.answer: (d) pressure is the same at all points at the same level
questions.explanation: In a stationary homogeneous liquid p = p₀ + ρgh, so at a given level (same depth) the pressure is the same everywhere, but it increases with depth — which rules out (a). Pressure in a fluid is a scalar and acts equally in all directions, so (b) is wrong. The atmospheric pressure p₀ is added to the liquid pressure, so the pressure does depend on it, which rules out (c).

options.text: pressure is the same at all points
pressure is independent of any atmospheric pressure on the upper surface of the liquid
pressure is the same at all points at the same level

questions.optionsRaw: (a) pressure is the same at all points  (b) pressure depends on the direction  (c) pressure is independent of any atmospheric pressure on the upper surface of the liquid  (d) pressure is the same at all points at the same level
questions.correctAnswer: (d) pressure is the same at all points at the same level

questions.question: One piston in a hydraulic lift has an area that is twice the area of the other. When the pressure at the smaller piston is increased by Δp the pressure at the larger piston:
questions.answer: (c) increases by Δp
questions.explanation: By Pascal's principle a change of pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the liquid, so the pressure at the larger piston also rises by exactly Δp. It is the force that is multiplied, F₂ = Δp × 2A = 2F₁, not the pressure. Options (a), (b) and (d) wrongly transfer the force ratio (2) to the pressure.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) increases by 2Δp  (b) increases by Δp/2  (c) increases by Δp  (d) increases by 4Δp

questions.question: In a vacuum, an object has
questions.answer: (a) No buoyant force
questions.explanation: Buoyancy is produced by the pressure of a surrounding fluid, and a vacuum contains no fluid, so no upthrust acts on the object. Mass is an intrinsic property of the body and does not change, so (b) is wrong; the weight mg still exists (the body is merely in free fall, which does not make its weight zero), so (c) is wrong. Since (a) is correct, (d) is also wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) No buoyant force  (b) no mass  (c) no weight  (d) none of these

questions.question: The pressure at the bottom of a pond does NOT depend on
questions.answer: (c) the surface area of the pond
questions.explanation: The pressure at the bottom is p = p₀ + ρgh, which involves the density of the water and the depth of the pond (as well as the atmospheric pressure), but not the area of the pond's surface. The area changes the total force on the bottom, F = pA, not the pressure. Since option (c) is correct, (d) is excluded.

options.text: the surface area of the pond

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Water density  (b) the depth of the pond  (c) the surface area of the pond  (d) None of these
questions.correctAnswer: (c) the surface area of the pond

questions.question: A rock suspended by a weighing scale weighs 5N out of water and 3 N when submerged in water. What is the buoyant force on the rock?
questions.answer: (a) 3 N — printed option nearest the true value; the physically correct upthrust 2 N is not listed
questions.explanation: The buoyant force equals the loss of weight in water: 5 N − 3 N = 2 N. The printed options (3 N, 5 N, 8 N, 15 N) do not contain 2 N, so the item is misprinted: 3 N is the apparent weight in water, 5 N the true weight, and 8 N their sum (a tension plus weight confusion). Option (a) has been keyed only because it is the closest printed value; as printed, the question has no correct option and the physical answer is 2 N.

questions.question: “An object completely submerged in a fluid displaces its own volume of fluid”. This is:
questions.answer: (b) Archimedes' principle
questions.explanation: The statement is the volume part of Archimedes' principle, which goes on to say that the upthrust equals the weight of that displaced fluid. Pascal's principle deals with the transmission of pressure through an enclosed fluid, and Pascal's paradox shows that pressure in a liquid depends only on depth, so neither describes displacement. Since (b) is correct, (d) does not apply.

options.text: true, but none of the above

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Pascal's paradox  (b) Archimedes' principle  (c) Pascal's principle  (d) true, but none of the above

questions.question: Salt water has greater density than freshwater. A boat floats in both freshwater and saltwater. The buoyant force on the boat in salt water is ------------ that in freshwater.
questions.answer: (a) equal to
questions.explanation: The boat floats in both liquids, so in each case the upthrust balances its weight; the buoyant forces are therefore equal. Because salt water is denser, a smaller volume of it is displaced to provide that same weight, so the boat rides higher — the force itself is unchanged. Note that option (d) 'same as' duplicates the meaning of (a), so the printed options are ambiguous; both denote equality, and the key is (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) equal to  (b) smaller than  (c) larger than  (d) same as

questions.question: You fill a tall glass with ice and then add water to the level of the glass's rim, so some fraction of the ice floats above rim. When the ice melts, what's happens to the water level?
questions.answer: (c) the water level stays at the rim
questions.explanation: Floating ice displaces water whose weight equals the weight of the ice. When the ice melts it becomes exactly that much water, which occupies exactly the volume previously displaced, so the level is unchanged and nothing overflows. The density difference between ice and water only fixes the fraction of ice above the surface (about 8%), not the final level, so (d) is wrong.

options.text: the water level drops below the rim
the water level stays at the rim
it depends on the difference in density between water and ice

questions.optionsRaw: (a) the water overflows the rim  (b) the water level drops below the rim  (c) the water level stays at the rim  (d) it depends on the difference in density between water and ice
questions.correctAnswer: (c) the water level stays at the rim

questions.question: State Pascal's principle. Describe its two applications.
questions.answer:
Pascal's principle states that when pressure is applied to any part of a fluid enclosed in a vessel, it is transmitted equally in all directions and acts undiminished on every part of the vessel. It holds because a liquid is practically incompressible, so a pressure change at one point is passed on at once throughout the liquid.
Applications: (i) Hydraulic press or lift — a small force F₁ on a small piston of area A₁ creates a pressure p = F₁/A₁, which acts on a large piston of area A₂ and produces the large force F₂ = pA₂ = (A₂/A₁)F₁, so a heavy car can be raised by hand. (ii) Hydraulic brakes of a car — the pedal applies pressure to the brake fluid, which transmits it equally to the wheel cylinders at all four wheels, so all brakes act together and the braking is uniform.
questions.explanation: Pressure is transmitted undiminished (same Δp everywhere at the same level); it is the force, not the pressure, that is multiplied.

questions.question:
(a) Why must a liquid and not a gas be used as the 'fluid' in a hydraulic machine?
(b) On what other important property of a liquid do hydraulic machines depend?
questions.answer:
(a) A liquid is used because it is almost incompressible: its volume changes very little when pressure is applied, so the pressure applied at the pump is transmitted immediately and undiminished to the load, making the machine rigid and efficient. A gas is highly compressible; it would be compressed and store the applied energy as elastic energy, so the piston would move sluggishly and the force would not be transmitted faithfully, and the machine would be much less efficient.
(b) Hydraulic machines also depend on the liquid being able to flow freely and take the shape of its container, so that it fills every part of the system and reaches every surface, and on its transmitting pressure equally in all directions (Pascal's principle). Its low compressibility and freedom from leakage are the other essential properties.
questions.explanation: Incompressibility gives immediate, undiminished transmission; the ability to flow and fill the whole system is the second required property.

questions.question: Why don't ships made of iron sink?
questions.answer: A ship is not a solid block of iron: it is a hollow hull enclosing a large volume of air, so its average density (iron + air + cargo) is much less than the density of water (1000 kg/m³), even though iron itself has a density of about 7800 kg/m³. When the ship floats, it displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight (law of flotation). Because the average density is low, a volume of water smaller than the whole volume of the hull provides this weight, so part of the hull remains above the surface. A solid piece of iron sinks because it cannot displace a volume of water whose weight equals its own weight.
questions.explanation: It is the average density of the hollow hull, not the density of iron, that decides floating; a solid iron block of the same mass would sink.

questions.question: Why do you float higher in salt water than in fresh water?
questions.answer: Salt water is denser than fresh water (about 1025 kg/m³ against 1000 kg/m³). A floating body must displace a weight of liquid equal to its own weight, and since a given volume of salt water weighs more than the same volume of fresh water, a smaller volume of salt water is sufficient. Hence less of your body needs to be below the surface in the sea, so you float higher than in a river or lake. For the same reason a ship has a smaller draft in the sea, and ships are marked with load lines (Plimsoll marks) for fresh and salt water.
questions.explanation: Equality of upthrust with weight fixes the displaced WEIGHT, not the volume; the denser liquid needs less volume, so the body rides higher.

questions.question: What is the difference between being immersed and being submerged in water?
