questions.answer: A body is immersed in a liquid when it is partly or wholly within the liquid, so immersion includes the case in which only part of the body is under the free surface — for example a floating block or a hydrometer. A body is submerged when it is completely under the surface, i.e. wholly immersed, as a stone at the bottom of a beaker. Every submerged body is therefore immersed, but an immersed body need not be submerged. In the partly immersed case the upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the immersed part only; in the fully submerged case the displaced volume equals the entire volume of the body, so the upthrust is the maximum possible for that body.
questions.explanation: Submerged = completely under the surface; immersed = partly or completely. The displaced volume differs in the two cases.

questions.question: Define surface tension and give its any two applications.
questions.answer:
Surface tension is the force per unit length acting along the free surface of a liquid, perpendicular to any line drawn on the surface, which tends to contract the surface to the smallest possible area; it arises from the cohesive forces between liquid molecules, which make the surface behave like a stretched elastic membrane. Its SI unit is N/m, and it is numerically equal to the surface energy per unit area (J/m²).
Applications: (i) Capillary rise — water rises in a narrow tube (and in soil pores and lamp wicks) because surface tension pulls the liquid up the tube, which supplies water to plant roots. (ii) Small dense objects such as a needle, razor blade or water strider can rest on water because the surface film supports them; detergents lower the surface tension and make such floating impossible, which is also why they help in washing.
questions.explanation: T = F/L, caused by cohesion; it decreases when the liquid is heated or a detergent is added.

questions.question: A swimmer dives off a raft in a pool. Does the raft rise or sink in the water? What happens to the water level in the pool? Give reasons for your answer.
questions.answer:
While the swimmer stands on the raft, the raft and swimmer together displace water whose weight equals their combined weight. When he dives off, the raft is relieved of his weight, so it needs to displace less water and it rises a little in the water (it becomes less deeply submerged).
For the pool level: before diving, the swimmer's whole weight is supported by buoyancy, so the water displaced on his account weighs as much as he does. After diving, if he is wholly under water he displaces only his own volume of water, and that water weighs less than he does (a swimmer is slightly denser than water), so the total displaced volume decreases and the water level in the pool falls slightly. If he floats at the surface after diving, he still displaces his own weight of water and the level is practically unchanged.
questions.explanation: The pool level is decided by the total displaced VOLUME; a floating body displaces its weight, a submerged body only its volume.

questions.question: Distinguish between flotation and upthrust.
questions.answer:
Upthrust (buoyant force) is the net upward force that a fluid exerts on a body immersed in it. By Archimedes' principle it equals the weight of the fluid displaced, F_b = ρ_f V_f g, and it acts on every body in a fluid, whether floating or sinking.
Flotation is the state in which a body remains at rest at the free surface of a liquid. It occurs only when the upthrust just balances the body's weight, which requires the average density of the body to be equal to or less than that of the liquid.
Thus upthrust is a force (newtons) present whenever a body is in a fluid, while flotation is a condition of equilibrium at the surface. A stone at the bottom of a pond experiences upthrust but does not float; a wooden block floats because its weight is less than the upthrust on it when fully immersed.
questions.explanation: Upthrust is a force (always present in a fluid); flotation is the equilibrium state in which upthrust equals weight.

questions.question: Discuss buoyancy in liquids and gases.
questions.answer:
Buoyancy is the upward force that a fluid exerts on a body placed in it. It arises because the pressure in a fluid increases with depth, p = p₀ + ρgh. Consider a cylinder of cross-sectional area A and height l, wholly submerged with its axis vertical. The downward force on its top face is p₁A and the upward force on its bottom face is p₂A, where p₂ − p₁ = ρg l. The net upward force is therefore
F_b = (p₂ − p₁)A = ρg l A = ρV g,
which is exactly the weight of the fluid displaced by the body — Archimedes' principle. The buoyant force acts vertically upward through the centre of buoyancy, the centre of gravity of the displaced fluid.

In liquids: the upthrust reduces the apparent weight of a body, W_app = W − F_b. If the average density of the body is less than that of the liquid, the upthrust at full immersion exceeds its weight, so the body rises and floats, displacing its own weight of liquid — a ship, an iceberg, a hydrometer. If the density is greater, the body sinks, as a stone does in water. If the densities are equal, the body stays in equilibrium wherever it is placed in the liquid, as a trimmed submarine does.

In gases: the same principle holds, but because the density of air is small (about 1.29 kg/m³) the upthrust is small and is usually neglected for ordinary objects. It becomes important for light, large-volume bodies. A helium balloon of volume V experiences F_b = ρ_air V g while its weight is only ρ_He V g plus the fabric, so it rises; a hot-air balloon works in the same way because hot air is less dense than the surrounding cool air. The usable lift is (ρ_air − ρ_gas)Vg − W_structure, and the balloon rises until the average density of the whole balloon equals that of the surrounding air.
questions.explanation: Buoyancy comes from the pressure difference between the lower and upper faces; the same F_b = ρ_f V g applies in liquids and gases, only the fluid density differs.

questions.question: Describe law of flotation in liquids and gases.
questions.answer:
The law of flotation states that the weight of a floating body is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, and that a body floats in a fluid when its weight is equal to or less than the upthrust on it when it is completely immersed — that is, when the average density of the body is not greater than the density of the fluid.

Reasoning: a floating body is in equilibrium, so the vertical forces on it must balance, giving upthrust = weight. By Archimedes' principle the upthrust equals the weight of the displaced fluid, hence W_body = W_displaced fluid, or mg = ρ_f V_sub g. The immersed fraction of the body is therefore V_sub/V = ρ_body/ρ_fluid.

Examples in liquids: an iceberg of density 917 kg/m³ floats in sea water of density 1025 kg/m³ with about 90% of its volume below the surface; a steel ship floats because its hollow hull gives an average density (steel + air + cargo) below that of water, and it sinks deeper as cargo is loaded until the displaced weight again equals the total weight; a hydrometer floats at a depth that indicates the density of the liquid; a submarine dives by admitting water into its ballast tanks (raising its average density above that of water) and rises by blowing the tanks.

In gases the same law applies. A balloon floats in air when the weight of the air it displaces equals its own weight, i.e. when (ρ_air − ρ_gas)V = m_structure. A hot-air balloon rises while the air inside is hotter and lighter than outside and settles at the level where its average density equals that of the surrounding air; a helium balloon rises until the fabric and payload make its average density equal to that of air. This explains balloons, airships and the neutral buoyancy of weather balloons.
questions.explanation: The law follows from equilibrium (upthrust = weight) plus Archimedes' principle; the fraction submerged equals the ratio of densities.

questions.question: Discuss surface tension with at least three experiments.
questions.answer:
Surface tension is the property by which the free surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched elastic membrane. A molecule inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions by its neighbours, but a molecule at the surface has neighbours only below and at the sides, so there is a net inward pull. The surface therefore tends to contract to the least possible area. Surface tension T is defined as the force per unit length acting along the surface, perpendicular to any line drawn on it: T = F/L, measured in N/m; it equals the surface energy per unit area (J/m²) and decreases as the temperature rises.

Experiment 1 (floating needle). A dry steel needle or razor blade is gently laid on water. Although steel is several times denser than water, the surface film bends and supports it, the needle resting in a small depression. Its weight is balanced by the vertical component of the tension along the deformed surface. If a drop of detergent is added, T falls, the film can no longer support the needle and it sinks.

Experiment 2 (soap film on a wire frame). A rectangular wire frame with a sliding wire of length L is dipped in soap solution. The film has two surfaces, so a force F = 2TL must be applied to hold the slider. If the slider is moved a distance x, the work done is Fx = 2TLx = T × (increase of area), which shows that T is the surface energy per unit area. When released, the film pulls the slider back, proving the contractile nature of the surface.

Experiment 3 (capillary rise). When a clean glass tube of radius r is dipped in water, the water rises to a height h. The upward pull of surface tension round the circumference, 2πrT cos θ, supports the weight of the column πr²hρg, giving T = rhρg/(2 cos θ). The experiment both demonstrates surface tension and provides a method of measuring it; mercury, whose surface is convex, is depressed instead.

Everyday evidence includes the spherical shape of raindrops and soap bubbles (least area for a given volume) and the domed surface of water heaped above the rim of a glass.
questions.explanation: Each experiment must be described with what is observed and why; the soap-film experiment also shows T as energy per unit area.

questions.question: Explain Archimedes principle and find gold purity by using density.
questions.answer:
Archimedes' principle states that when a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it. For a body of volume V fully submerged in a fluid of density ρ_f, F_b = ρ_f V g, and the apparent weight is W_app = W_air − F_b. The principle follows from the increase of pressure with depth: the upward force on the lower surface of a submerged body exceeds the downward force on its upper surface by exactly the weight of the displaced fluid.

Gold purity by density. Pure gold has a density of 19,300 kg/m³, much greater than that of the usual adulterants (silver 10,500 kg/m³, copper 8900 kg/m³), so an alloy of gold with these metals has a smaller density than pure gold. The density of an ornament is found by weighing it twice:
(1) Weigh it in air, W_air, and in water, W_water; the loss of weight is the upthrust F_b = W_air − W_water.
(2) Volume V = F_b/(ρ_w g), with ρ_w = 1000 kg/m³.
(3) Density ρ = m/V = (W_air/g)/(F_b/ρ_w g) = W_air ρ_w/(W_air − W_water).
The ratio ρ/ρ_gold gives the fraction of pure gold, and 24 × that fraction gives the purity in carats.

Worked example: an ornament weighs 25.0 N in air and 23.7 N in water. Then F_b = 1.3 N, V = 1.3/(1000 × 9.8) = 1.33 × 10⁻⁴ m³, m = 25.0/9.8 = 2.55 kg, so ρ = 2.55/1.33 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.92 × 10⁴ kg/m³. Purity = 19,200/19,300 ≈ 0.995, i.e. about 99.5% (nearly 24 carat); an ornament of the same weight containing much silver would show a distinctly smaller density.

This is the method Archimedes is said to have used to test King Hiero's crown. Its limitation is that it measures the average density, so a hollow ornament can give a false low value.
questions.explanation: F_b = W_air − W_water gives the volume, and combined with the weight in air it gives the density; compare with 19,300 kg/m³ for pure gold.

questions.question: In a hydraulic press a force of 20 N is applied to a piston of area 0.20 m². The area of the other piston is 2.0 m². What is (a) the pressure transmitted through the fluid; (b) the force on the piston?
questions.answer:
Given: F₁ = 20 N; A₁ = 0.20 m²; A₂ = 2.0 m².
(a) Pressure transmitted:
Formula: p = F₁/A₁.
Substitution: p = 20/0.20.
Calculation: p = 100 Pa.
Result: p = 100 Pa.
(b) Force on the large piston:
Formula: F₂ = pA₂ (Pascal's principle).
Substitution: F₂ = 100 × 2.0.
Calculation: F₂ = 200 N.
Result: F₂ = 200 N.
The printed answer (200 N, 100 Pa) lists the two results in the reverse of the order asked, but the values agree.
questions.explanation: The pressure is the same at both pistons; the force ratio equals the area ratio (10), so 20 N becomes 200 N.

questions.question: The pressure in a water pipe in the ground floor of a building is 4 × 10⁵ Pa but three floors up it is only 2 × 10⁵ Pa. What is the height between the ground floor and the third floor? The water in the pipe may be assumed to be stationary; density of water = 1 × 10³ Kg/m³
questions.answer:
Given: p₁ = 4 × 10⁵ Pa; p₂ = 2 × 10⁵ Pa; ρ = 1 × 10³ kg/m³; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: p₁ − p₂ = ρgh, so h = (p₁ − p₂)/(ρg).
Substitution: h = (4 × 10⁵ − 2 × 10⁵)/(1 × 10³ × 9.8) = 2 × 10⁵/9800.
Calculation: h = 20.4 m.
Result: h ≈ 20 m, which agrees with the printed answer (20 m); the printed value corresponds to taking g = 10 m/s², which gives exactly 20 m.
questions.explanation: The fall of pressure with height in a stationary liquid is Δp = ρgh; using g = 10 gives the printed 20 m.

questions.question: The small piston of hydraulic press has an area of 10.0 cm². If the applied force is 50.0 N, what must the area of the large piston to exert a pressing force of 4800N?
questions.answer:
Given: A₁ = 10.0 cm²; F₁ = 50.0 N; F₂ = 4800 N.
Formula: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so A₂ = A₁F₂/F₁.
Substitution: A₂ = 10.0 × 4800/50.0.
Calculation: 4800/50.0 = 96; A₂ = 10.0 × 96 = 960 cm².
Result: A₂ = 960 cm², which agrees with the printed answer (960 cm²).
questions.explanation: Pascal's principle gives F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂; the areas may be left in cm² as long as both are in the same unit.

questions.question: Mechanical advantage of a hydraulic jack is 420. Find the weight of the heaviest automobile that can be lifted by an applied force of 55 N.
questions.answer:
Given: MA = 420; effort F = 55 N.
Formula: MA = load/effort, so load = MA × F.
Substitution: load = 420 × 55.
Calculation: load = 23,100 N.
Result: load = 2.31 × 10⁴ N. The printed answer (23000 N) is this value rounded to two significant figures; the exact product is 23,100 N.
questions.explanation: MA = load/effort, so the load is the effort multiplied by 420; note the printed value is rounded.

questions.question: A flat -bottom river barge is 30 ft wide, 85 ft long and 15 ft. deep, (a) how many m³ of water will displace while the top stays 1 m above the water.? (b) What load in tons will the barge contain under these conditions if the empty barge weighs 160 tons in dry dock?
questions.answer:
Given: width = 30 ft; length = 85 ft; depth = 15 ft; freeboard = 1 m ≈ 3 ft; empty barge = 160 tons; 1 ft³ of fresh water weighs 62.4 lb.
(a) With 1 m ≈ 3 ft above water, the submerged depth = 15 − 3 = 12 ft.
Formula: V = width × length × submerged depth.
Substitution: V = 30 × 85 × 12 = 30,600 ft³.
Calculation: 30,600 ft³ = 30,600 × 0.02832 = 866 m³ ≈ 3.1 × 10⁴ ft³.
Result: the barge displaces about 3.1 × 10⁴ ft³ (≈ 870 m³) of water, agreeing with the printed answer (3.1 × 10⁴ ft³).
(b) Weight of the displaced water = 30,600 × 62.4 = 1.91 × 10⁶ lb = 955 tons (1 ton = 2000 lb). By the law of flotation this equals the weight of the barge plus its load.
Calculation: load = 955 − 160 = 795 tons ≈ 800 tons.
Result: load ≈ 800 tons, agreeing with the printed answer (800 tons).
Note: taking 1 m = 3.281 ft exactly would give a submerged depth of 11.72 ft, V = 2.99 × 10⁴ ft³ (846 m³) and a load of about 686 metric tonnes (755 short tons); the printed values follow from the 1 m ≈ 3 ft approximation and short tons.
questions.explanation: Volume of displaced water = submerged volume; the load is the weight of that water minus the empty weight of the barge, with 1 ton taken as 2000 lb.

questions.question: A canal lock gate is 20 m wide and 10 m deep. Calculate the thrust acting on it assuming that the water in the canal is in level with the top of the gate. Density of water is 1000 kg/m³
questions.answer:
Given: width b = 20 m; depth h = 10 m; ρ = 1000 kg/m³; g = 9.8 m/s². The water surface is level with the top of the gate, so the pressure rises from 0 at the top to ρgh at the bottom.
Formula: average pressure p_av = ρg(h/2); thrust F = p_av × area = ρg(h/2)(bh) = ½ρgbh².
Substitution: F = ½ × 1000 × 9.8 × 20 × (10)².
Calculation: F = 0.5 × 1000 × 9.8 × 20 × 100 = 9.8 × 10⁶ N.
Result: F = 9.8 × 10⁶ N (about 1000 tonnes weight). The printed answer (9.8 × 10⁴ N) is too small by a factor of 100 — it corresponds to a gate area of only 2 m². With b = 20 m and h = 10 m the thrust must be 9.8 × 10⁶ N.
questions.explanation: The pressure varies linearly with depth, so use the average pressure at mid-depth (½ρgh) multiplied by the gate area bh.

questions.question: A tank 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2 m deep is filled to the brim with paraffin (density 800 kg /m³). Calculate the pressure on the base? What is the thrust on the base?
questions.answer:
Given: length = 4 m; width = 3 m; depth h = 2 m; ρ = 800 kg/m³; g = 9.8 m/s².
Pressure on the base:
Formula: p = ρgh.
Substitution: p = 800 × 9.8 × 2.
Calculation: p = 15,680 Pa ≈ 1.6 × 10⁴ Pa.
Result: p ≈ 1.6 × 10⁴ Pa, agreeing with the printed answer (16000 Pa), which is obtained with g = 10 m/s².
Thrust on the base:
Formula: F = pA, with A = 4 × 3 = 12 m².
Substitution: F = 15,680 × 12.
Calculation: F = 1.88 × 10⁵ N ≈ 1.9 × 10⁵ N.
Result: F ≈ 1.9 × 10⁵ N. The printed thrust (19200 N) is too small by a factor of 10: 16,000 × 12 = 192,000 N = 1.92 × 10⁵ N.
questions.explanation: Pressure depends only on depth (ρgh), while the thrust is that pressure multiplied by the base area; check the power of ten in the printed thrust.

questions.question: A rectangular boat is 4.0 m wide, 8.0 m long, and 3.0 m deep. (a) How much water will it displace if the top stays 1.0 m above the water? (b) What load will the boat contain under these conditions if the empty boat weighs 8.60×10⁴ N in dry dock? (Weight density of water = 9800 N/m³)
questions.answer:
Given: width 4.0 m; length 8.0 m; depth 3.0 m; freeboard 1.0 m; empty weight 8.60 × 10⁴ N; weight density of water 9800 N/m³.
(a) Submerged depth = 3.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 m.
Formula: V = width × length × submerged depth.
Substitution: V = 4.0 × 8.0 × 2.0.
Calculation: V = 64.0 m³.
Result: V = 64.0 m³, which agrees with the printed answer (64.0 m³).
(b) Formula: upthrust = weight density × V; load weight = upthrust − empty weight.
Substitution: upthrust = 9800 × 64.0 = 6.272 × 10⁵ N; load = 6.272 × 10⁵ − 8.60 × 10⁴.
Calculation: load = 5.41 × 10⁵ N.
Result: load = 5.41 × 10⁵ N, which agrees with the printed answer (5.41 × 10⁵ N).
questions.explanation: The displaced volume uses only the submerged part of the hull; the load is the upthrust minus the weight of the empty boat.

questions.question: A hot air balloon has a volume of 2200 m³. The density of air at temperature of 20 °C is 1.205 kg/m³. The density of the hot air inside the balloon at a temperature of 100 °C is 0.946 kg / m³. How much weight can the hot air can lift?
questions.answer:
Given: V = 2200 m³; density of cool air ρ_c = 1.205 kg/m³; density of hot air ρ_h = 0.946 kg/m³; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula: upthrust (weight of displaced cool air) = ρ_c V g; weight of the hot air inside = ρ_h V g; lift = (ρ_c − ρ_h)Vg.
Substitution: upthrust = 1.205 × 2200 × 9.8; hot-air weight = 0.946 × 2200 × 9.8.
Calculation: upthrust = 25,980 N; hot-air weight = 20,396 N; lift = 5584 N ≈ 5.59 × 10³ N (a mass of about 570 kg).
Result: the balloon can lift about 5.59 × 10³ N, agreeing with the printed answer (5590 N); the small difference comes from taking g = 9.81 m/s² in the printed value.
questions.explanation: Lift equals the difference between the upthrust on the balloon and the weight of the hot air inside; the payload is not included in this figure.

questions.question: A spherical balloon has a radius of 7.15 m and is filled with helium. How large a cargo can it lift, assuming that the skin and structure of the balloon have a mass of 930 kg? Neglect the buoyant force on the cargo volume itself.
questions.answer:
Given: r = 7.15 m; mass of skin and structure m_s = 930 kg; density of air ρ_air = 1.29 kg/m³; density of helium ρ_He = 0.179 kg/m³.
Formula: V = (4/3)πr³; cargo mass = (ρ_air − ρ_He)V − m_s; cargo weight = cargo mass × g.
Substitution: V = (4/3) × π × (7.15)³ = 1531 m³; cargo mass = (1.29 − 0.179) × 1531 − 930 = 1701 − 930.
Calculation: cargo mass = 771 kg; cargo weight = 771 × 9.8 = 7.56 × 10³ N.
Result: the balloon can lift about 7.7 × 10² kg, i.e. 7.6 × 10³ N. The printed answer (920 kg, 9 × 10³ N) is about 19% larger; it follows only if the density of helium is taken as about 0.09 kg/m³ instead of 0.179 kg/m³. With the standard densities used above the cargo is ≈ 770 kg.
questions.explanation: The net lift is the upthrust on the whole balloon minus the weight of the helium and of the structure; the helium mass must not be omitted.

questions.question: For an incompressible fluid, the flow rate is
questions.answer: (b) constant throughout the pipe.
questions.explanation: In steady flow of an incompressible fluid the mass entering any section per second equals the mass leaving it; since the density is constant, the volume flow rate Q = A v must be the same at every cross-section. So the flow rate is constant along the pipe, although the speed changes from place to place. Options (a) and (c) confuse flow rate with speed or with area, and (d) is wrong because a definite answer exists.

options.text: greater for the larger parts of the pipe.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) equal for all surfaces.  (b) constant throughout the pipe.  (c) greater for the larger parts of the pipe.  (d) none of the above

questions.question: Bernoulli's principle states that for horizontal flow of a fluid through a tube, the sum of the pressure and energy of motion per unit volume is
questions.answer: (c) constant
questions.explanation: For steady horizontal flow the height term is the same at both points, so Bernoulli's equation reduces to P + ½ρv² = constant; this sum is the pressure plus the kinetic energy per unit volume. It is constant along the tube, not increasing, decreasing or varying with time, because steady flow means the velocity at each point does not change with time.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) increasing with time  (b) decreasing with time  (c) constant  (d) varying with time

questions.question: Which of the following is associated with the law of conservation of energy in fluids?
questions.answer: (b) Bernoulli's principle
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation is obtained by applying the work-energy theorem to a moving fluid: the work done by the pressure forces appears as change of kinetic plus potential energy per unit volume, so it is conservation of energy written for a fluid. Archimedes' and Pascal's principles belong to fluid statics, and the equation of continuity follows from conservation of mass, not energy.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Archimedes' principle  (b) Bernoulli's principle  (c) Pascal's principle  (d) equation of continuity

questions.question: As the speed of a moving fluid increases, the pressure in the fluid
questions.answer: (c) decreases
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant requires that at the same height an increase of speed v be accompanied by a decrease of pressure P, because the sum of the two terms stays constant. The pressure therefore falls as the fluid speeds up; it does not rise or stay constant, and viscosity only causes an extra loss of energy, it does not reverse this relation for ideal streamline flow.

options.text: may increase or decrease, depending on the viscosity

questions.optionsRaw: (a) increases  (b) remains constant  (c) decreases  (d) may increase or decrease, depending on the viscosity

questions.question: If the cross-sectional area of a pipe decreases, what happens to the fluid velocity?
questions.answer: (a) Increases
questions.explanation: By the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ for an incompressible fluid, the product of area and speed must stay constant, so a smaller area forces a larger speed for the same volume flow rate. This is why water from a partly closed tap or a nozzle comes out faster. Density cancels out of the incompressible continuity equation, so the answer does not depend on it.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Increases  (b) Decreases  (c) Remains the same  (d) Depends on the fluid density

questions.question: A sky diver falls through the air at terminal velocity. The force of air resistance on him is
questions.answer: (b) equal to his weight
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity is the constant speed reached when the upward drag has grown until it exactly balances the downward weight, so the net force and hence the acceleration are zero. At that stage the air resistance equals his weight, not half or twice it, and it can be determined because the motion is stated to be at terminal velocity.

options.text: Cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) half his weight  (b) equal to his weight  (c) twice his weight  (d) Cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.question: Wind speeding up as it blows over the top of a hill
questions.answer: (b) decreases atmospheric pressure there.
questions.explanation: The air is forced to speed up as it crosses the hill, and along a streamline at nearly the same height Bernoulli's equation gives P + ½ρv² = constant; a larger v therefore means a smaller P. This low pressure over the crest explains why strong winds on hill tops are associated with reduced pressure and why roofs can be lifted in a gale. Options (a), (c) and (d) ignore the link between speed and pressure.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Increases atmospheric pressure there.  (b) decreases atmospheric pressure there.  (c) doesn't affect atmospheric pressure there.  (d) equal's atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: A fluid is undergoing “incompressible” flow. This means that:
questions.answer: (e) the density cannot change with time or location
questions.explanation: Incompressible means the volume of a given mass of fluid cannot be squeezed, so its density stays the same as it moves and as time passes; that is option (e). Options (a) and (b) define steady flow, option (c) describes uniform flow, and option (d) would mean no pressure differences at all, so none of them is what incompressibility means.

options.text: the pressure at a given point cannot change with time
the velocity at a given point cannot change with time
the velocity must be the same everywhere
the pressure must be the same everywhere
the density cannot change with time or location

questions.optionsRaw: (a) the pressure at a given point cannot change with time  (b) the velocity at a given point cannot change with time  (c) the velocity must be the same everywhere  (d) the pressure must be the same everywhere  (e) the density cannot change with time or location
questions.correctAnswer: (e) the density cannot change with time or location

questions.question: A fluid is undergoing steady flow. Therefore:
questions.answer: (c) the velocity at any given point does not vary with time
questions.explanation: Steady flow means the velocity field is independent of time: at a fixed point in space the speed and direction are always the same, though the fluid elements passing through may be speeding up or slowing down elsewhere. A given molecule can change its velocity as it moves to a new point (a), and neither the pressure (b) nor the density (d) has to be uniform in steady flow.

options.text: the velocity of any given molecule of fluid does not change
the pressure does not vary from point to point
the velocity at any given point does not vary with time
the density does not vary from point to point

questions.optionsRaw: (a) the velocity of any given molecule of fluid does not change  (b) the pressure does not vary from point to point  (c) the velocity at any given point does not vary with time  (d) the density does not vary from point to point
questions.correctAnswer: (c) the velocity at any given point does not vary with time

questions.question: The equation of continuity for fluid flow can be derived from the conservation of:
questions.answer: (b) mass
questions.explanation: The continuity equation ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂ states that the mass of fluid crossing every section per second is the same, which is conservation of mass for a steady flow with no sources or sinks. Conservation of energy gives Bernoulli's equation instead. Conservation of volume holds only as a consequence of constant density in an incompressible fluid, and pressure is not a conserved quantity.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) energy  (b) mass  (c) volume  (d) pressure

questions.question: What is difference between streamline and turbulent flow?
questions.answer: In streamline (laminar) flow every particle that passes a given point follows the same path and has the same velocity as the particles before it, so the motion is smooth, orderly and can be drawn as streamlines that never cross. In turbulent flow the velocity at a point changes irregularly with time, eddies and whirlpools appear and the streamlines break up and cross one another. Laminar flow occurs at low speed, high viscosity and low Reynolds number (Re below about 1000 in a pipe); turbulent flow occurs at high speed, low viscosity and Re above about 2000. Laminar flow needs only a small driving pressure, while turbulent flow offers much greater resistance to motion because of the eddies, and it mixes the fluid rapidly.
questions.explanation: Key contrast: in laminar flow the velocity at each point is constant in time and streamlines do not cross; in turbulent flow the velocity fluctuates randomly and eddies form. A common mistake is to say laminar flow has no viscosity.

questions.question: Would a drinking straw work in space where there is no gravity? Explain.
questions.answer: Yes, provided the spacecraft cabin still contains air at normal pressure. A straw works by a pressure difference, not by gravity: sucking lowers the pressure in the mouth, and the greater pressure of the surrounding air on the free surface of the drink pushes the liquid up the straw. Gravity actually opposes the rise, because the liquid has to be lifted through a height h (a pressure ρgh is needed), so its absence makes drinking easier. The practical problem is that without gravity the liquid does not settle at the bottom of the container but floats about as globules, so it may not stay around the lower end of the straw. If the straw is inside an enclosed drink bag, an astronaut can drink normally; in the vacuum outside the cabin there would be no pressure to push the liquid and the straw would not work.
questions.explanation: Common mistake: thinking suction pulls the liquid. The liquid is pushed up by the external (cabin) pressure acting on its free surface; gravity is not required and actually hinders the rise.

questions.question: Why do airplanes take off into wind?
questions.answer: An aircraft takes off into the wind so that the speed of air relative to its wings is the ground speed plus the wind speed. Lift depends on the airspeed over the wing, L = ½ρ(v_top² − v_bottom²)A, and not on the ground speed. With a headwind the wing already experiences a high airspeed while the aircraft is still moving slowly along the runway, so the lift needed to leave the ground is produced at a lower ground speed; the take-off run is therefore shorter and the aircraft can clear obstacles sooner. The headwind also gives better steering and control at low ground speed. For the same reason aircraft land into the wind, which lowers the touchdown speed and shortens the landing run.
questions.explanation: Key point: lift depends on airspeed relative to the wing, not ground speed. A headwind adds to the airspeed, so the required lift is reached at a smaller ground speed and the runway needed is shorter.

questions.question: Describe terminal velocity in liquids.
questions.answer: When a body falls through a liquid, three forces act on it: its weight W downwards, the buoyant force U upwards and the viscous drag F upwards. The drag increases with speed according to Stokes' law, F = 6πηrv. At first W is greater than U + F, so the body accelerates; as its speed grows the drag grows too, until W = U + F and the net force becomes zero. From then on the body moves with a constant maximum speed called its terminal velocity. For a sphere, v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), so the terminal velocity increases with the square of the radius and with the difference of densities, and decreases as the viscosity increases. This is why a steel ball sinks quickly in water while a tiny air bubble rises slowly, and why raindrops reach only a few metres per second.
questions.explanation: Essential point: terminal velocity is reached when weight = buoyancy + drag, so the acceleration is zero although the body still moves. The strong r² dependence is often forgotten.

questions.question: Discuss the significance of Reynolds number.
questions.answer: The Reynolds number Re = ρvd/η = vd/ν is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow, and being dimensionless it characterises the flow itself rather than any particular fluid. Its main significance is that it predicts whether the flow will be laminar or turbulent: for flow through a pipe, Re below about 1000 gives steady laminar flow, Re above about 2000 gives turbulent flow, and in between the flow is unstable. A large Re (high speed, large pipe, low viscosity) means inertia dominates and eddies form, while a small Re means viscosity damps out disturbances. Engineers use Re to design pipes, pumps, aircraft and ships, and to test scale models, because two flows with the same Re behave in the same way (dynamic similarity).
questions.explanation: Key idea: Re = ρvd/η compares inertial with viscous forces; it is dimensionless, and the laminar-to-turbulent transition occurs near a critical value of about 2000 for pipe flow.

questions.question: State Bernoulli's principle.
questions.answer: Bernoulli's principle states that for the steady, streamline flow of an incompressible and non-viscous fluid, the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is constant at every point along a streamline: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. The three terms are called the static pressure, the dynamic pressure ½ρv² and the potential term ρgh, and their sum is the total pressure. Equivalently, where the fluid moves faster its pressure is lower, and where it moves slower its pressure is higher. The principle is a statement of the conservation of energy per unit volume for a flowing fluid, and it holds only for steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow along a streamline.
questions.explanation: State the equation P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant together with its conditions: steady, streamline, incompressible, non-viscous flow. Forgetting the assumptions is the usual mistake.

questions.question: Give two applications of Bernoulli's principle.
questions.answer: Two applications are the atomizer and the venturi meter. In an atomizer, air is blown across the top of a vertical tube dipping into a liquid; the fast air lowers the pressure above the tube, and the atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface in the bottle pushes the liquid up the tube, where the air stream breaks it into a fine spray. In a venturi meter the fluid is forced through a narrow throat; by continuity its speed rises and by Bernoulli's principle its pressure falls, and measuring the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat gives the flow rate from ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). The same principle explains the lift on an aerofoil, the action of a filter pump or Bunsen burner, the draught in a chimney and the swing of a spinning ball.
questions.explanation: Each application must show the chain: constriction or spin gives higher speed, higher speed gives lower pressure, and the pressure difference produces the observed effect.

questions.question: ‘Fluid flow is turbulent rather than laminar’, support this statement.
questions.answer: In everyday situations the Reynolds number of a flow is usually far above the critical value, so turbulence is the rule rather than the exception. Water flowing at only 1 m/s through a 5 cm pipe has Re = ρvd/η ≈ 1000 × 1 × 0.05/10⁻³ = 5 × 10⁴, twenty-five times the critical value of about 2000, so eddies are bound to appear. Rivers, winds, smoke plumes, ocean currents and blood in the aorta are all turbulent. Rough internal surfaces, bends, valves and sudden changes of cross-section trip the flow into turbulence, and high speed or low viscosity makes it even more likely. Laminar flow survives only in narrow tubes, at low speeds, or in very viscous liquids such as honey and glycerine. Turbulence also mixes the fluid and greatly increases the resistance to motion, which is why it dominates practical designs.
questions.explanation: Support the statement with high Reynolds numbers, roughness, sudden changes of section, high speed and low viscosity, and with concrete examples such as rivers, smoke and blood flow.

questions.question: Discuss importance of Stokes law.
questions.answer: Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid: F = 6πηrv. It is important for several reasons. It allows the terminal velocity of raindrops, dust particles, blood cells and sedimenting particles to be calculated, which explains why fine dust stays suspended for hours while sand settles quickly. It is the basis of the falling-sphere (Stokes) viscometer, in which the measured terminal speed of a steel ball gives the coefficient of viscosity of a liquid. It is also used in the analysis of sedimentation and centrifugation, in the design of filters and in Millikan's oil-drop experiment, where the drag on a charged droplet allows its charge to be found. The law is valid only for a smooth sphere, laminar flow and low Reynolds number, but it is the starting point for the theory of motion through a viscous medium.
questions.explanation: Key formula F = 6πηrv. Its importance lies in measuring viscosity, terminal velocity, sedimentation and the charge of an electron in Millikan's experiment.

questions.question: Justify spin of ball in Bernoulli’s principle.
questions.answer: When a ball spins as it moves through the air, the layer of air next to its surface is dragged round with it by friction. On one side of the ball the surface moves in the same direction as the air stream, so the relative speed of the air there is increased; on the opposite side the surface moves against the stream, so the relative speed is decreased. By Bernoulli's principle, P + ½ρv² = constant, the pressure is lower on the side where the air moves faster. The resulting pressure difference produces a net sideways force, which pushes the ball towards the low-pressure side. This is called the Magnus effect. It explains why a spinning cricket or football curves in flight, why a table-tennis ball with top spin dips, and why a golf ball with back spin gains lift.
questions.explanation: Magnus effect: spin makes the relative air speed higher on one side, so by Bernoulli's principle the pressure there is lower and the ball is pushed sideways towards that side.

questions.question: Derive equation of continuity. Also show its physical significance.
questions.answer:
Consider a tube of varying cross-section through which a fluid flows steadily. Let A₁ and A₂ be the areas of two sections, v₁ and v₂ the speeds of the fluid there and ρ₁ and ρ₂ the densities. In a small time Δt the mass entering at section 1 is Δm₁ = ρ₁A₁v₁Δt and the mass leaving at section 2 is Δm₂ = ρ₂A₂v₂Δt. Since the flow is steady, no fluid accumulates between the sections, so conservation of mass requires Δm₁ = Δm₂, giving ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂. This is the equation of continuity. For an incompressible fluid ρ₁ = ρ₂, and therefore A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, or A v = constant = Q.
Physical significance: (i) it is the law of conservation of mass written for a flowing fluid; (ii) the volume flow rate Q is the same at every cross-section of the tube; (iii) the speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, which is why water speeds up when the end of a hose is partly closed and why a river slows down where it widens; (iv) it is the basis of the design of nozzles, carburettors and venturi meters and of the study of blood flow, where the aorta branches into billions of capillaries of very large total area, so the blood slows to a few mm/s. For a gas the density term must be kept, giving ρ A v = constant.
questions.explanation: Key idea: conservation of mass for steady flow. For an incompressible fluid A v = constant, so the speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

questions.question: Derive Bernoulli’s equation.
questions.answer:
Assumptions: the flow is steady and streamline, the fluid is incompressible and non-viscous, and we follow a fixed mass of fluid along a streamline.
Consider a pipe whose cross-section and height change, and follow a volume ΔV of fluid from point 1 (area A₁, pressure P₁, speed v₁, height h₁) to point 2 (area A₂, pressure P₂, speed v₂, height h₂). The mass of this element is Δm = ρΔV.
Work done by pressure forces: the fluid behind section 1 pushes the element forward through Δx₁, doing work P₁A₁Δx₁ = P₁ΔV, while the fluid ahead of section 2 pushes back through Δx₂, doing work −P₂A₂Δx₂ = −P₂ΔV. Net work by pressure, W = (P₁ − P₂)ΔV.
Change in kinetic energy: ΔK = ½Δm(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ρΔV(v₂² − v₁²).
Change in potential energy: ΔU = Δm g(h₂ − h₁) = ρΔV g(h₂ − h₁).
By the work-energy theorem the net work equals the change in mechanical energy:
(P₁ − P₂)ΔV = ½ρΔV(v₂² − v₁²) + ρΔV g(h₂ − h₁).
Dividing throughout by ΔV and rearranging,
P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂,
that is, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline. This is Bernoulli's equation.
The three terms are the pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume, so the equation is a statement of conservation of energy for a flowing fluid. For horizontal flow (h₁ = h₂) it reduces to P + ½ρv² = constant: where the fluid moves faster the pressure is lower, which explains aerofoil lift, the atomizer, the venturi meter and the swing of a spinning ball. The equation neglects viscous losses, compressibility and turbulence, so it applies only to steady, streamline flow of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid.
questions.explanation: Key idea: apply the work-energy theorem to a volume ΔV of fluid; the net pressure work (P₁ − P₂)ΔV equals the change in kinetic plus potential energy per unit volume.

questions.question: Discuss viscous force in fluids.
questions.answer:
When a real fluid flows, adjacent layers move with different speeds, so there is relative motion between them. Because of the cohesive forces between molecules and the exchange of molecules between neighbouring layers, each layer exerts a tangential frictional force on the layer next to it which opposes their relative motion. This internal friction is called the viscous force.
For laminar flow between two parallel layers of area A separated by a distance dx and moving with a velocity difference dv, Newton's law of viscosity gives F = ηA(dv/dx), where dv/dx is the velocity gradient and η is the coefficient of viscosity. Its SI unit is Pa·s (N·s m⁻²) and it is a measure of the resistance of a fluid to flow: honey and glycerine have large viscosities, water and air much smaller ones. In liquids η decreases as the temperature rises because the cohesive forces weaken, whereas in gases η increases with temperature because the molecular momentum transfer becomes faster.
Viscous force is responsible for the parabolic velocity profile of flow in a pipe, for the drag on a body moving through a fluid (Stokes' law F = 6πηrv for a sphere) and hence for terminal velocity, and for the pressure drop along a pipe. It converts mechanical energy into heat, and it must be overcome in pumping, lubrication and the flow of blood through fine vessels.
questions.explanation: Key idea: Newton's law of viscosity F = ηA(dv/dx). Viscosity is internal friction between adjacent layers of the fluid, caused by cohesion and molecular interchange, not merely friction with the pipe wall.

questions.question: Define fluid dynamics and explain its significance in the study of fluids. How does it differ from fluid statics?
questions.answer:
Fluid dynamics is the branch of fluid mechanics that deals with fluids in motion: with the velocity, pressure and energy of a flowing fluid and with the forces that cause or resist the flow. Its basic tools are the equation of continuity (conservation of mass), Bernoulli's equation (conservation of energy) and the laws of viscosity and turbulence.
Its significance is very wide. It allows the flow of water, oil and gas in pipes, nozzles and pumps to be calculated and the required pipe sizes and pumping powers to be designed. It explains the lift on aircraft wings, the swing of a spinning ball, and the working of carburettors, atomizers, venturi meters and filter pumps. It describes the circulation of blood, the flow of rivers, ocean currents and weather systems, and it is essential in the design of ships, cars, dams, turbines and aeroplanes. Without fluid dynamics the safe and efficient transport of water, fuel and air would be impossible.
Fluid statics, on the other hand, deals with fluids at rest. It uses pressure, Pascal's law, Archimedes' principle and the result that pressure depends only on depth, P = hρg. In a static fluid there is no relative motion of layers, so there are no shear or viscous forces and only normal pressure acts. In fluid dynamics the fluid is moving, viscous shear appears and the pressure is no longer fixed by depth alone: Bernoulli's equation shows that pressure also depends on speed. Fluid statics is therefore the special case of fluid dynamics with v = 0.
questions.explanation: Key distinction: statics treats fluids at rest, where pressure depends only on depth and there are no shear forces; dynamics treats moving fluids, where viscosity and speed-dependent pressure must be included.

questions.question: Discuss the concept of Reynolds number and its significance in fluid dynamics. Explain how Reynolds number relates to the transition between laminar and turbulent flow.
questions.answer:
The Reynolds number is a dimensionless parameter defined by Re = ρvd/η = vd/ν, where ρ is the density of the fluid, v the speed of flow, d the diameter of the pipe (or some other characteristic length) and η the coefficient of viscosity; ν = η/ρ is the kinematic viscosity. It represents the ratio of the inertial forces (of order ρv²d²) to the viscous forces (of order ηvd), and therefore indicates which of the two dominates the flow.
Its significance is that it characterises the flow rather than the particular fluid. Small Re means viscous forces dominate: disturbances are damped out and the flow is smooth and laminar. Large Re means inertial forces dominate: disturbances grow, eddies form and the flow becomes turbulent. Because Re is dimensionless, two flows with the same Re behave similarly even if they involve different fluids and different sizes; this is the principle of dynamic similarity, used to test scale models of aircraft, ships and dams in wind tunnels and towing tanks.
For flow through a straight pipe the transition occurs as follows. For Re below about 1000 the flow is laminar and Poiseuille's law holds. Between about 1000 and 2000 the flow is unstable: a small disturbance neither dies out nor grows. Above about 2000 the flow becomes turbulent, with random velocity fluctuations, eddies and a much larger resistance. In Reynolds' classic experiment, dye injected into the stream first moves as a straight thread (laminar), then wavers, and finally breaks up and mixes throughout the pipe (turbulent) as the speed, and hence Re, is increased.
questions.explanation: Key idea: Re = ρvd/η compares inertial and viscous forces. Laminar flow at low Re, turbulent flow above the critical value (about 2000 for pipe flow), with an unstable transition region in between.

questions.question: Two spherical raindrops of equal size are falling through air at a velocity of 0.08 m/s. If the drops join together forming a large spherical drop, what will be the new terminal velocity?
questions.answer:
Given:
Two equal spherical drops, each at terminal velocity v = 0.08 m/s, merge into a single spherical drop.
Formula:
At terminal velocity v_t ∝ r² (Stokes' law), and the volume is conserved: (4/3)πR³ = 2 × (4/3)πr³, so R = 2^(1/3) r.
Substitution:
v′ = v (R/r)² = 0.08 × (2^(1/3))² = 0.08 × 2^(2/3).
Calculation:
2^(2/3) = 1.587, so v′ = 0.08 × 1.587 = 0.127 m/s.
Result:
v′ ≈ 0.13 m/s, which agrees with the printed answer (0.13 m/s).
questions.explanation: Key relation: terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, and joining two equal drops gives R = 2^(1/3) r, so the speed increases by the factor 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59.

questions.question: Calculate the viscous drag on a drop of oil of 0.1 mm radius falling through air at tis terminal velocity. (Viscosity of air = 1.8×10⁻⁵ Pa. s; density of oil = 850 kg / m³)
questions.answer:
Given:
r = 0.1 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m; η(air) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s; ρ(oil) = 850 kg/m³; the density of air is negligible.
Formula:
Terminal velocity v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η); Stokes' drag F = 6πηrv_t.
Substitution:
v_t = 2(1.0 × 10⁻⁴)²(850)(9.8)/(9 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵); F = 6π(1.8 × 10⁻⁵)(1.0 × 10⁻⁴)(1.03).
Calculation:
v_t = (2 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ × 8330)/(1.62 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.03 m/s;
F = 6 × 3.1416 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.03 = 3.49 × 10⁻⁸ N.
Result:
F ≈ 3.49 × 10⁻⁸ N, in agreement with the printed 3.48 × 10⁻⁸ N (the small difference is only round-off).
Check: at terminal velocity the drag must equal the weight, (4/3)πr³ρg = (4/3)π(10⁻⁴)³(850)(9.8) = 3.49 × 10⁻⁸ N, which confirms the result.
questions.explanation: Key step: first find the terminal speed from Stokes' law, v_t = 2r²ρg/(9η), then use F = 6πηrv_t; at terminal velocity the drag also equals the weight, which provides a check.

questions.question: What area must a heating duct have if air moving 3.0 m/s along it can replenish the air every 15 minutes in a room of volume 300 m³. Assume air density remains constant.
questions.answer:
Given:
V = 300 m³; t = 15 min = 900 s; v = 3.0 m/s.
Formula:
Volume flow rate Q = V/t; from Q = A v, A = Q/v; for a circular duct, d = √(4A/π).
Substitution:
Q = 300/900 = 0.333 m³/s; A = 0.333/3.0; d = √(4 × 0.111/3.1416).
Calculation:
A = 0.111 m² ≈ 0.11 m²; d = √0.1415 = 0.376 m.
Result:
A ≈ 0.11 m² and d ≈ 0.38 m. The printed area (0.11 m²) agrees; the printed value 0.33 m for the diameter is a book error, since 0.33 m is √A (the side of a square duct), not the diameter of a circular one. Discrepancy noted.
questions.explanation: Key formulas: Q = V/t and Q = A v. Check the second printed answer with d = √(4A/π); it gives 0.38 m, not the printed 0.33 m.

questions.question: Water circulates throughout a house in a hot-water heating system. If the water is pumped at a speed of 0.50 m/s through a 4.0 cm diameter pipe in the basement under a pressure of 3.0 atm, what will be the flow speed and pressure in a 2.6 cm diameter pipe on the second floor 5.0 m above? Assume the pipes do not divide into branches.
questions.answer:
Given:
d₁ = 4.0 cm, v₁ = 0.50 m/s, P₁ = 3.0 atm; d₂ = 2.6 cm; h₂ − h₁ = 5.0 m; ρ = 1000 kg/m³; 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
Formula:
Continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = v₁(d₁/d₂)².
Bernoulli P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂.
Substitution:
v₂ = 0.50 × (4.0/2.6)² = 0.50 × 2.367;
P₂ = P₁ − ρg(h₂ − h₁) + ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²)
= 3.0 − (1000 × 9.8 × 5.0)/(1.01 × 10⁵) + 500(0.25 − 1.40)/(1.01 × 10⁵) atm.
Calculation:
v₂ = 1.18 m/s ≈ 1.2 m/s;
P₂ = 3.0 − 0.485 − 0.006 = 2.51 atm.
Result:
v₂ ≈ 1.2 m/s and P₂ ≈ 2.5 atm, agreeing with the printed (1.2 m/s, 2.5 atm). The pressure drops because the water gains kinetic energy and is lifted 5.0 m.
questions.explanation: Use continuity for the speed and Bernoulli for the pressure; the pressure falls by ρgΔh ≈ 0.48 atm for the height and by a small ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) term for the speed increase.

questions.question: What is the volume rate of flow of water from a 1.85 cm diameter faucet if the pressure head is 12 m?
questions.answer:
Given:
d = 1.85 cm = 1.85 × 10⁻² m; pressure head h = 12 m; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula:
Speed of efflux v = √(2gh); volume flow rate Q = A v = (πd²/4)v.
Substitution:
v = √(2 × 9.8 × 12) = √235.2; A = π(1.85 × 10⁻²)²/4.
Calculation:
v = 15.3 m/s; A = 2.69 × 10⁻⁴ m²;
Q = 2.69 × 10⁻⁴ × 15.3 = 4.12 × 10⁻³ m³/s.
Result:
Q ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻³ m³/s (about 4.1 L/s). The printed answer is 4.6 × 10⁻³ m³/s, which is about 11% larger and is not obtained from the printed data; it would require a head of about 15 m or a diameter of about 1.95 cm. Discrepancy noted.
questions.explanation: Key formulas: Torricelli's law v = √(2gh) and Q = A v. The printed value 4.6 × 10⁻³ m³/s does not follow from d = 1.85 cm and h = 12 m.

questions.question: The stream of water emerging from a faucet ‘neck down’ as it falls. The cross-sectional area is 1.2 cm² and 0.35 cm². The two levels are separated by a vertical distance of 45 mm as shown in figure. At what rate does water flow from the tap? [The tap's opening has area 1.2 cm², the lower section of the stream has area 0.35 cm², and the two levels are 45 mm apart.]
questions.answer:
Given:
A₁ = 1.2 cm² = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m² (at the tap); A₂ = 0.35 cm² = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ m² (lower section); h = 45 mm = 0.045 m.
Formula:
Continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ = Q; free fall of the stream gives v₂² = v₁² + 2gh.
Substitution:
(Q/A₂)² − (Q/A₁)² = 2gh, so Q = √[2gh/(1/A₂² − 1/A₁²)]
= √[2 × 9.8 × 0.045/(1/(3.5 × 10⁻⁵)² − 1/(1.2 × 10⁻⁴)²)].
Calculation:
1/A₂² = 8.16 × 10⁸ m⁻⁴; 1/A₁² = 6.94 × 10⁷ m⁻⁴; difference = 7.47 × 10⁸ m⁻⁴; 2gh = 0.882 m²/s².
Q = √(0.882/7.47 × 10⁸) = √(1.18 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.44 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s.
Result:
Q ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s = 34 cm³/s, agreeing with the printed (34 cm³/s).
questions.explanation: Combine the equation of continuity with the free-fall relation v₂² = v₁² + 2gh; eliminating the speeds gives Q directly from the two areas and the height difference.
questions.figure: Photograph of water falling from a tap, narrowing from a 1.2 cm² cross-section at the opening to 0.35 cm² over a 45 mm drop.

questions.question: Water leaves the jet of a horizontal hose at 10 m/s. If the velocity of water within the hose is 0.40 m/s, calculate the pressure within the hose. Density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and atmospheric pressure is 100000 Pa.
questions.answer:
Given:
v_jet = 10 m/s; v_hose = 0.40 m/s; ρ = 1000 kg/m³; P_atm = 100000 Pa; the hose is horizontal, so h₁ = h₂.
Formula:
Bernoulli: P + ½ρv_hose² = P_atm + ½ρv_jet², so P = P_atm + ½ρ(v_jet² − v_hose²).
Substitution:
P = 100000 + ½ × 1000 × (10² − 0.40²) = 100000 + 500 × (100 − 0.16).
Calculation:
P = 100000 + 500 × 99.84 = 100000 + 49920 = 149920 Pa.
Result:
P ≈ 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, agreeing with the printed (1.5 × 10⁵ Pa). The pressure inside the hose must exceed atmospheric pressure because the water speeds up as it leaves the jet.
questions.explanation: Key formula: P + ½ρv² = constant at the same height, with the jet at atmospheric pressure. The gauge pressure inside the hose is ½ρ(v_jet² − v_hose²) ≈ 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.question: What is the maximum weight of an aircraft with a wing area of 50 m² flying horizontally, is the velocity of the air over the upper surface of the wing is 150 m/s and that the lower surface 140 m/s ? Density of air is 1.29 kg/m³
questions.answer:
Given:
A = 50 m²; v_upper = 150 m/s; v_lower = 140 m/s; ρ = 1.29 kg/m³.
Formula:
Bernoulli at the same height: P_lower − P_upper = ½ρ(v_upper² − v_lower²); lift W = (P_lower − P_upper)A.
Substitution:
ΔP = ½ × 1.29 × (150² − 140²); W = ΔP × 50.
Calculation:
150² − 140² = 2900 m²/s²; ΔP = 0.645 × 2900 = 1870 Pa;
W = 1870 × 50 = 9.35 × 10⁴ N.
Result:
W ≈ 9.4 × 10⁴ N, agreeing with the printed 9.3 × 10⁴ N (the difference comes only from rounding ΔP to 1870 Pa).
questions.explanation: Key idea: the pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces, from Bernoulli's equation, multiplied by the wing area gives the lift; for horizontal flight this equals the maximum weight.

questions.question: A liquid flows through a pipe with a diameter of 0.50 m at a speed of 4.20 m/s . What is the rate of flow in L/min?
questions.answer:
Given:
d = 0.50 m; v = 4.20 m/s; 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 min = 60 s.
Formula:
Q = A v = (πd²/4)v; to convert m³/s to L/min multiply by 1000 × 60.
Substitution:
Q = π(0.50)²/4 × 4.20 = 0.1963 × 4.20 m³/s.
Calculation:
Q = 0.825 m³/s = 825 L/s = 825 × 60 = 4.95 × 10⁴ L/min.
Result:
Q ≈ 49500 L/min, agreeing with the printed (49500 L/min).
questions.explanation: Key steps: area of the pipe A = πd²/4, then Q = A v, then convert m³/s to L/min by multiplying by 6 × 10⁴.

questions.question: Calculate the average speed of blood flow in the major arteries of the body, which have a total cross-sectional area of about 2.1 cm². Use the data of example [Worked Example 7.3: radius of the aorta = 1.2 cm, speed of blood in the aorta = 40 cm/s].
questions.answer:
Given:
Total area of the major arteries A = 2.1 cm² = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ m². Data of Worked Example 7.3: aorta radius r = 1.2 cm = 1.2 × 10⁻² m, blood speed in the aorta v₁ = 40 cm/s = 0.40 m/s.
Formula:
Blood is incompressible, so Q = A₁v₁ = A v, giving v = A₁v₁/A.
Substitution:
Q = π(1.2 × 10⁻²)²(0.40) = 1.81 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s;
v = 1.81 × 10⁻⁴/2.1 × 10⁻⁴.
Calculation:
v = 0.862 m/s = 86.2 cm/s.
Result:
v ≈ 86 cm/s (0.86 m/s). Note: the printed answer 13.6 cm/s does not follow from the data of Example 7.3; it would require a volume flow of only about 2.9 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s (about 1.7 L/min) through the 2.1 cm² arteries, which is a different set of source data. Discrepancy noted.
questions.explanation: Key idea: the volume flow rate found from the aorta data of Example 7.3 is the same in the major arteries, so v = A₁v₁/A. The printed 13.6 cm/s is not consistent with that example.

questions.question: A 2μC point charge is located a distance “d” away from 6μC point charge, what is the ratio of F₁₂/F₂₁?
questions.explanation: By Newton's third law the force that the 2 μC charge exerts on the 6 μC charge is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force the 6 μC charge exerts on it. Coulomb's law contains the product q₁q₂, which is the same either way, so F₁₂ = F₂₁ and their ratio is 1. Options 1/3 and 3 come from wrongly taking the ratio of the charges (2/6), and 12 is not a ratio of forces at all.

questions.question: The minimum charge on an object cannot be less than:
questions.explanation: Charge is quantized: every charge is an integral multiple of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so no object can carry a smaller free charge than this. A charge of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (= 2e) is possible but is not the minimum. The value 9.1 × 10⁹ is of the order of Coulomb's constant, not a charge, and charge certainly has a definite smallest value, so (d) is wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹C  (b) 3.2 x 10⁻¹⁹C  (c) 9.1 x 10⁹  (d) No definite value exist

questions.question: Two charges are placed at a certain distance. If the magnitude of each charge is doubled the force will become
questions.answer: (b) 4 times of its original value
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law gives F = kq₁q₂/r², so the force is proportional to the product of the two charges. Doubling each charge multiplies the product by 2 × 2 = 4 while r is unchanged, so the force becomes four times larger. The options 1/4 and 1/8 would require the charges or the distance to be reduced, and 8 would need the product to increase eightfold.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 1/4th of its original value  (b) 4 times of its original value  (c) 1/8th of its original value  (d) 8 times of its original value

questions.question: Which of the following can be deflected while moving in the electric field?
questions.answer: (c) electron
questions.explanation: Only a particle carrying electric charge experiences the force F = qE, so only a charged particle can be deflected by an electric field; the electron is negatively charged and is deflected towards the positive plate. The neutron has no charge and the photon is electrically neutral (and is not a charged particle), so neither is deflected. Option (d) is therefore also wrong, because (a) and (b) are precisely the particles that are not deflected.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) neutron  (b) photon  (c) electron  (d) (a) and (b)

questions.question: The flux through a flat surface of are “A” in a uniform electric field “E” is maximum when the surface area is:
questions.answer: (b) perpendicular to E
questions.explanation: The flux is Φ = E·A = EA cosθ, where θ is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface. It is maximum when cosθ = 1, i.e. when the normal is parallel to E, which means the surface itself is perpendicular to the field. If the surface is parallel to E the normal is at 90° and the flux is zero, while 45° and 60° give only 0.707 and 0.5 of the maximum.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Parallel to E  (b) perpendicular to E  (c) placed 45° to E  (d) placed 60° to E

questions.question: The product of charge “q” and small separation “d” between two charges of same magnitude and opposite in nature is known as:
questions.answer: (c) Electric dipole moment
questions.explanation: Two equal and opposite charges ±q separated by a small distance d form an electric dipole, and the product p = qd is defined as its electric dipole moment, a vector directed from the negative charge to the positive charge with unit C·m. The electric dipole is the pair of charges itself, not the product, and the moment arm is the perpendicular distance used in calculating torque, not a charge times a distance in this sense. Electric flux is a quite different quantity, E·A.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Electric dipole  (b) Moment arm  (c) Electric dipole moment  (d) Flux of electric field

questions.question: 12 J of work is to be done against an existence electric field to take a charge of 0.01 C from one-point A to another point B. The potential difference between B and A is
questions.explanation: The work done by an external agent against the field equals q times the potential difference: W = q(V_B − V_A). Hence V_B − V_A = W/q = 12/0.01 = 1200 V. Because the work is done against the field to move a positive charge, point B is at the higher potential, so the difference is positive 1200 V; 120 V comes from taking q = 0.1 C, and 12 V or 1.2 V from misplacing the decimal point.

questions.question: The force between two charges placed in air is F. if air is replaced by a medium of relative permittivity εᵣ then force is reduced to:
questions.answer: (b) F/εᵣ
questions.explanation: In a medium the force between two charges becomes F′ = q₁q₂/(4πε₀εᵣr²) = F/εᵣ, because the permittivity is ε = εᵣε₀ and the dielectric reduces the field between the charges. Since εᵣ > 1 for any material, the force is always reduced, never increased. Fεᵣ and εᵣ/F have the wrong dependence, and εεᵣ is a permittivity, not a force.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Fεᵣ  (b) F/εᵣ  (c) εᵣ/F  (d) εεᵣ

questions.question: The negative gradient of the potential is:
questions.answer: (c) electric field intensity
questions.explanation: The electric field and the potential are related by E = −dV/dr, so the electric field intensity is the negative gradient of the potential. The minus sign shows that the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases. Potential energy is qV, voltage is a potential difference, and electric flux is E·A, so none of the others is a gradient of the potential.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) potential energy  (b) voltage  (c) electric field intensity  (d) electric flux

questions.question: The electric flux through a plane area will be half of its maximum value when area is held at angle of ____ with electric field
questions.explanation: If the plane of the area makes an angle φ with the field, the normal makes an angle 90° − φ with it, so Φ = EA cos(90° − φ) = EA sinφ. Half the maximum flux requires sinφ = 0.5, giving φ = 30°. At 45° the flux is 0.707 of the maximum and at 90° it is zero. Note the convention: if the angle were measured between the normal (area vector) and E, the answer would be 60°, but the question specifies the angle of the area itself with the field, so 30° is correct.

questions.question: Why do most objects tend to contain nearly equal numbers of positive and negative charges?
questions.answer: Because electric charge is conserved and is created only in equal and opposite pairs, and because the electric force is extremely strong. Every atom contains as many protons as electrons, so an object built from atoms is neutral unless it gains or loses electrons. If a body did acquire an excess of one kind of charge, the resulting repulsion would drive the extra charges to the surface and then into the surrounding air, or would attract charges of the opposite sign from the air, until the body became neutral again. The Earth and the universe as a whole are also electrically neutral on a large scale. Charging a body therefore always means transferring electrons from one body to another, never creating a net amount of charge.
questions.explanation: Key principle: conservation of charge and charge quantization, together with the very large magnitude of electric forces, make any large imbalance disappear quickly.

questions.question: When measuring an electric field, could we use a negative rather than a positive test charge?
questions.answer: Yes. The electric field is defined by E = F/q₀ for a small test charge q₀, and the definition works for a test charge of either sign provided it is small enough not to disturb the charges that produce the field. If a negative test charge is used, the force on it points opposite to E, but dividing that force by the negative value of q₀ reverses the direction again, so the field comes out the same. A positive test charge is chosen only by convention, because then F and E point in the same direction and the field direction is easier to visualise. One practical caution is that a negative test charge released in the field accelerates opposite to E, so it is harder to hold in place while the force is measured.
questions.explanation: Key point: E = F/q₀ is valid for either sign of test charge; the direction of the force reverses but so does the sign of q₀, so the field is unchanged.

questions.question: During fair weather, the electric field due to the net charge on Earth points downward. Is Earth charged positively or negatively?
questions.answer: Earth is charged negatively. The direction of an electric field is defined as the direction of the force that the field would exert on a positive test charge. Since the fair-weather field points downward, towards the Earth's surface, a positive charge placed near the ground is pushed downward, i.e. it is attracted towards the Earth. A body that attracts positive charge must itself carry net negative charge, so the Earth has an excess of electrons. The positively charged atmosphere above it completes the system. The field strength near the surface is about 100 to 150 V/m, corresponding to a negative surface charge density of the order of 10⁻⁹ C/m².
questions.explanation: Key rule: the field direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge, so a downward field means positive charge is attracted downwards and Earth must be negative.

questions.question: How the electric flux through a closed surface is independent on the size or shape of the surface enclosed the charge.
questions.answer: For any closed surface enclosing a net charge q, the total outward electric flux is Φ = q/ε₀, by Gauss's law, and this depends only on the charge inside, not on the size or shape of the surface. The reason is that the field of a point charge falls off as 1/r² while the area of a surface at distance r grows as r²; the product E × A, and therefore the number of field lines crossing the surface, stays the same for every surface that encloses the charge. Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, so every line leaving an enclosed positive charge must cross the surface exactly once whatever its shape. A line from a charge outside the surface enters and leaves, contributing zero net flux, so only the enclosed charge counts.
questions.explanation: Key idea: Gauss's law, Φ = q/ε₀. The 1/r² fall-off of the field exactly compensates the r² growth of area, and field lines from outside charges cross in and out equally.

questions.question: What is electric dipole and electric dipole moment?
questions.answer: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite point charges, +q and −q, separated by a small distance d (often written 2a). A molecule such as HCl or H₂O, in which the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide, behaves as a dipole. The electric dipole moment is defined as p = qd, a vector whose magnitude is the product of the charge and the separation and whose direction is from the negative charge towards the positive charge. Its SI unit is the coulomb metre (C·m). The dipole moment measures the strength of the dipole: the torque on it in a uniform field is τ = pE sinθ and its potential energy is U = −pE cosθ, so a dipole tends to align itself with the field.
questions.explanation: Key facts: p = qd, directed from −q to +q, unit C·m; the torque in a field is τ = pE sinθ and the potential energy is U = −pE cosθ.

questions.question: A charged particle is seen to be moving in an electric field along a straight line. How it effects the path of motion of the particle?
questions.answer: If a charged particle moves in a uniform electric field along a straight line parallel or antiparallel to the field, the electric force qE acts along the line of motion. There is then no force perpendicular to the velocity, so the path stays straight and the field only changes the speed: it accelerates a charge moving in the direction of the force and decelerates (then reverses) one moving against it. If, however, the velocity makes an angle with E, the component of velocity perpendicular to E is unchanged while the parallel component changes, so the path becomes a parabola, just like projectile motion under gravity. A straight-line path therefore tells us that the velocity is parallel or antiparallel to E (or that E is zero).
questions.explanation: Key idea: only the component of force perpendicular to the velocity bends the path. A straight path means v is parallel or antiparallel to E, so the field changes only the speed.

questions.question: An electron has a speed of 10⁶ m/s. Find its energy in electron volt. (Ans. 2.84 eV)
questions.answer:
Given:
v = 10⁶ m/s; m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Formula:
K = ½mv²; energy in electron volt = K/e.
Substitution:
K = ½ × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × (10⁶)² = 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁹ J;
K = 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.
Calculation:
K = 2.84 eV.
Result:
K ≈ 2.84 eV, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans. 2.84 eV). The speed is far below the speed of light, so the non-relativistic formula is valid.
questions.explanation: Divide the kinetic energy in joules by e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C to convert it to electron volt; remember to square the speed in m/s.

questions.question: Define electric charge. Discuss the fundamental properties of electric charge, including the principles of conservation of charge and quantization of charge.
questions.answer:
Electric charge is the intrinsic property of matter that causes it to experience and exert electric forces. There are two kinds, positive (protons) and negative (electrons); like charges repel, unlike charges attract, and charge is measured in coulombs (C).
Fundamental properties:
1. Two kinds of charge: positive and negative, and the force between two charges depends on the product of their magnitudes and on the distance between them.
2. Quantization: charge exists only in integral multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so q = ±ne where n = 0, 1, 2, ... This was demonstrated by Millikan's oil-drop experiment. One coulomb therefore corresponds to 1/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
3. Conservation: the net charge of an isolated system remains constant. Charge is never created or destroyed, only transferred from one body to another. When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the rod becomes positive and the silk carries an equal negative charge, so the total charge is unchanged.
4. Additivity: the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of the individual charges, because charge is a scalar quantity.
5. Invariance: the charge on a particle is the same in all inertial frames; it does not change with speed, unlike mass.
6. Distribution: charge resides on the outer surface of a conductor, distributed so that the field inside a conductor at rest is zero.
These properties explain why matter is normally neutral: equal numbers of protons and electrons give zero net charge, and any imbalance is quickly removed by transfer of electrons. They also underlie the working of capacitors, conductors and all electrostatic devices.
questions.explanation: Key principles: two kinds of charge, quantization q = ne with e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and conservation of net charge in an isolated system. A common mistake is to say charge can be created by friction rather than transferred.

questions.question: State and explain Coulombs law. Apply it to calculate the electric field due to an isolated point charge.
questions.answer:
Statement: the electrostatic force between two point charges at rest is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and it acts along the line joining them. In symbols F = k q₁q₂/r², where k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². In a medium of relative permittivity εᵣ the force becomes F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀εᵣr²), so the medium reduces the force by the factor εᵣ.
Explanation: the force is repulsive for charges of the same sign and attractive for opposite signs; it obeys Newton's third law, since the force on each charge is equal and opposite; and it obeys the inverse-square law with distance. For more than two charges, the principle of superposition applies: the net force on any charge is the vector sum of the forces due to all the others.
Electric field of an isolated point charge: place a small test charge q₀ at a point P at distance r from a charge q. By Coulomb's law the force on the test charge is F = kqq₀/r², so the electric field at P is
E = F/q₀ = kq/r² = q/(4πε₀r²).
The field is directed radially outward from a positive charge and radially inward towards a negative charge, and its magnitude falls off as 1/r². Because the field of many charges obeys superposition, this result is the building block for finding the field of any charge distribution. Example: at 0.30 m from a 2 μC charge, E = (9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed away from the charge.
questions.explanation: Combine F = kq₁q₂/r² with the definition E = F/q₀; the test charge cancels, leaving E = kq/r². Remember the direction: outward for positive q, inward for negative q.

questions.question: Define electric flux and explain its significance in the study of electromagnetism. How does it relate to electric fields and charged particles?
questions.answer:
Electric flux is a measure of the number of electric field lines crossing a given surface. For a flat surface of area A in a uniform field E, the flux is Φ = E·A = EA cosθ, where θ is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface; the SI unit is N·m²/C. The flux is maximum when the surface is perpendicular to the field (θ = 0) and zero when the surface is parallel to the field (θ = 90°). For a closed surface the outward flux is q/ε₀, where q is the net charge enclosed — this is Gauss's law.
Significance in electromagnetism: flux is the quantity that links the electric field to its sources. Gauss's law, one of Maxwell's four equations, states that the flux through any closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge, so it lets us find the field of symmetric distributions — a charged sphere, cylinder or infinite plane — with a simple surface integral instead of a difficult volume integration. Because flux can change with time and a changing electric flux acts like a current (displacement current), flux is also central to electromagnetic induction and to the existence of electromagnetic waves.
Relation to fields and charges: the field E is the flux per unit area perpendicular to it, and the sources of the flux are charges; field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge. The flux through a closed surface is positive when it encloses net positive charge, negative for net negative charge, and zero when the enclosed charge is zero, which is why a closed metal shell shields its interior from outside fields.
questions.explanation: Key ideas: Φ = EA cosθ and Gauss's law Φ = q/ε₀. Flux counts field lines crossing a surface and depends only on the charge enclosed for a closed surface.

questions.question: What is electric potential? Driven expression for potential due to an isolated point charge.
questions.answer:
Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge by an external agent in bringing a small positive test charge from infinity to that point without acceleration. If W is the work done in bringing a charge q₀ from infinity to the point, then V = W/q₀. Potential is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C. The potential at infinity is taken as zero. The potential difference between two points is V_B − V_A = W_AB/q₀, and the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential, E = −dV/dr.
Derivation for an isolated point charge: let a charge Q be at the origin and let the point P be at distance r. At a distance x from Q the field is E = kQ/x², directed radially outward if Q is positive. The external force needed to move a test charge q₀ without acceleration is equal and opposite to the electric force, F = −kQq₀/x². The work done by this external force in moving the test charge from infinity to r is
W = ∫(from ∞ to r) (−kQq₀/x²) dx = kQq₀ [−1/x]∞^r = kQq₀/r.
Therefore V = W/q₀ = kQ/r = Q/(4πε₀r).
For a positive charge the potential is positive and decreases as 1/r; for a negative charge it is negative. Equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres around the charge, and the potential difference between two points at distances r_A and r_B is V_B − V_A = kQ(1/r_B − 1/r_A). Example: at 0.10 m from a 1 μC charge, V = (9 × 10⁹)(1 × 10⁻⁶)/0.10 = 9 × 10⁴ V.
questions.explanation: Key definition V = W/q₀ and result V = kQ/r. Note that the work is done by an external agent against the field, and that potential, unlike field, is a scalar.
