questions.question: Define an electric dipole. Derive formula for the electric field due to an electric dipole at a point “P” placed on its axial line.
questions.answer:
An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite point charges, +q and −q, separated by a small distance 2a. Its electric dipole moment is p = q × 2a, a vector directed from the negative charge towards the positive charge; its SI unit is C·m.
Derivation for the axial line: let the charges be at A (−q) and B (+q) with the centre O between them, so OB = OA = a. Take a point P on the axis on the side of the positive charge B, at distance r from O, with r much greater than a.
The field at P due to +q at B is E₊ = kq/(r − a)², directed away from B, i.e. along OP.
The field at P due to −q at A is E₋ = kq/(r + a)², directed towards A, i.e. opposite to OP.
Since the two fields are along the same line but in opposite directions and E₊ is larger, the net field is
E = E₊ − E₋ = kq[1/(r − a)² − 1/(r + a)²].
Combining the fractions,
E = kq[(r + a)² − (r − a)²]/(r² − a²)² = kq(4ar)/(r² − a²)².
Since p = q(2a), this can be written E = 2kpr/(r² − a²)².
For a short dipole, r is much greater than a, so r² − a² ≈ r² and
E = 2kp/r³ = p/(2πε₀r³).
The field is directed along the dipole moment, from −q towards +q, and falls off as 1/r³, faster than the 1/r² field of a single charge. For the same distance the axial field is twice the equatorial field, which is kp/r³ and points opposite to p. Example: for p = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C·m at r = 0.10 m, E = 2 × 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁹/(0.10)³ = 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C.
questions.explanation: Key steps: E₊ − E₋ along the axis, then the approximation r >> a giving E = 2kp/r³. Remember the axial field is twice the equatorial field kp/r³.

questions.question: Calculate the value of two equal charges if they repel one another with a force of 0.1 N when situated 50 cm apart in a vacuum. (b) What would be the size of the charges if they were situated in an insulating liquid whose permittivity was ten times that of a vacuum?
questions.answer:
Given:
F = 0.1 N; r = 50 cm = 0.50 m; q₁ = q₂ = q; k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²; for part (b) εᵣ = 10.
Formula:
F = kq²/r², so q = √(Fr²/k); in a medium F = kq²/(εᵣr²), so q′ = q√εᵣ.
Substitution:
q = √(0.1 × 0.50²/9 × 10⁹) = √(0.025/9 × 10⁹);
q′ = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ × √10.
Calculation:
q = √(2.78 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ C;
q′ = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.162 = 5.27 × 10⁻⁶ C.
Result:
(a) q ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ C = 1.7 μC each.
(b) q′ ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻⁶ C = 5.3 μC each.
These agree with the printed answers (1.7 μC, 5.3 μC). In the liquid the force is reduced tenfold, so the charges must be √10 times larger to give the same force.
questions.explanation: Key formula F = q²/(4πε₀εᵣr²). In a medium of εᵣ = 10 the charges must be √10 times larger to keep the same force.

questions.question: How far apart must two protons be if the magnitude of the electrostatic force acting on either one due to the other is equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force on a proton at Earth’s surface? (mass of proton = 1.67 X 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge of proton = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; g = 9.8 m/s²; k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Formula:
Electrostatic force = weight of one proton: ke²/r² = mg, so r = e√(k/mg).
Substitution:
r = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × √[9 × 10⁹/(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 9.8)].
Calculation:
mg = 1.64 × 10⁻²⁶ N; k/mg = 5.50 × 10³⁵ m²/C²; √(k/mg) = 7.42 × 10¹⁷ m/C;
r = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 7.42 × 10¹⁷ = 0.119 m.
Result:
r ≈ 0.119 m, agreeing with the printed (0.119 m). At this separation each force is about 1.6 × 10⁻²⁶ N.
questions.explanation: Set ke²/r² = mg and solve for r; the charge and mass of a single proton are used for both particles because the forces are on one proton due to the other.

questions.question: An electron of charge 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C is situated in a uniform electric field of intensity 1200-volt cm⁻¹. Find the force on it, its acceleration, and the time it takes to travel 2 cm from rest (electronic mass, m = 9.1 x 10⁻³¹ kg).
questions.answer:
Given:
q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; E = 1200 V cm⁻¹ = 1200/0.01 = 1.2 × 10⁵ V/m; m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg; s = 2 cm = 0.02 m; u = 0.
Formula:
F = qE; a = F/m; s = ½at², so t = √(2s/a).
Substitution:
F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.2 × 10⁵;
a = 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁴/9.1 × 10⁻³¹;
t = √(2 × 0.02/2.11 × 10¹⁶).
Calculation:
F = 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ N;
a = 2.11 × 10¹⁶ m/s²;
t = √(1.90 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 1.38 × 10⁻⁹ s.
Result:
F ≈ 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, a ≈ 2.1 × 10¹⁶ m/s², t ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁹ s, agreeing with the printed (1.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, 2.12 × 10¹⁶ m s⁻², 1.37 × 10⁻⁹ s). Note: the book prints the acceleration unit as ms², which is a typographical error for m/s².
questions.explanation: Convert V/cm to V/m first (multiply by 100), then use F = qE, a = F/m and s = ½at². The book's unit ms² is a misprint for m/s².

questions.question: An alpha particle (the nucleus of a helium atom) has a mass of 6.64 X 10⁻²⁷ kg and a charge of 2e. What are the (a) magnitude and (b) direction of the electric field that will balance the gravitational force on the particle?
questions.answer:
Given:
m = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; q = 2e = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; g = 9.8 m/s².
Formula:
For balance qE = mg, so E = mg/q.
Substitution:
E = (6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ × 9.8)/(3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹).
Calculation:
E = 6.51 × 10⁻²⁶/3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.03 × 10⁻⁷ N/C.
Result:
(a) E ≈ 2.03 × 10⁻⁷ N/C.
(b) The electric force must act upward to balance the downward weight; since the alpha particle is positive, the field must point upward, i.e. vertically away from the Earth. This agrees with the printed answer (2.03 × 10⁻⁷ N/C, directed upwards).
questions.explanation: Balance weight with electric force: qE = mg. For a positive charge the field direction is the same as the force direction, so E points upward.

questions.question: A proton and an electron form two corners of an equilateral triangle of side length 2.0 X 10⁻⁶ m. What is the magnitude of the net electric field these two particles produce at the third corner?
questions.answer:
Given:
Proton (+e) and electron (−e) at two corners of an equilateral triangle; side r = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Formula:
Each charge produces E = ke/r² at the third corner. The two field vectors make an angle of 120° with each other (one points away from the proton, the other towards the electron), so
E_net = √(E² + E² + 2E² cos120°) = E.
Substitution:
E = 9 × 10⁹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)².
Calculation:
E = 1.44 × 10⁻⁹/4.0 × 10⁻¹² = 360 N/C; E_net = 360 N/C.
Result:
E_net ≈ 3.6 × 10² N/C, agreeing with the printed (3.6 × 10² N/C). The resultant is parallel to the line joining the proton and the electron, directed away from the proton.
questions.explanation: Both fields have equal magnitude ke/r² and are 120° apart, so their vector sum equals either one. A common mistake is to add them as if they were parallel.

questions.question: Figure shows two charged particles on an x axis: -q=-3.20 X10⁻¹⁹ C at x = -3.00 m and q =3.20 X10⁻¹⁹ C at x = 3.00 m. What are the (a) magnitude and (b) direction (relative to the positive direction of the x axis) of the net electric field produced at point P at y = 4.00 m? [Charges lie on the x-axis: −q = −3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C at x = −3.00 m and q = +3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C at x = +3.00 m; point P is on the y-axis at y = 4.00 m.]
questions.answer:
Given:
q = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C at x = +3.00 m; −q at x = −3.00 m; P at y = 4.00 m; k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Formula:
Each charge gives E = kq/r² with r = √(3.00² + 4.00²) = 5.00 m. The vertical components cancel and the horizontal components both point in the −x direction, so E_net = 2(kq/r²) × (3.00/5.00).
Substitution:
E = 9 × 10⁹ × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹/(5.00)² = 1.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ N/C each;
E_net = 2 × 1.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.600.
Calculation:
E_net = 1.38 × 10⁻¹⁰ N/C.
Result:
(a) E_net ≈ 1.38 × 10⁻¹⁰ N/C.
(b) The field points in the −x direction, i.e. 180° from the positive x-axis, agreeing with the printed answer (1.38 × 10⁻¹⁰ N/C, in the −x direction).
questions.explanation: Use symmetry: the two equal fields have equal and opposite vertical components, which cancel, and equal horizontal components pointing towards −x, which add with cosθ = 3/5.
questions.figure: Cartesian axes with −q at x = −3.00 m and +q at x = +3.00 m on the x-axis, and point P at y = 4.00 m on the y-axis.

questions.question: A proton and an electron form two corners of an equilateral triangle of side length 5 μm. What is the magnitude of the net electric field these two particles produce at the third corner?
questions.answer:
Given:
Proton (+e) and electron (−e); side r = 5 μm = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Formula:
E = ke/r² for each charge; as in the previous question the two field vectors are 120° apart, so E_net = E.
Substitution:
E = 9 × 10⁹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/(5.0 × 10⁻⁶)².
Calculation:
E = 1.44 × 10⁻⁹/2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ = 57.6 N/C.
Result:
E_net ≈ 58 N/C (≈ 5.8 × 10¹ N/C), parallel to the line joining the proton and the electron and directed away from the proton. The book prints no answer for this question; the value is smaller than in the 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m case because the side is 2.5 times longer, so each field falls by 2.5² = 6.25.
questions.explanation: Same geometry as the previous numerical, but with a larger side: E scales as 1/r², and the 120° vector sum again equals the magnitude of either field.

questions.question: The square surface shown in figure measures 3.2 mm on each side. It is immersed in a uniform electric field with magnitude E =1800 N/C and with field lines at an angle of θ = 35° with a normal to the surface, as shown. Take that normal to be directed “outward”, as though the surface were one face of a box. Calculate the electric flux through the surface. [Square of side 3.2 mm; E = 1800 N/C; the field lines make 35° with the outward normal.]
questions.answer:
Given:
Side a = 3.2 mm = 3.2 × 10⁻³ m; E = 1800 N/C; θ = 35° between the field and the outward normal.
Formula:
Φ = E·A = EA cosθ.
Substitution:
A = (3.2 × 10⁻³)² = 1.024 × 10⁻⁵ m²;
Φ = 1800 × 1.024 × 10⁻⁵ × cos35°.
Calculation:
Φ = 0.018432 × 0.8192 = 1.51 × 10⁻² N·m²/C.
The field lines enter the surface while the normal points outward, so the flux is negative: Φ = −1.5 × 10⁻² N·m²/C.
Result:
Φ ≈ −1.5 × 10⁻² N·m²/C, agreeing with the printed (−1.5 × 10⁻² N·m²/C).
questions.explanation: Determine the sign from the direction of the field relative to the outward normal: field entering gives negative flux; the magnitude is EA cosθ.
questions.figure: Square plate of side 3.2 mm in a uniform field whose lines make 35° with the outward normal drawn on the plate.

questions.question: An electron is liberated from the lower of two large parallel metal plates separated by a distance h = 2 cm. The upper plate has a potential of 2400 volts relative to the lower. How long does the electron take to reach it?
questions.answer:
Given:
h = 2 cm = 0.020 m; V = 2400 V; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg; the electron starts from rest.
Formula:
E = V/h; a = eE/m; h = ½at², so t = √(2h/a).
Substitution:
E = 2400/0.020 = 1.2 × 10⁵ V/m;
a = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(1.2 × 10⁵)/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹);
t = √(2 × 0.020/2.11 × 10¹⁶).
Calculation:
a = 2.11 × 10¹⁶ m/s²;
t = √(1.90 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 1.38 × 10⁻⁹ s.
Result:
t ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁹ s (about 1.4 ns). Note: the printed bracket answer 1.2 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ is the electric field E = V/h, not the time asked for; the time is 1.38 × 10⁻⁹ s. Discrepancy in the printed answer noted.
questions.explanation: The printed answer is actually the field E = V/h; to answer the question, use a = eE/m and h = ½at², which gives t = 1.4 × 10⁻⁹ s.

questions.question: Two large parallel metal plates are 1.5 cm apart and have charges of equal magnitudes but opposite signs on their facing surfaces. Take the potential of the negative plate to be zero. If the potential halfway between the plates is then 5.0 V, what is the electric field in the region between the plates?
questions.answer:
Given:
d = 1.5 cm = 0.015 m; potential of the negative plate = 0; potential at the midpoint (0.75 cm from either plate) = 5.0 V.
Formula:
The field between large parallel plates is uniform, so the potential changes linearly with distance: E = ΔV/d.
Substitution:
The potential rises from 0 at the negative plate to 5.0 V at the midpoint, so across the whole gap ΔV = 2 × 5.0 = 10 V;
E = 10/0.015.
Calculation:
E = 667 V/m.
Result:
E ≈ 6.7 × 10² V/m, agreeing with the printed (6.7 × 10² V/m), directed from the positive plate to the negative plate.
questions.explanation: Because E is uniform, V is linear in distance; the full plate separation carries twice the midpoint potential, so E = 2 × 5.0/0.015.

questions.question: The capacitance of a capacitor is NOT influenced by:
questions.answer: (a) Plate thickness
questions.explanation: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε₀εᵣA/d, so the capacitance depends on the plate area A, the plate separation d and the nature of the dielectric through εᵣ. Plate thickness does not appear in the formula, so changing it does not change C. Options (b), (c) and (d) all change the capacitance, so (a) is the factor with no influence.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Plate thickness  (b) Plate area  (c) Plate separation  (d) Nature of the dielectric

questions.question: What is the value of capacitance of a capacitor which has a voltage of 4V and has 16C of charge?
questions.answer: (b) 4F
questions.explanation: By definition C = Q/V. Substituting Q = 16 C and V = 4 V gives C = 16/4 = 4 F. The distractors correspond to subtracting or mis-dividing the data; only 4 F satisfies Q = CV, since 4 F × 4 V = 16 C.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 2F  (b) 4F  (c) 6F  (d) 8F

questions.question: Capacitors are used in electric power supply system to:
questions.answer: (a) Improve power factor
questions.explanation: Most industrial loads are inductive, so the current lags the voltage and the power factor is low. Capacitors draw a leading current that cancels part of the lagging reactive current, raising the power factor towards unity (power-factor correction). Reduced line current is only a consequence of this correction, and capacitors are not used as switching devices. Hence (a) is the standard purpose.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Improve power factor  (b) Reduce line current  (c) Provide voltage stability  (d) switching

questions.question: In a variable capacitor, capacitance can be varied by:
questions.answer: (a) Turning the rotatable plates in or out
questions.explanation: A variable (tuning) capacitor has fixed plates and a set of plates that can be rotated between them. Turning the rotor changes the overlapping area A, and since C = ε₀εᵣA/d the capacitance varies continuously. Changing the plates or their material would give only fixed values, and the plates are rotated, not slid. Hence (a).

options.text: Turning the rotatable plates in or out

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Turning the rotatable plates in or out  (b) Changing the plates  (c) Sliding the rotatable plates  (d) Changing the material of plates
questions.correctAnswer: (a) Turning the rotatable plates in or out

questions.question: Energy stored in the capacitor is:
questions.answer: (b) E = ½ CV²
questions.explanation: The work done in charging a capacitor is W = ∫v dq = ∫(q/C)dq = Q²/2C, and with Q = CV this becomes E = ½CV². Options (a) and (d) are dimensionally wrong because the voltage is not squared, and (c) is twice the correct value. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) E = ¼ CV  (b) E = ½ CV²  (c) E = CV²  (d) E = ½ CV

questions.question: The time constant of a series RC circuit consisting of 100μF capacitor in series with a 100Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: For a series RC circuit the time constant is τ = RC = (100 Ω)(100 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 1.0 × 10⁻² s = 0.01 s = 10 ms. The value 0.1 s would require R = 1 kΩ, and options (b) and (d) confuse the prefix milli with centi. Hence (c).

questions.question: The charging of a capacitor through a resistance follows:
questions.answer: (c) exponential law
questions.explanation: While charging, q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)), and while discharging q = Q₀e^(−t/RC); both the charge and the current change exponentially with time, the rate being set by τ = RC. Neither a linear nor a square-law relation describes this curve. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) linear law  (b) square law  (c) exponential law  (d) none of the above

questions.question: When the total charge in a capacitor is doubled, the energy stored
questions.answer: (d) is quadrupled
questions.explanation: For a given capacitor the stored energy is E = Q²/2C, so E ∝ Q². Doubling Q therefore multiplies the energy by 2² = 4, i.e. it becomes four times larger. 'Doubled' would be correct only if E were proportional to Q, which is not the case at fixed capacitance. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) remains the same  (b) is doubled  (c) is halved  (d) is quadrupled

questions.question: The capacitance C is charged through a resistor R. The time constant of the charging circuit is given by:
questions.answer: (c) RC
questions.explanation: The time constant is the time in which the charge reaches 63% of its final value; putting t = τ in q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) gives 0.63Q₀ only when τ = RC. The product RC has the unit of seconds (Ω × F = s). C/R and R/C are not times, and 1/RC is a rate with unit s⁻¹. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) C/R  (b) 1/RC  (c) RC  (d) R/C

questions.question: Capacitor blocks:
questions.answer: (b) direct current
questions.explanation: When a steady d.c. source is connected, the capacitor charges once and then no further current flows, so direct current is blocked after the brief charging transient. With a.c. the capacitor charges and discharges every half cycle, so alternating current passes; its reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls as the frequency rises. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) alternating current  (b) direct current  (c) both alternating and direct current  (d) neither alternating nor direct current

questions.question: State the factors on which the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor depends.
questions.answer: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is C = ε₀εᵣA/d, where A is the area of each plate, d is the separation between the plates and εᵣ is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of the medium between them. Hence C depends on: (i) the area of the plates — C ∝ A, so larger plates give greater capacitance; (ii) the separation between the plates — C ∝ 1/d, so bringing the plates closer increases C; (iii) the nature of the dielectric — C ∝ εᵣ, so inserting a dielectric of higher permittivity increases C. The thickness or material of the metal plates, and the charge or voltage applied, do not appear in the formula and therefore do not affect the capacitance.
questions.explanation: Key relation C = ε₀εᵣA/d; a common mistake is to think that the charge stored or the applied voltage changes the capacitance — it does not, since C is fixed by geometry and dielectric.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by dielectric constant (relative permittivity). State two physical properties desirable in a material to be used as the dielectric in acapacitor.
questions.answer: The dielectric constant (relative permittivity) of a dielectric is the ratio of the capacitance of a capacitor with the dielectric between its plates to the capacitance of the same capacitor with vacuum (or air) between them: εᵣ = C/C₀ = ε/ε₀. It is a pure number with no unit and is always greater than 1 (about 1.0006 for air and about 6 for mica). Because C = εᵣC₀, a dielectric multiplies the capacitance by εᵣ. Two desirable properties are: (i) a high dielectric constant, so that a large capacitance is obtained in a small space; (ii) a high dielectric strength, i.e. the material must withstand a strong electric field without breaking down or sparking. Low dielectric loss, good insulation resistance and thermal stability are additional desirable properties.
questions.explanation: Key idea: εᵣ = C/C₀, dimensionless; students often wrongly attach units to εᵣ or confuse dielectric constant with dielectric strength.

questions.question: Drive expressions for the combined capacitance of two capacitors (a) connected in series, (b) connected in parallel.
questions.answer:
(a) Series: the same charge Q is deposited on both capacitors. The potential differences are V₁ = Q/C₁ and V₂ = Q/C₂, and the total is V = V₁ + V₂ = Q(1/C₁ + 1/C₂). Since V = Q/C_s, it follows that 1/C_s = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂, or C_s = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). The series combination is always smaller than the smaller capacitance.
(b) Parallel: both capacitors have the same potential difference V, so Q₁ = C₁V and Q₂ = C₂V. The total charge is Q = Q₁ + Q₂ = (C₁ + C₂)V. Since Q = C_pV, the combined capacitance is C_p = C₁ + C₂, which is larger than either capacitance.
questions.explanation: Key point: series capacitors carry the same charge and their reciprocals add; parallel capacitors share the same voltage and their capacitances add — the opposite of resistors.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the energy stored in a capacitor C when there is a potential difference V between the plates.
questions.answer: Let the capacitor be charged to a final charge Q at potential difference V, so that Q = CV. At some instant let the charge be q, when the potential difference is v = q/C. To add a further charge dq, work must be done against the repulsion of the existing charge: dW = v dq = (q/C)dq. The total work done in raising the charge from 0 to Q is W = ∫₀^Q (q/C)dq = (1/C)(Q²/2) = Q²/2C. This work is stored as electric potential energy, so U = Q²/2C. Using Q = CV gives U = ½CV², and using V = Q/C gives the equivalent form U = ½QV. The energy resides in the electric field between the plates.
questions.explanation: Key derivation: integrate dW = v dq with v = q/C; the common error is to write W = QV, which ignores that the voltage rises from zero to V during charging.

questions.question: A capacitor gets a charge of 50C when it is connected to a battery of emf 5 V. Calculate the capacity of the capacitor.
questions.answer:
Given: Q = 50 C, V = 5 V.
Formula: the capacity (capacitance) is the charge stored per unit potential difference, C = Q/V.
Substitution: C = 50 C / 5 V.
Calculation: C = 10 F.
Result: the capacity of the capacitor is 10 F. This is an extremely large capacitance, since one farad means one coulomb stored per volt; practical capacitors are rated in microfarads, nanofarads or picofarads, so the given data are only of textbook interest.
questions.explanation: Key formula C = Q/V; 10 F is an enormous capacitance, so such a value is only of textbook interest, practical capacitors being rated in μF, nF or pF.

questions.question: Calculate combined capacitance of capacitors in series and in parallel.
questions.answer:
Capacitors in series:
Consider two capacitors C₁ and C₂ connected in series across a supply V. The same charge Q is deposited on the facing plates of the series combination, so the potential differences are V₁ = Q/C₁ and V₂ = Q/C₂. By Kirchhoff's loop rule, V = V₁ + V₂ = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂. If C_s is the single capacitance that would store the same charge Q at the same total voltage, V = Q/C_s. Therefore 1/C_s = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂, or C_s = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). For n capacitors, 1/C_s = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … + 1/Cₙ. The equivalent capacitance in series is smaller than the smallest individual capacitance, because the same charge is shared across a larger effective separation.

Capacitors in parallel:
When C₁ and C₂ are connected in parallel, the same potential difference V is applied to each, and the charges are Q₁ = C₁V and Q₂ = C₂V. The total charge supplied by the source is Q = Q₁ + Q₂ = (C₁ + C₂)V. If C_p is the equivalent capacitance, Q = C_pV, hence C_p = C₁ + C₂, and for n capacitors C_p = C₁ + C₂ + … + Cₙ. In parallel the equivalent capacitance is larger than the largest individual capacitance, because the effective plate area is increased.

Worked example: for C₁ = 10 μF and C₂ = 40 μF, the series combination gives C_s = (10 × 40)/(10 + 40) = 8 μF, while in parallel C_p = 50 μF. In a series combination the reciprocal formula must be used, and the smaller capacitance carries the larger share of the voltage.
questions.explanation: Key point: series capacitances add as reciprocals while parallel capacitances add directly; the series result must always be smaller than the smallest capacitance, which serves as a quick check.

questions.question: Prove that energy stored in a capacitor is E = ½ CV²
questions.answer:
Consider a capacitor of capacitance C being charged from rest to a final potential difference V, so that its final charge is Q = CV. At an intermediate stage let the charge be q, when the potential difference is v = q/C. The work needed to bring an extra charge dq from the negative plate to the positive plate against this potential difference is dW = v dq = (q/C)dq. The total work done in raising the charge from zero to Q is W = ∫₀^Q (q/C)dq = (1/C)[q²/2]₀^Q = Q²/2C. This work is stored in the capacitor as electric potential energy, so U = Q²/2C. Substituting Q = CV gives U = ½CV², which is the required result; substituting V = Q/C gives the alternative form U = ½QV.
Graphical proof: plotting the potential difference v against the charge q gives a straight line through the origin. The work done is the area under this line from 0 to Q, i.e. area = ½ × base × height = ½QV, which again gives U = ½CV².
The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates. For a parallel-plate capacitor the energy density is u = ½ε₀εᵣE², so that U = u × Ad = ½ε₀εᵣE²(Ad).
Example: a 100 μF capacitor charged to 50 V stores U = ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × (50)² = 0.125 J; if its charge is doubled, the energy becomes four times larger because U ∝ Q².
questions.explanation: Key derivation: integrate dW = v dq with v = q/C, or take the area under the v–q graph; the common mistake is to use W = QV, which overestimates the stored energy by a factor of two.

questions.question: Describe the factors affecting the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor?
questions.answer:
For a parallel-plate capacitor the capacitance is C = ε₀εᵣA/d, where A is the area of each plate, d is their separation, ε₀ is the permittivity of free space and εᵣ is the relative permittivity of the dielectric between the plates. Three factors therefore affect the capacitance.
(1) Area of the plates: C is directly proportional to A. Doubling the area doubles the capacitance, because a larger area can hold more charge at the same potential difference. This is why practical capacitors use long foil strips rolled up or many interleaved plates.
(2) Separation between the plates: C is inversely proportional to d. Reducing the separation increases the capacitance, because the same charge then produces a stronger field and a smaller potential difference. The separation cannot be made too small, however, or the dielectric will break down.
(3) Nature of the dielectric: C is directly proportional to εᵣ. Inserting a dielectric multiplies the capacitance by εᵣ, because the polarized dielectric partly cancels the field and lowers the potential difference for the same charge. Mica (εᵣ ≈ 6) or ceramic (εᵣ up to several hundred) therefore gives a much larger capacitance than air (εᵣ ≈ 1).
The thickness of the plates and the metal used for them do not appear in the formula, so they do not affect C; temperature and applied voltage influence C only through changes in the dielectric.
Example: a capacitor with A = 0.01 m² and d = 1 mm in air has C = (8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(0.01)/(10⁻³) ≈ 88.5 pF; with mica (εᵣ = 6) between the plates it becomes about 531 pF.
questions.explanation: Key relation C = ε₀εᵣA/d; remember that capacitance is fixed by geometry and dielectric, not by the charge or voltage applied.

questions.question: The capacitance of air-filled parallel-plate capacitor is 1.3 pF. If the separation of the plates is doubled and wax is inserted between them. The new capacitance is 2.6 pF. Find the dielectric constant of the wax.
questions.answer:
Given: C_air = 1.3 pF, new separation d′ = 2d, new capacitance C′ = 2.6 pF, dielectric = wax.
Formula: C_air = ε₀A/d and C′ = εᵣε₀A/d′ = εᵣε₀A/(2d) = εᵣC_air/2.
Substitution: 2.6 pF = εᵣ × 1.3 pF / 2.
Calculation: εᵣ = 2 × 2.6/1.3 = 4.0.
Result: the dielectric constant of the wax is 4.0, which agrees exactly with the printed answer (Ans. 4.0).
questions.explanation: Key formula C = ε₀εᵣA/d; doubling d alone would halve C to 0.65 pF, so the wax must multiply it by 4 to reach 2.6 pF.

questions.question: Three capacitors have capacitances 10, 50 and 25 μF respectively as shown in figure. Calculate (i) charge on each when connected in parallel to a 250 V supply (ii) total capacitance and (iii) potential difference across each when connected in series.
questions.answer:
Given: C₁ = 10 μF, C₂ = 50 μF, C₃ = 25 μF, V = 250 V.
(i) In parallel each capacitor has the full 250 V: Q = CV.
Q₁ = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 250 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ C = 2.5 mC.
Q₂ = 50 × 10⁻⁶ × 250 = 12.5 × 10⁻³ C = 12.5 mC.
Q₃ = 25 × 10⁻⁶ × 250 = 6.25 × 10⁻³ C = 6.25 mC.
(ii) C_p = C₁ + C₂ + C₃ = 10 + 50 + 25 = 85 μF (matches the printed 85 μF).
(iii) In series: 1/C_s = 1/10 + 1/50 + 1/25 = 0.10 + 0.02 + 0.04 = 0.16 μF⁻¹, so C_s = 6.25 μF. The common charge is Q = C_sV = 6.25 × 10⁻⁶ × 250 = 1562.5 μC = 1.5625 mC.
V₁ = Q/C₁ = 1562.5/10 = 156.25 V (across 10 μF).
V₂ = Q/C₂ = 1562.5/50 = 31.25 V (across 50 μF).
V₃ = Q/C₃ = 1562.5/25 = 62.5 V (across 25 μF).
Check: 156.25 + 31.25 + 62.5 = 250 V.
Result: (i) 2.5 mC, 12.5 mC and 6.25 mC; (ii) 85 μF; (iii) 156.25 V, 31.25 V and 62.5 V (i.e. 156.25 V, 62.5 V, 31.25 V for the 10, 25 and 50 μF capacitors).
Discrepancy: the book prints 6.75 mC for the charge on the 25 μF capacitor, but 25 μF × 250 V = 6.25 mC, so 6.75 mC is a printing slip; the other printed answers agree exactly.
questions.explanation: Key checks: in parallel Q = CV with the same V for all; in series the charge is common, Q = C_sV, and the voltages must add up to the supply voltage (they do: 250 V).
questions.figure: Fig. 9.9: C₁ = 10 μF, C₂ = 50 μF and C₃ = 25 μF in parallel across a 250 V supply (upper diagram), and the same three capacitors reconnected in series across 250 V with V₁, V₂, V₃ marked (lower diagram).

questions.question: Three capacitors are connected through a potential difference of 100 volts as shown in figure. Find the charges and potential difference across each capacitor. [C₁ = 2 μF is in series with the parallel combination of C₂ = 1 μF and C₃ = 3 μF; the network is connected across the 100 V supply, with V₁ across C₁ and V₂ across the parallel pair.]
questions.answer:
Given: C₁ = 2 μF in series with the parallel pair C₂ = 1 μF and C₃ = 3 μF, total potential difference V = 100 V.
Formula: C_p = C₂ + C₃; C_eq = C₁C_p/(C₁ + C_p); Q = C_eqV; V = Q/C.
Substitution: C_p = 1 + 3 = 4 μF; C_eq = (2 × 4)/(2 + 4) = 8/6 = 1.33 μF.
Calculation: Q₁ = Q_total = 1.33 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 1.33 × 10⁻⁴ C = 133 μC.
V₁ = Q₁/C₁ = 133/2 = 66.7 V.
V₂ (across the parallel pair) = 100 − 66.7 = 33.3 V.
Q₂ = C₂V₂ = 1 × 33.3 = 33.3 μC and Q₃ = C₃V₂ = 3 × 33.3 = 100 μC.
Check: Q₂ + Q₃ = 133 μC = Q₁.
Result: Q₁ = 133 μC (V₁ = 66.7 V), Q₂ = 33.3 μC and Q₃ = 100 μC, with V₂ = 33.3 V across each of them.
Discrepancy: the printed answers (160 μC, 60 μC, 100 μC, V₁ = 80 V, V₂ = 20 V) correspond exactly to C₂ = 3 μF and C₃ = 5 μF (then C_p = 8 μF, C_eq = 1.6 μF, Q₁ = 160 μC, V₁ = 80 V, V₂ = 20 V, Q₂ = 60 μC, Q₃ = 100 μC). The scanned figure shows 1 μF and 3 μF, so the printed figure values and the printed answer key are inconsistent with each other.
questions.explanation: Key method: reduce the parallel pair first, then treat the network as two capacitors in series so that C₁ and the pair carry the same charge; the voltages must add to 100 V.

questions.question: Capacitor is charged through a large non-reactive resistance by a battery of constant voltage V. For this arrangement, if the capacitor has a capacitance of 10 μ F and the resistance is 1 M Ω, calculate the time taken for the capacitor to receive 90% of its final charge.
questions.answer:
Given: C = 10 μF = 10 × 10⁻⁶ F, R = 1 MΩ = 1 × 10⁶ Ω, q/Q₀ = 90% = 0.90.
Formula: q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)), so t = RC ln[1/(1 − q/Q₀)].
Substitution: RC = (1 × 10⁶)(10 × 10⁻⁶) = 10 s; t = 10 ln[1/(1 − 0.90)] = 10 ln 10.
Calculation: ln 10 = 2.303, so t = 10 × 2.303 = 23.0 s.
Result: the capacitor takes about 23 s to receive 90% of its final charge, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans. 23s).
questions.explanation: Key relation q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)); note that 90% charge needs 2.3 time constants, while one time constant gives only 63%.

questions.question: What capacitance is required to store energy of 10 kWh at a potential difference of 1000 V?
questions.answer:
Given: E = 10 kWh = 10 × 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 × 10⁷ J, V = 1000 V.
Formula: E = ½CV², so C = 2E/V².
Substitution: C = 2 × 3.6 × 10⁷ / (1000)².
Calculation: C = 7.2 × 10⁷ / 1.0 × 10⁶ = 72 F.
Result: a capacitance of 72 F is required, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans. 72 F).
questions.explanation: Key conversion: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; then C = 2E/V². Such a huge capacitance shows why energy is stored chemically in batteries rather than in capacitors.

questions.question: A 2.0 μF capacitor and a 4.0 μF capacitor are connected in parallel across a 300 V potential difference. Calculate the total energy stored in the capacitors.
questions.answer:
Given: C₁ = 2.0 μF, C₂ = 4.0 μF in parallel, V = 300 V.
Formula: C_p = C₁ + C₂ and E = ½C_pV².
Substitution: C_p = 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 μF; E = ½ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ × (300)².
Calculation: E = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 9.0 × 10⁴ = 0.27 J.
Result: the total energy stored is 0.27 J, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans. 0.27J).
questions.explanation: Key point: in parallel the capacitances add, and the same 300 V appears across each; the energy could also be found as ½C₁V² + ½C₂V² = 0.09 + 0.18 = 0.27 J.

questions.question: A 12.0-V battery is connected to a capacitor, resulting in 54.0 μC of charge stored on the capacitor. How much energy is stored in the capacitor?
questions.answer:
Given: V = 12.0 V, Q = 54.0 μC = 54.0 × 10⁻⁶ C.
Formula: E = ½QV (equivalently E = Q²/2C with C = Q/V = 4.5 μF).
Substitution: E = ½ × 54.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 12.0.
Calculation: E = 27.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 12.0 = 3.24 × 10⁻⁴ J.
Result: the energy stored is 3.24 × 10⁻⁴ J, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans. 3.24 × 10⁻⁴ J).
questions.explanation: Key formula E = ½QV, which avoids first calculating C; the equivalent check is C = Q/V = 4.5 μF and E = ½CV² = 3.24 × 10⁻⁴ J.

questions.question: Kirchhoff's laws are useful in determining:
questions.answer: (a) current flowing in a circuit
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule give a set of simultaneous equations from which the unknown currents in a network are determined, and the voltage drops then follow from V = IR. Power follows once the currents are known (P = I²R), but the laws are not a power principle, and they determine far more than emf alone. Hence the standard answer is (a).

options.text: emf and voltage drops in a circuit

questions.optionsRaw: (a) current flowing in a circuit  (b) emf and voltage drops in a circuit  (c) power in a circuit  (d) only emf in a circuit

questions.question: The resistance of a superconductor is:
questions.answer: (d) zero
questions.explanation: Below its critical temperature a superconductor suffers an abrupt transition to a state of exactly zero electrical resistance, so a current once started persists without any applied voltage. Zero resistance is not infinite resistance, and the property does not change from one conductor to another. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) finite  (b) infinite  (c) changes with every conductor  (d) zero

questions.question: Reciprocal of resistance is called:
questions.answer: (a) conductance
questions.explanation: Conductance is defined as G = 1/R and is measured in siemens (S), so a large conductance means a small resistance. Resistivity is a material property given by ρ = RA/L, resonance is a condition of a tuned circuit, and capacitance is charge per unit potential difference. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) conductance  (b) resistivity  (c) resonance  (d) capacitance

questions.question: The graphical representation of Ohms law is:
questions.answer: (d) straight line
questions.explanation: Ohm's law states V = IR, so at constant temperature V is directly proportional to I; a graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals R (and a graph of I against V has slope 1/R). A parabola, hyperbola or ellipse would imply a non-linear relation between V and I. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) parabola  (b) hyperbola  (c) ellipse  (d) straight line

questions.question: A potential difference is applied across the ends of a wire. If the potential difference is doubled, then the drift velocity of free electrons will:
questions.answer: (b) be doubled
questions.explanation: The drift velocity is v_d = eEτ/m, and the field inside a wire of length L is E = V/L, so v_d ∝ V. Doubling the potential difference doubles the field and therefore doubles the drift velocity, since τ and the number of free electrons per unit volume are unchanged. Quadrupling would need four times the voltage. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) be quadrupled  (b) be doubled  (c) be halved  (d) remain unchanged

questions.question: Internal resistance is the resistance offered by:
questions.answer: (d) source of emf
questions.explanation: Internal resistance is the resistance of the source of emf itself — the electrolyte and electrodes of a cell, or the windings of a generator — to the current it supplies. It causes the terminal voltage to fall below the emf according to V = ε − Ir. A capacitor, a resistor or a connecting conductor is an external component. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Capacitor  (b) resistor  (c) Conductor  (d) source of emf

questions.question: Power dissipation in a resistor can be calculated using which formula:
questions.answer: (b) P = I² × R
questions.explanation: For a resistor P = I²R = V²/R = VI, so options (a), (b) and (c) are all correct expressions and the question is imperfectly set with three valid answers. Option (b) is the form that follows directly from Joule's law of heating for a resistor. Option (d), P = R/(V × I), has the wrong dimensions and can never be valid. Since a single key must be given, (b) is marked.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) P = V² / R  (b) P = I² × R  (c) P = V × I  (d) P = R / (V × I)

questions.question: What is a potentiometer primarily used for?
questions.answer: (c) Measuring potential difference (voltage)
questions.explanation: A potentiometer compares an unknown potential difference (or the emf of a cell) with the potential drop across a known length of a uniform wire, using the null method so that no current is drawn from the source under test. It is not an ammeter, a charge meter or a resistance meter, although it can be used indirectly to compare emfs and to find an internal resistance. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Measuring electric current  (b) Measuring electric charge  (c) Measuring potential difference (voltage)  (d) Measuring electric resistance

questions.question: A heat-sensitive device whose resistivity changes with the change in temperature is called:
questions.answer: (c) thermistor
questions.explanation: A thermistor is a semiconductor device (usually a metal-oxide) whose resistance changes markedly with temperature, falling in the NTC type and rising in the PTC type; it is used as a temperature sensor. An ordinary conductor or resistor shows only a slight temperature dependence, and a thermometer is the measuring instrument, not the sensing element. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) conductor  (b) resistor  (c) thermistor  (d) thermometer

questions.question: A wire of uniform area of cross-section A length L and resistance R is cut into two parts. The resistivity of each part:
questions.answer: (d) remains same
questions.explanation: Resistivity ρ = RA/L is a property of the material and depends on its nature and temperature, not on the size or shape of the specimen. Cutting the wire changes L and A of each piece (and hence its resistance), but the material is unchanged, so ρ stays the same. Hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Becomes zero  (b) is halved  (c) Is doubled  (d) remains same

questions.question: Why is the terminal voltage of a cell less than its emf?
questions.answer: The emf ε of a cell is the energy converted per unit charge by the source, i.e. the potential difference across its terminals when no current is drawn. Every real cell also has an internal resistance r. When the cell supplies a current I to an external circuit, that same current passes through r and produces a potential drop Ir inside the cell, which appears as heat. The terminal voltage is therefore V = ε − Ir, which is less than ε whenever I is not zero, and the deficit ε − V = Ir is called the lost volts. Only on open circuit (I = 0) does the terminal voltage equal the emf. Example: a 12 V battery of internal resistance 0.5 Ω delivering 4 A gives V = 12 − (4)(0.5) = 10 V.
questions.explanation: Key relation V = ε − Ir; the internal drop exists only while current flows, so an open-circuit voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.question: Why is a potentiometer preferred over a voltmeter for determining the emf of a cell?
questions.answer: A potentiometer uses the null method: at the balance point no current is drawn from the cell under test, so there is no potential drop Ir across its internal resistance and the balancing length gives the true emf, ε = kl (k is the potential gradient). A voltmeter, by contrast, must draw some current to deflect; because its resistance is finite it measures the terminal voltage V = ε − Ir, which is always less than the emf. The potentiometer also behaves as an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance at balance, is very sensitive (it can detect a few microvolts), and compares the unknown emf directly with the potential drop along a uniform wire, so it needs no calibration against another meter. A voltmeter is only portable and quicker to read.
questions.explanation: Key idea: null method draws no current, so the reading is the emf and not the terminal voltage; a voltmeter always draws current.

questions.question: Nichrome and copper wires of same length and same radius are connected in series. Current I is passed through them. Which wire gets heated up more? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: The nichrome wire gets heated up much more. In series the same current I flows through both wires, so the rate of heat production is P = I²R, and R = ρL/A. Since L and the radius (hence A) are the same, R ∝ ρ, so the wire of greater resistivity has the greater resistance and dissipates more power. The resistivity of nichrome (about 1.0–1.5 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m) is roughly 60–100 times that of copper (1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m), so for the same current the nichrome wire produces far more heat. Nichrome also resists oxidation and keeps its strength when red hot, which is why it is used in heating elements, whereas copper is used for connecting wires where heating is undesirable.
questions.explanation: Key point: in series the current is common, so P = I²R makes the higher-resistivity material the hotter one; a common error is to compare voltages instead.

questions.question: Explain why the terminal potential of a battery decreases when the current drawn from it in increased?
questions.answer: Every cell has an internal resistance r in series with its emf ε, so when a current I is drawn the terminal potential difference is V = ε − Ir. As the current drawn increases, the product Ir increases and the terminal voltage therefore falls; the lost volts Ir appear as heat inside the cell, at the rate I²r. The fall may be slightly greater than a straight line suggests, because the internal resistance rises as the cell warms up and the emf itself falls slowly as the active material is used up. The graph of V against I is consequently a straight line of slope −r with intercept ε. Example: a cell of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω gives 2.0 V on open circuit but only 1.5 V when it supplies 1 A.
questions.explanation: Key relation V = ε − Ir; the internal drop grows with current, so terminal voltage falls while the emf stays (nearly) constant.

questions.question: What are thermistors? Write their importance.
questions.answer: A thermistor is a temperature-sensitive resistor made from a semiconducting metal oxide (such as a sintered mixture of manganese, nickel and cobalt oxides) whose resistance changes greatly with temperature. In the common negative temperature coefficient (NTC) type the resistance falls as the temperature rises, often almost exponentially; in the positive temperature coefficient (PTC) type it rises. Because the change is large (several per cent per kelvin) and the response is fast, thermistors are important as temperature sensors and are used in thermometers, fire alarms, oven and refrigerator thermostats, air-conditioning control, liquid-level detection, protection of motors against overheating, and as inrush-current limiters in power supplies. They are small, cheap, rugged and need only simple circuits.
questions.explanation: Key idea: a semiconductor whose resistance is strongly temperature dependent (NTC resistance falls with heating); do not confuse it with an ordinary resistor, whose variation is small.

questions.question: State Kirchhoff's Laws.
questions.answer:
Kirchhoff's laws are two rules that follow from the conservation of charge and of energy and are used to solve electrical networks.
(1) Kirchhoff's current law (junction rule): the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it, ΣI_in = ΣI_out, because charge cannot accumulate at a point; equivalently, the algebraic sum of the currents at a junction is zero.
(2) Kirchhoff's voltage law (loop rule): the algebraic sum of the potential differences around any closed loop is zero, or the sum of the emfs in a loop equals the sum of the potential drops, Σε = ΣIR. This follows from conservation of energy, since a charge taken round a closed loop returns to the same potential.
These laws are used to find unknown currents and potential differences in circuits that cannot be reduced by simple series and parallel combinations.
questions.explanation: Key point: the junction rule expresses conservation of charge and the loop rule conservation of energy; signs of emf and IR terms must be taken consistently round the loop.

questions.question: If Copper and Aluminum wires of the same length have same resistance, which has the larger diameter? And why?
questions.answer: The aluminium wire has the larger diameter. The resistance of a wire is R = ρL/A, so for the same length L and the same resistance R the required area is A = ρL/R, i.e. A ∝ ρ. The resistivity of aluminium (about 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) is greater than that of copper (about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m), so an aluminium wire must have a larger cross-sectional area, and since A = πd²/4, a larger diameter, to offer the same resistance. Quantitatively d_Al/d_Cu = √(2.8/1.7) ≈ 1.28, so the aluminium wire must be about 28% thicker than the copper wire. This is why aluminium power lines are made thicker (often with a steel core) than the equivalent copper conductors.
questions.explanation: Key relation R = ρL/A with R and L fixed gives A ∝ ρ; higher resistivity means a thicker wire for the same resistance.

questions.question: What is the difference between potential difference and emf?
questions.answer: Potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them through a component, V = W/Q; it represents electrical energy converted into other forms per coulomb. Emf of a source is the work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge round the complete circuit, ε = W/Q; it is the energy supplied per coulomb. Emf is a property of the source itself, whereas potential difference is measured across a component and depends on the current flowing. On open circuit the terminal potential difference equals the emf, but when current flows V = ε − Ir, so the potential difference is always less than the emf. Both are measured in volts (J C⁻¹), but the emf is the cause and the potential difference the effect.
questions.explanation: Key distinction: emf is energy given to each coulomb by the source, potential difference is energy taken from each coulomb by a component; both have the unit volt.

questions.question: State the principle of working of a meter bridge. Explain how it is used to find an unknown resistance.
questions.answer:
Principle: A metre bridge works on the principle of the Wheatstone bridge, which is balanced (zero current through the galvanometer) when the ratio of the resistances of two adjacent arms equals the ratio of the other two: P/Q = R/S. In the bridge a uniform resistance wire one metre long is stretched along a scale; the unknown resistance R is placed in the left gap and a standard resistance S in the right gap, with a cell and a galvanometer connected between the midpoints.
Working: A jockey is pressed on the wire and moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection. If the balancing length measured from the left end is l (in cm), the resistance of the left part of the wire is proportional to l and that of the right part to (100 − l). Since the two parts of the wire form the other two arms, balance gives R/S = l/(100 − l), so R = S l/(100 − l). As S and l are known, R is calculated.
Procedure and precautions: Make tight connections; press the jockey gently and locate the null point accurately; measure l from the end to which the unknown resistance is connected; interchange the resistances in the gaps and repeat so that the two results can be averaged and end errors eliminated; choose S of the same order as R so that the balance point lies near the middle of the wire.
Example: with S = 15 Ω in the right gap and balance at l = 62.5 cm, R = 15 × 62.5/37.5 = 25 Ω.
questions.explanation: Key relation R/S = l/(100 − l); the balance point should lie near the middle of the wire for greatest accuracy, and interchanging the gaps removes end corrections.

questions.question: Define thermoelectricity. Explain the working of a Fire Alarm system using thermistor.
questions.answer:
Thermoelectricity: When two wires of different metals are joined to form a closed circuit with the two junctions kept at different temperatures, a small emf is set up and a current flows round the circuit. This production of emf (and hence current) by a temperature difference between the junctions of two dissimilar metals is called thermoelectricity, and the emf is called the thermoelectric emf (Seebeck effect). The emf depends on the pair of metals and on the temperature difference between the junctions.
Fire alarm using a thermistor: A thermistor is a semiconductor device whose resistance changes strongly with temperature; in the NTC type the resistance falls as the temperature rises. In a fire alarm the thermistor is connected in series with a relay coil (and a buzzer or bell) across a supply, usually as one arm of a potential divider. At normal room temperature the thermistor is cool and its resistance is high, so only a small current flows and the relay is not energised. When a fire raises the temperature, the resistance of the thermistor falls sharply, the current in the circuit increases, the relay operates and closes the contacts of the alarm bell or buzzer, giving the warning. A variable resistor is included to set the temperature at which the alarm operates.
Advantages: the thermistor is very sensitive (a few per cent change of resistance per kelvin), responds quickly, has no moving parts and is cheap and reliable. Example: a thermistor whose resistance falls from 10 kΩ at 25 °C to 1 kΩ at 80 °C can easily switch a relay set to operate at a few milliamperes.
questions.explanation: Key idea: an NTC thermistor loses resistance on heating, so the current through the relay rises and the alarm operates; the variable resistor sets the threshold.

questions.question: Define resistivity. Explain dependence of resistivity on temperature.
questions.answer:
Resistivity: The resistivity ρ of a material is the resistance of a conductor of that material having unit length and unit area of cross-section. From R = ρL/A, ρ = RA/L. Its SI unit is the ohm metre (Ω m). Resistivity depends on the nature of the material and on its temperature, but not on the dimensions of the specimen.
Metals: Current is carried by free electrons, and resistance arises from their collisions with the vibrating lattice ions. As the temperature rises the ions vibrate more vigorously, the relaxation time τ between collisions decreases, and since ρ = m/(ne²τ) the resistivity increases. Over a moderate range the increase is nearly linear: ρ = ρ₀(1 + αΔT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (about 4 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ for copper). In a superconductor ρ falls abruptly to zero below the critical temperature.
Semiconductors: Here the number density n of charge carriers increases very rapidly with temperature (more carriers are freed across the energy gap), and this effect outweighs the decrease in τ, so the resistivity decreases as the temperature rises; α is negative. This is the basis of the thermistor.
Alloys: In alloys such as manganin and constantan the resistivity is high and almost independent of temperature, so they are used for standard resistors and shunts.
Example: a 10 K rise in temperature increases the resistivity of copper by about 4%, whereas a thermistor may change by several per cent for each kelvin.
questions.explanation: Key relation ρ = m/(ne²τ): in metals n is fixed and τ falls with temperature (ρ rises), while in semiconductors n rises faster than τ falls (ρ decreases).

questions.question: What is a rheostat? How can we use a rheostat as a potential divider?
questions.answer:
A rheostat is a variable resistor consisting of a long coil of resistance wire (nichrome or constantan) wound on an insulating cylinder, with a sliding contact or wiper that can be moved along the coil. Moving the slider changes the length of wire included in the circuit and hence the resistance, so a rheostat is used to control the current in a circuit or to obtain a variable potential difference. It has three terminals: the two ends of the coil and the slider.
As a potential divider: the two ends of the rheostat are connected across a fixed supply V, so that a steady current I flows through the whole coil. The output is taken between one end of the coil and the slider. If the resistance between that end and the slider is R₁ and the remaining part is R₂, with R₁ + R₂ = R, the output potential difference is V_out = IR₁ = V R₁/(R₁ + R₂). As the slider is moved, R₁ varies continuously from 0 to R, so V_out varies smoothly from 0 to V. This arrangement is called a potential divider, and it is used to apply any desired fraction of the supply voltage to a load, as in volume controls, lamp dimmers and the setting of bias voltages.
Practical note: for good control the rheostat resistance should be much smaller than the resistance of the load; otherwise the load current itself changes the division of voltage.
questions.explanation: Key relation V_out = V R₁/(R₁ + R₂); the rheostat is connected across the supply, not in series with the load, when used as a potential divider.

questions.question: State the underlying principle of a potentiometer. Describe briefly, giving the necessary circuit diagram, how a potentiometer is used to measure the internal resistance of a given cell?
questions.answer:
Principle: When a steady current I flows through a uniform wire of resistance per unit length λ, the potential difference across a length l is V = Iλl, so V ∝ l. The potential difference between any two points of the wire is therefore proportional to the length between them, and the wire behaves as a continuously variable source of known potential difference. A cell connected in opposition to this potential difference gives no galvanometer deflection when the two are exactly equal (null method).
Circuit: A driver cell E with a key K is connected across the potentiometer wire AB. The cell of unknown internal resistance r is connected with its positive terminal to A, and its negative terminal through a galvanometer G to the jockey; a resistance box R and a key K₂ are connected in parallel with this cell (so that R can be switched across it).
Procedure: (1) With K₂ open, no current is drawn from the cell, so its terminal potential difference equals its emf ε. The jockey is moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection at a length l₁; then ε = k l₁. (2) K₂ is closed, so the cell now sends a current through R; its terminal potential difference becomes V = ε − Ir, and the new balance length l₂ gives V = k l₂. Dividing, ε/V = l₁/l₂.
Derivation: With the key closed the current in the cell is I = ε/(R + r), so V = IR = εR/(R + r). Hence ε/V = (R + r)/R = 1 + r/R = l₁/l₂, which gives r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂.
Thus, knowing R and the two balance lengths, the internal resistance of the cell is calculated.
questions.explanation: Key relations ε = kl₁ (open key) and V = kl₂ (with shunt R), leading to r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂; the cell must be connected with the same polarity as the driver cell.

questions.question: The storage battery of a car has an emf of 12 V. If the internal resistance of the battery is 0.5Ω, what is the maximum current that can be drawn from the battery?
questions.answer:
Given: emf ε = 12 V, internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω.
Formula: I = ε/(R + r); the current is maximum when the external resistance R = 0 (short circuit), i.e. I_max = ε/r.
Substitution: I_max = 12 V / 0.5 Ω.
Calculation: I_max = 24 A.
Result: the maximum (short-circuit) current is 24 A, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: 24A). In practice such a current would damage the battery and is limited by the small resistance of the connecting cables.
questions.explanation: Key formula I = ε/(R + r); maximum current occurs at zero external resistance.

questions.question: A negligibly small current is passed through a wire of length 12m and uniform cross-section 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², and its resistance is measured to be 6.0 Ω. What is the resistivity of the material at the temperature of the experiment?
questions.answer:
Given: L = 12 m, A = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², R = 6.0 Ω.
Formula: R = ρL/A, so ρ = RA/L.
Substitution: ρ = (6.0 Ω)(4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m²) / 12 m.
Calculation: ρ = 24 × 10⁻⁷ / 12 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.
Result: the resistivity is 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m).
questions.explanation: Key rearrangement ρ = RA/L; the measured value is typical of an alloy such as nichrome rather than a pure metal.

questions.question: In a potentiometer arrangement, a cell of emf 1.20 V gives a balance point at 40.0 cm length of the wire. If the cell is replaced by another cell and the balance point shifts to 74.0 cm, what is the emf of the second cell?
questions.answer:
Given: ε₁ = 1.20 V at l₁ = 40.0 cm; l₂ = 74.0 cm for the second cell.
Formula: for the same potential gradient k, ε = kl, so ε₂/ε₁ = l₂/l₁.
Substitution: ε₂ = 1.20 V × 74.0 cm / 40.0 cm.
Calculation: ε₂ = 1.20 × 1.85 = 2.22 V.
Result: the emf of the second cell is 2.22 V, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: 2.22 V).
questions.explanation: Key relation ε ∝ balance length because the potential gradient along the wire is constant; the driver cell and its rheostat setting must not be disturbed between the two readings.

questions.question:
(a) Three resistors 1 Ω, 2 Ω, and 3 Ω are combined in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?
(b) If the combination is connected to a battery of emf 24 V and negligible internal resistance, obtain the potential drop across each resistor.
questions.answer:
(a) Given: R₁ = 1 Ω, R₂ = 2 Ω, R₃ = 3 Ω in series.
Formula: R_s = R₁ + R₂ + R₃.
Substitution: R_s = 1 + 2 + 3.
Calculation: R_s = 6 Ω.
Result: the total resistance is 6 Ω, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: 6 Ω).
(b) Given: emf = 24 V, internal resistance negligible, R_s = 6 Ω.
Formula: I = V/R_s and V = IR for each resistor.
Substitution: I = 24 V / 6 Ω = 4 A.
Calculation: V₁ = (4 A)(1 Ω) = 4 V; V₂ = (4 A)(2 Ω) = 8 V; V₃ = (4 A)(3 Ω) = 12 V.
Result: the potential drops are 4 V, 8 V and 12 V, which agree with the printed answers (Ans: V₁ = 4 V, V₂ = 8V, V₃ = 12V); the three add up to the supply voltage, 24 V.
questions.explanation: Key checks: resistances add in series; the current is common, so the p.d. across each resistor is proportional to its resistance and the drops must sum to 24 V.

questions.question:
From the given circuit find the value of I.
Six wires meet at one common junction. The labelled currents and their directions relative to the junction are: top branch 0.4 A directed away from the junction; upper-left branch 0.2 A directed towards the junction; upper-right branch 0.6 A directed towards the junction; lower-right branch 0.5 A directed away from the junction; bottom branch 0.7 A directed towards the junction; lower-left branch carries the unknown current I, the arrow being drawn towards the junction.
questions.answer:
Given (currents towards the junction taken as positive): 0.2 A, 0.6 A and 0.7 A enter; 0.4 A and 0.5 A leave; the unknown I is drawn entering.
Formula: Kirchhoff's junction rule, ΣI_in = ΣI_out.
Substitution: 0.2 + 0.6 + 0.7 + I = 0.4 + 0.5.
Calculation: 1.5 + I = 0.9, so I = −0.6 A.
Result: the magnitude is I = 0.6 A, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: I = 0.6A). The negative sign means the current actually flows away from the junction along the lower-left branch, opposite to the direction of the arrow drawn in the figure.
questions.explanation: Key rule: total current into a junction equals total current out; the 1.5 A entering must be balanced by 0.9 A plus the unknown, giving 0.6 A leaving.
questions.figure: Six-resistor star network meeting at a single junction: 0.4 A (top branch, arrow away from junction), 0.2 A (upper-left, arrow towards junction), 0.6 A (upper-right, arrow towards junction), 0.5 A (lower-right, arrow away), 0.7 A (bottom, arrow towards junction), and I on the lower-left branch with its arrow drawn towards the junction.

questions.question: In a meter bridge with a standard resistance of 15 Ω in the right gap, the ratio of balancing length is 5:3. Find the value of the other resistance.
questions.answer:
Given: standard resistance S = 15 Ω in the right gap; ratio of the balancing lengths l₁ : l₂ = 5 : 3, where l₁ is adjacent to the unknown resistance P and l₂ adjacent to S.
Formula: at balance P/S = l₁/l₂, so P = S l₁/l₂.
Substitution: P = 15 Ω × 5/3.
Calculation: P = 75/3 = 25 Ω.
Result: the unknown resistance is 25 Ω, which agrees with the printed answer (Ans: P = 25 Ω). The balancing lengths are 62.5 cm and 37.5 cm, which add up to the full metre of the wire as they should.
questions.explanation: Key relation P/S = l₁/l₂; the ratio 5:3 corresponds to balance lengths 62.5 cm and 37.5 cm, whose sum must be 100 cm.

questions.question:
By using KVL find Current flowing through 10 Ω resistance.
Circuit: three loops side by side. Top wire carries, from left to right, 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 12 Ω. The vertical branch between loop 1 and loop 2 contains 15 Ω; the vertical branch between loop 2 and loop 3 contains 8 Ω. The left branch contains a 4 V battery with its positive (long) terminal upwards; the right branch contains a 6 V battery with its positive (long) terminal upwards. The loop currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ are drawn clockwise.
questions.answer:
Assumed loop directions: I₁, I₂ and I₃ are all taken clockwise, as drawn in the figure.
Given: R_top = 5 Ω, 10 Ω, 12 Ω; vertical branches 15 Ω and 8 Ω; emfs 4 V (left) and 6 V (right), both with the positive terminal upwards.
Formulae (KVL, sum of drops = sum of emfs):
Loop 1: 5I₁ + 15(I₁ − I₂) = 4, i.e. 20I₁ − 15I₂ = 4.
Loop 2: 10I₂ + 8(I₂ − I₃) + 15(I₂ − I₁) = 0, i.e. −15I₁ + 33I₂ − 8I₃ = 0.
Loop 3: 12I₃ + 6 + 8(I₃ − I₂) = 0, i.e. −8I₂ + 20I₃ = −6 (the 6 V battery is traversed from + to − in the clockwise sense, so it is a drop).
Substitution and calculation: from loop 1, I₁ = (4 + 15I₂)/20 = 0.2 + 0.75I₂; from loop 3, I₃ = (8I₂ − 6)/20 = 0.4I₂ − 0.3. Substituting in loop 2: −15(0.2 + 0.75I₂) + 33I₂ − 8(0.4I₂ − 0.3) = 0, that is −3 − 11.25I₂ + 33I₂ − 3.2I₂ + 2.4 = 0, so 18.55I₂ = 0.6 and I₂ = 0.0323 A. The other currents are I₁ = 0.224 A and I₃ = −0.287 A (the negative sign means I₃ actually flows anticlockwise).
Result: the current through the 10 Ω resistor is I₂ = 0.0323 A ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻² A, flowing from left to right along the top wire, i.e. clockwise round the middle loop.
Discrepancy: the book prints 0.0341 A (clockwise). With the printed values (15 Ω, 8 Ω, 5 Ω, 10 Ω, 12 Ω, 4 V and 6 V) the solution is 0.0323 A, so the printed value is about 5% high, probably through rounding or an answer-key slip; the direction (clockwise) agrees. Check: 20(0.2243) − 15(0.0323) = 4.0 V and −8(0.0323) + 20(−0.2871) = −6.0 V, so both outer loops are satisfied.
questions.explanation: Key method: assign clockwise mesh currents, write KVL for each loop with the shared-branch currents (I₁ − I₂) and (I₂ − I₃), and solve the three simultaneous equations; the 10 Ω current is simply I₂.
questions.figure: Three-loop network: top wire has 5 Ω (left), 10 Ω (middle) and 12 Ω (right); the vertical branch between loops 1 and 2 has 15 Ω; the vertical branch between loops 2 and 3 has 8 Ω; the left branch has a 4 V battery (positive terminal up) and the right branch a 6 V battery (positive terminal up); loop currents I₁, I₂, I₃ are marked clockwise.

questions.question: Two simple pendulums A and B with same lengths, and equal amplitude of vibrations, but the mass of A is twice the mass of B, their period are T_A and T_B and energies are E_A and E_B respectively. Choose the correct statement.
questions.answer: (a) T_A = T_B and E_A > E_B
questions.explanation: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g), which contains no mass, so equal lengths give equal periods, T_A = T_B. This eliminates (b) and (c). The energy of an oscillator is E = ½mω²A², so at the same length (same ω) and the same amplitude the energy is proportional to mass; A is twice as heavy, hence E_A > E_B, which eliminates (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) T_A = T_B and E_A > E_B  (b) T_A < T_B and E_A > E_B  (c) T_A > T_B and E_A < E_B  (d) T_A = T_B and E_A < E_B

questions.question: In order to double the period of a simple pendulum:
questions.answer: (b) Its length should be quadrupled
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g) shows that T ∝ √L, so doubling T requires L to become four times larger. Doubling the length only multiplies the period by √2, and the mass does not appear in the formula at all, so (a), (c) and (d) are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Its length should be doubled  (b) Its length should be quadrupled  (c) The mass should be doubled  (d) The mass should be quadrupled

questions.question: A simple harmonic oscillator has amplitude A and time period t. Its maximum speed is:
questions.answer: (d) 2πA/t
questions.explanation: The maximum speed of an oscillator is v_max = ωA, and ω = 2π/T = 2π/t, so v_max = 2πA/t. Options (a) and (b) omit the factor π, and (c) uses 4π, which would correspond to a wrong angular frequency; 4A/t is the average speed over one quarter cycle, not the maximum speed.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 4A/t  (b) 2A/t  (c) 4πA/t  (d) 2πA/t

questions.question: A spring attached by a load of weight W is vibrating with a period T. If the spring is divided in four equal parts and the same load is suspended from one of these parts, the new time period is:
questions.explanation: The spring constant is inversely proportional to the length, so cutting the spring into four equal parts makes each part four times stiffer: k′ = 4k. Since T = 2π√(m/k), the new period is T′ = T/√4 = T/2. Getting T/4 would require a 16-fold increase in stiffness, while 2T and 4T wrongly assume the spring becomes softer.

questions.question: The total energy of a particle executing simple harmonic motion is proportional to:
questions.answer: (d) square of amplitude of motion
questions.explanation: The total energy of a harmonic oscillator is E = ½mω²A² = ½kA², so it is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude, not to the amplitude itself. Since v_max = ωA, E = ½mv_max² is proportional to the square of the maximum velocity, not to the maximum velocity, so (b) is also wrong. The energy varies as the square of the frequency for a fixed amplitude, so (a) is wrong too.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) frequency of oscillation  (b) maximum velocity of motion  (c) amplitude of motion  (d) square of amplitude of motion

questions.question: A child swinging on a swing in sitting position, stands up, then the time period of the swing will:
questions.answer: (b) decrease
questions.explanation: A swing behaves as a pendulum whose period is T = 2π√(L/g), where L is the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass. Standing up raises the child's centre of mass, so the effective length L decreases and the period decreases. The mass of the child does not change the period, so (d) is incorrect, and the period certainly does not stay the same.

options.text: increases if the child is long and decreases if the child is short

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Increase  (b) decrease  (c) remains the same  (d) increases if the child is long and decreases if the child is short

questions.question: If a body oscillates at the angular frequency ω_d of the driving force, then the oscillations are called:
questions.answer: (a) Forced oscillations
questions.explanation: When a body is made to oscillate by a periodic external force and settles into motion at the frequency of that force, the motion is forced oscillation. Free oscillations occur at the natural frequency of the body, not at ω_d. Maintained oscillations are kept going by a small periodic supply of energy but still occur at the natural frequency, and coupled oscillations involve energy exchange between two connected oscillators.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Forced oscillations  (b) Coupled oscillations  (c) Free oscillations  (d) Maintained oscillations

questions.question: A simple harmonic oscillator with a natural frequency ω_N is force to oscillate with a driving frequency ω_d. The Resonance occurred when:
questions.answer: (c) ω_N = ω_d
questions.explanation: Resonance is defined as the condition in which the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the oscillator, ω_d = ω_N; the amplitude then reaches its maximum. Option (d) describes a near-resonance condition in which the amplitude is large but not maximum, so it is only an approximation. The inequalities in (a) and (b) give small amplitudes on either side of the peak.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) ω_N < ω_d  (b) ω_N > ω_d  (c) ω_N = ω_d  (d) ω_N ≈ ω_d

questions.question: In vehicles, shock absorber reduced the jerks:
questions.answer: (d) All of these
questions.explanation: A shock absorber is a damped oscillator: its piston forces oil through small holes, so the damping force opposes the motion and removes energy from each bounce. The damping effect arises precisely because a fraction of the mechanical energy is lost as heat in every cycle, and the practical result is that the jerks and continued bouncing of the vehicle are reduced. All three statements are therefore correct.

options.text: The shock absorber is the application of damped oscillations.
Damping effect is due to the fractional loss of energy
Shock absorbers in vehicles reduced jerk

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The shock absorber is the application of damped oscillations.  (b) Damping effect is due to the fractional loss of energy  (c) Shock absorbers in vehicles reduced jerk  (d) All of these

questions.question: A heavily damped system has a fairly flat resonance curve in:
questions.answer: (b) An amplitude frequency graph
questions.explanation: Resonance is shown by plotting the steady-state amplitude against the driving frequency. Heavy damping lowers the peak and broadens it, so the amplitude-frequency curve becomes fairly flat over a wide range of frequencies. Acceleration-time, velocity-time and distance-time graphs describe the motion at a single frequency and do not display a resonance peak at all.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) An acceleration time graph  (b) An amplitude frequency graph  (c) Velocity time graph  (d) Distance-time graph

questions.question: Explain the concept of periodic motion to oscillatory motion. Discuss the terms period, frequency, and amplitude.
questions.answer: Periodic motion repeats itself exactly in equal intervals of time, such as the motion of a clock hand or a swinging pendulum. Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is a special periodic motion in which the body moves to and fro about a fixed mean (equilibrium) position, so its displacement alternately increases and decreases, as for a mass on a spring or a plucked guitar string. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory: uniform circular motion is periodic but not oscillatory. Period T is the time for one complete oscillation, measured in seconds. Frequency f is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T, measured in hertz (Hz). Amplitude A is the maximum displacement from the mean position, measured in metres; it is not the total distance 4A travelled in one cycle.
questions.explanation: Keep the hierarchy clear: oscillatory motion is a subset of periodic motion. Amplitude is a maximum displacement from equilibrium, not the peak-to-peak distance or the path length per cycle.

questions.question: Explain the concept of phase and phase difference in oscillatory motion. Discuss how phase is related to the position and time in an oscillating system.
questions.answer: The phase of an oscillating body describes the state of its motion (position and direction) at any instant. It is the argument of the sine function, θ = ωt + φ, where ω = 2π/T is the angular frequency and φ the initial phase (epoch), fixed by the initial conditions; phase is measured in radians. Two oscillators of the same frequency have a phase difference Δφ = φ₂ − φ₁, which stays constant with time. Phase is related to position by x = A sin(ωt + φ) = A sin θ, so equal phases mean equal displacements and velocities, while a phase difference of π means opposite displacements. Phase is related to time because one cycle corresponds to a phase change of 2π, so Δφ = (2π/T)Δt = ωΔt. A time lag of T/4 therefore gives Δφ = π/2, and a lag of T/2 gives Δφ = π.
questions.explanation: Phase is an angle-like quantity measured in radians, and a phase difference of 2π corresponds to one full period. A common mistake is to treat phase as a time or as a displacement.

questions.question: Explain the concept of damping and its effects on oscillatory motion. Discuss the types of damping, such as over-damping, under-damping, and critical-damping
questions.answer: Damping is the gradual decrease in the amplitude and energy of an oscillatory motion caused by resistive forces such as friction, air resistance or viscous drag. For slow motion the damping force is proportional to velocity, F_d = −bv, so mechanical energy is continuously converted into heat and the amplitude decays exponentially, A = A₀ exp(−bt/2m), while the period changes little for light damping. There are three cases. Under-damping: the body oscillates with steadily decreasing amplitude. Over-damping: the damping force is so large that the body returns to equilibrium without oscillating, and very slowly. Critical damping: the smallest damping for which no oscillation occurs; the body returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without overshooting. Critical damping is used in galvanometers, door closers and shock absorbers, whereas over-damping makes a system sluggish.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is whether the system oscillates while returning: under-damped oscillates, critically damped returns fastest without oscillating, over-damped returns slowly without oscillating.

questions.question: Discuss the concept of resonance frequency and its relationship to the natural frequency of an oscillating system.
questions.answer: Every oscillating system has a natural frequency f₀ at which it oscillates freely once displaced, fixed by its inertia and restoring force; for a mass-spring system f₀ = (1/2π)√(k/m). When a periodic driving force of frequency f_d acts, the system ultimately oscillates at f_d, and the steady-state amplitude is A = (F₀/m)/√((ω₀² − ω_d²)² + (bω_d/m)²). Resonance frequency is the driving frequency at which this amplitude is maximum. For light damping it is practically the natural frequency, f_res ≈ f₀ (more exactly f_res = √(ω₀² − b²/2m²)/2π, slightly below f₀), and heavier damping lowers the peak a little further. At resonance the driving force is in step with the velocity, so it does positive work every cycle and the energy transfer is greatest. That is why a swing pushed at its natural rate rises to a large amplitude, and why a bridge can be destroyed by wind or marching soldiers.
questions.explanation: Resonance is about the driving frequency matching the natural frequency, not about the largest driving force. Light damping puts the resonance peak almost exactly at f₀; heavy damping lowers and shifts it slightly.

questions.question: Discuss the factors that affect the period of a simple pendulum. Explain how the length of the pendulum, the acceleration due to gravity, mass and the amplitude of oscillation influence the period.
questions.answer: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g). Length: T ∝ √L, so the period increases with length; four times the length doubles the period. Acceleration due to gravity: T ∝ 1/√g, so a stronger g gives a shorter period, which is why a pendulum clock runs slow on a mountain or on the Moon. Mass: the period is independent of the mass of the bob, because the restoring force (mg sin θ) and the inertia both contain m and cancel, leaving a = −(g/L)x. Amplitude: for small oscillations (θ below about 10°) the period is practically independent of amplitude (isochronism), but for large swings it increases slightly as T ≈ 2π√(L/g)(1 + θ₀²/16 + …), because the restoring force is then no longer proportional to the displacement. Temperature and air resistance also produce small corrections.
questions.explanation: Mass cancels because it appears in both the restoring force and the inertia; the simple formula is exact only in the small-angle limit, where sin θ ≈ θ.

questions.question: Define simple harmonic motion (SHM). Discuss the key characteristics of a system undergoing SHM.
questions.answer: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is the to-and-fro motion of a body about a fixed mean position in which its acceleration is directly proportional to its displacement from that position and is always directed towards it: a = −ω²x, or equivalently F = −kx. The minus sign expresses the restoring nature of the force. For motion starting at the mean position, the displacement is x = A sin(ωt + φ), where A is the amplitude, ω = 2π/T the angular frequency and (ωt + φ) the phase.
